events.title: From crane rental to marine transport: How this third-gen leader is steering his family business up the value chain
events.summary: Led by Michael Ang, Tiong Woon Corporation, multiple award winners at the Singapore Corporate Awards 2026, is investing in talent and engineering expertise to take on haulage and large-scale projects Tiong Woon Corporation chief executive officer Michael Ang is steering the third-generation family business beyond its crane-rental roots. It is past midnight in Pasir Ris. With sections of the road closed to traffic, massive precast girders are lifted, manoeuvred into position and lowered onto their supports for a new flyover. Beam-launching work like this is usually done overnight, when there is enough space to move heavy equipment safely with minimal disruption to other road users. Behind the operation is Tiong Woon Corporation, whose role in projects like this reflects how far the business has moved beyond its beginnings in crane rental and transport. In recent years, the 48-year-old family business has expanded into engineering and marine services, allowing it to take on bigger and more complex projects. Its fleet has grown with that ambition: The company now operates several hundred cranes, with the single largest rated at 2,200 tonnes. “A lot of people still perceive Tiong Woon as purely a crane rental company,” says chief executive officer Michael Ang. “Crane rental is still our core business, but we also offer marine, transport and engineering services. We want to show our clients and stakeholders that we can provide a more integrated solution.” For Ang, who joined the company 23 years ago, the transformation is also part of his role as the third-generation leader of his family business. Tiong Woon’s first 300-tonne crane, acquired from Soon Douglas in 1987. His grandfather, the late Ang Choo Kim, founded Tiong Woon in 1978 with a single 20-tonne crane. Two years later, the business was incorporated as Tiong Woon Crane & Transport by the next generation of the family. Today, Ang represents the third generation of leadership, while his father, Ang Kah Hong, serves as executive chairman and his uncle, Ang Kha King, remains on the board as an executive director. His family’s involvement across several generations has deepened his understanding of how far the company has evolved from its beginnings as a crane and transport operator. Over the past five years, Tiong Woon has worked towards an integrated model that combines its heavy lift equipment with its haulage and marine fleet and engineering expertise. Instead of supplying a crane or vehicle, it aims to take on more parts of a project and provide customers with a more complete heavy lift solution. For contractors and project owners, that can mean dealing with one company rather than coordinating several across different stages of a job. The Tiong Woon team dismantling a 200-tonne gantry crane at PSA Singapore, an example of the more integrated heavy-lift work the company now undertakes. The company is also expanding into new sectors. Oil and gas, petrochemical and construction firms have traditionally made up the bulk of its customer base. Data centres, semiconductors and biopharmaceuticals are newer targets. In February 2026, the company announced more than $40 million worth of projects across the semiconductor, public infrastructure and biopharmaceutical sectors, ranging from crane deployment to lifting engineering and project support. But taking on more complex work requires more than a larger fleet and workforce. Today, the company has about 1,300 employees across Singapore and markets including Malaysia, Thailand, India and Saudi Arabia, and is looking to hire more crane operators, engineers and technicians as the business expands. As the company tries to move up the value chain, its next stage of growth will depend not only on adding physical assets, but on building the human expertise needed to take on bigger projects and new revenue streams. A 4,500-tonne module being loaded out at Laem Chabang, Thailand, where Tiong Woon is expanding its heavy-lift capabilities. In the last financial year ended June 2026 (FY2026), the wage bill reached $65 million, about a third of revenue. “Our single largest investment is actually our human capital,” says group chief financial officer William Tan. The challenge is particularly apparent in Singapore, where Tiong Woon has more cranes than operators, Tan says, reflecting the shortage of skilled trades workers in the built environment sector. Knowing when to move, and when to wait In December 2023, Tiong Woon formed a strategic alliance in Thailand with Netherlands-headquartered heavy lift specialist Mammoet and acquired heavy lift, haulage and transportation equipment to strengthen its capabilities and position in the market. The move reflects the broader direction of the business: using the heavy lift expertise it has built in Singapore over decades as a base to take on a larger and more complex role in overseas projects.

events.title: This building will cost more than $1 billion. What do we know about it?
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts This National Security Office Precinct will cost more than $1 billion. What do we know about it? Some details about the National Security Office Precinct were revealed to Senate estimates in May. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) A stone's throw from Parliament House, six giant cranes have been working on the biggest Commonwealth construction project in Canberra in almost 40 years. The development of a National Security Office Precinct has been heralded by the federal government as a solution to "critical accommodation and capability requirements" of several agencies. Despite the huge scale of the project, many of the details have been kept secret. We know the precinct in Barton will be utilised by a range of Commonwealth entities. That includes the Office of National Intelligence and the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT). In Senate estimates in May, we heard some details that there may be more to come. Construction of the National Security Office Precinct in Canberra continues. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) "We are engaging with other agencies as part of the development for the precinct going forward," Nick McClintock of the Department of Finance, which is leading the development, said. Next to the main buildings, there will also be hospitality and retail venues, servicing both the wider public and workers in the precinct. Up to 5,000 workers are expected to be based at the precinct. At the sod turning for the project, Finance Minister and ACT Senator Katy Gallagher said a "purpose built" and "specifically designed" building was needed to allow the national intelligence community "to do the work they need to do in a changing world". "[It's] clearly needed in terms of our national security agencies being able to work in a facility that actually allows them to do their job properly." Senator Katy Gallagher says the up-coming building will be more secure. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) She said the precinct would be "more appropriate" and "more secure" than existing buildings, with several government agencies reaching, or at, capacity. The project's price tag has not been revealed because of "commercial-in-confidence and national security sensitivities". But, we know it will cost at least $1 billion. "It is the most significant investment we've seen in the territory in a long time," Senator Gallagher said in 2023. The total cost of the precinct is expected to be revealed publicly once it's completed. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) She also told Senate estimates: "it is a very significant infrastructure spend" and has also described it as a "multi-year billion-dollar investment". The final cost is expected to be revealed publicly, but only after construction is completed. The precinct is the biggest Commonwealth construction project in Canberra since the development of the new Parliament House, which opened in 1988. Senator Gallagher has previously rejected claims Canberra had missed out on its fair share in recent federal budgets, pointing to the precinct as an example of spending in the territory. Construction is expected to be completed by the end of 2028, with the precinct starting to be occupied from 2029. The federal government has said the project will support more than 10,000 jobs over the construction period, which commenced in late 2024. The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is consolidating its presence in the ACT into two new buildings. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Due to the "security requirements" of the project, it was exempt from needing the green light of the public works committee, which scrutinises major public capital expenditure projects. We also haven't seen any artist impressions or plans for the precinct, which means we won't know exactly what it will look like for a while yet. The precinct is being built on the site of a former car park. What happens to the buildings after agencies move out? A Department of Finance spokesperson said as existing buildings were "privately owned commercial properties", their future use is a commercial decision for the landlords. We know DFAT is consolidating its presence in the ACT into two new buildings — the precinct and another new building also being built in Barton. The head office of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade will be vacated. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) It means its current head office, the RG Casey building, will be vacated. The lease is due to run out in 2031, and as noted by the department, its future after that will be up to the private landlord. It was revealed in Senate estimates in June that staff will be moved into the new precinct as soon as they are "reasonably able to".

events.title: Trump bears down on Zelensky as Russia keeps up attacks on Ukraine
events.summary: President Trump's announcement Sunday about an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine referred to a potential deal that includes each side stopping attacks on oil refineries — and he expects Volodymyr Zelensky to abide by it, a White House official said. The official said if attacks on oil refineries cease, a deal to stop hitting power plants and energy grids could come next. Why it matters: Trump appears to be singlehandedly trying to will a partial ceasefire into existence. But for now Russia hasn't accepted any kind of ceasefire — and Ukraine wants one that forbids attacks on power plants. Reality check: The "refinery for refinery" proposal, as the official dubbed it, is lopsided. A Ukrainian official told Axios that the country has a single oil refinery which the Russians have attacked multiple times and isn't fully functional. Russia, by contrast, has a vast network of refineries. "We import diesel and gas. What we need is for the Russians to stop attacking our electricity grid," the Ukrainian official said. "The Russians are thinking about" it, the White House official said. "We will know soon if they are ready." Case in point: Hours after Trump's announcement, Russia conducted strikes on power plants in Ukraine, according to Ukrainian media. What he said: Trump's Truth Social post sounded at first like a major breakthrough. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" he wrote. It appears much more tenuous than that. Zelensky said the announced ceasefire "was news for me." State of play: After reaching a deal with Russia Friday to lift diesel sanctions, Trump remains focused on stopping Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. He believes the strikes are driving up U.S. gas prices. White House officials warn that Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries are hurting Zelensky's relationship with Trump more than they're damaging Russia. "Trump is really mad. He feels Zelensky is taking the U.S. for granted," the White House official said. Zoom in: Amid the crisis with Ukraine, presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have put their planned trip to Moscow on hold, at least until they get clarity on whether Ukraine and the Europeans are ready to agree to a new unified proposal for Putin. A Ukrainian official told Axios on Friday that during a meeting with U.S. negotiators in Miami on Friday, Witkoff and Kushner threatened that Trump could stop sharing U.S. intelligence if it continued to ignore his requests. A U.S. official denied that, saying Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainians that the U.S. was a strong partner, providing munitions and intelligence. Ukraine therefore shouldn't take actions that hurt American consumers, the two said. On Sunday, the Financial Times reported that the U.S. told European countries it might stop selling weapons to Ukraine through NATO if Ukraine continues to strike Russian refineries.

events.title: Insurer underpaid hundreds of NSW accident victims in 'mind blowing' error
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NRMA Insurance underpaid hundreds of injured motorists in NSW since 2019 NRMA Insurance initially estimated that about 700 people had been underpaid, a number later revised down to 400. ( Facebook: NRMA Insurance ) Hundreds of people injured in car accidents have been repaid by NRMA Insurance after the company miscalculated some compulsory third party benefits since 2019. The company said 700 people were impacted but the number was later revised down to 400. Neither the insurer nor the State Insurance Regulatory Authority noticed the error. NRMA Insurance has been forced to repay hundreds of people who were injured in motor vehicle accidents, after failing to correctly calculate some compulsory third party (CTP) benefits since 2019. The original error was not detected by the insurer, nor was it noticed by NSW's State Insurance Regulatory Authority (SIRA), despite it having previously launched an audit of the company's practices. Instead, the mistake was spotted by a lawyer who realised their client's weekly payments did not add up. Neither the insurer nor the State Insurance Regulatory Authority picked up on the original error. ( Supplied ) Initially, NRMA Insurance estimated about 700 people who had been injured in motor vehicle accidents had been underpaid, before revising the number down to 400. However, the company told the ABC it had also identified a "further cohort" of people it believed were owed interest, after previously receiving lump sum payments. Greens MP Abigail Boyd said NRMA Insurance, a trading name of Insurance Australia Limited, should have been capable of indexing payments correctly. "It actually blows my mind," she said. Ms Boyd says it was "extraordinary" that NRMA had not discovered the issue itself. ( Four Corners: Rob Hill ) She said it was "particularly extraordinary" that NRMA had not discovered the issue itself. "You have this massive power differential between these insurers and these injured people who are going through some of the worst times of their lives. "[Yet] it's somehow expected that [the victims] are the ones, or their lawyers … that will pick up these errors." Under the state's CTP scheme, people injured in motor vehicle accidents are entitled to income support payments if they are unable to work as a result. It starts at 95 per cent of their pre-accident weekly earnings, before dropping to a maximum of 85 per cent from 14 weeks onwards, depending on their capacity to work. The payments, made by CTP insurers like NRMA Insurance, are supposed to be adjusted twice a year, in line with average weekly earnings. The insurer markets itself as a "help company". ( Supplied: NRMA ) However NRMA Insurance, which markets itself as "a help company", acknowledged it had incorrectly applied this principle, costing the average affected claimant $940. "We became aware in late April this year, through a customer's legal representative, that the statutory indexation may not have been correctly applied to weekly benefit payments for customers who continued receiving payments more than 78 weeks after their accident," a spokesperson said. "Our investigation confirmed an error in the application of indexation in our system, which has been corrected. We apologised to the customer, paid the amount outstanding (and interest) and notified the regulator." NRMA Insurance, which is a separate entity to the NRMA, said it had recently completed the process of repaying customers, along with the interest they were owed. "We sincerely apologised to all affected customers," the spokesperson said. This is not the first time NRMA Insurance has failed to properly pay the required weekly benefits to people who have been injured in motor vehicle accidents. In February 2023, SIRA issued a letter of censure to the company, after finding it had contravened NSW legislation, and its licence conditions by underpaying more than 2,000 customers. NRMA Insurance repaid more than $735,000 to those affected, but it was not fined. In March the same year, another censure letter was issued over the late processing of weekly benefits. No fine was issued. And in June 2023, SIRA sent another censure letter to NRMA Insurance over delays in commencing weekly payments. No financial penalty was imposed. In 2023, NRMA Insurance had to repay more than $735,000 to people injured in car accidents. ( ABC News: Adriane Reardon ) Ms Boyd said SIRA's enforcement actions to date had given NRMA Insurance little incentive to raise its standards.

events.title: Mexican president urges residents to shelter as Hurricane Simon approaches
events.summary: The Mexican community of Cabo Corrientes faces the risk of a direct hit as the Category 4 storm churns off Jalisco. Mexican President ‌‌Claudia Sheinbaum has urged residents along the Pacific Ocean to stay indoors as Hurricane Simon’s powerful winds and heavy rains pound coastal communities. As of Sunday, the hurricane’s eye was moving offshore of Mexico’s Jalisco state, with winds of at least 240km/h (150mph). list 1 of 4 Powerful storm floods US Northeast, causes power outages list 2 of 4 Hurricane Polo lashes Mexico as Nolo strengthens near Hawaii list 3 of 4 Isaias weakens after making landfall in US Gulf Coast as hurricane list 4 of 4 Hurricane Simon strengthens to Category 4 off Mexico’s Pacific coast Torrential rain has already battered residents living between the Sierra Madre mountain range and the ocean. Communities in hilly and mountainous areas have been warned to brace for mudslides. Simon reached Category 4 strength, on a scale of five, on Saturday, as part of an unusually active Pacific hurricane season. “With the approaching impact of Category 4 Hurricane Simon, we urge residents of coastal municipalities ‌‌in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to remain sheltered until authorities officially declare that the danger has passed,” Sheinbaum wrote in a post on the social media platform X on Sunday. In a midday advisory , the United States’ National Hurricane Center (NHC) warned that Simon could produce “additional rainfall totals of 8 to 16 inches (20 to 41 cm) over portions of southwestern Mexico”. Precipitation totals as high as 76 cm (30 inches) were possible in areas of Michoacan, Colima, and Jalisco until Monday. It’s not clear whether the storm will make landfall. But the greatest risk of a direct hit lies at the moment with Cabo Corrientes, a town that sits on a cape in Jalisco, jutting into the Pacific Ocean. Mexico’s National Civil Protection ⁠⁠Coordination (CNPC) placed 28 municipalities in Jalisco and Colima under its highest cyclone alert level, while another 93 municipalities were under a ⁠⁠high alert level, according to civil protection bulletins. Classes were suspended in the affected areas, and efforts to evacuate residents were under way. Businesses in popular tourist destinations like Puerto Vallarta boarded up windows and placed sandbags at entrances as the storm approached. Jalisco’s Governor Pablo Navarro warned that the high-powered hurricane was creating “high-risk marine conditions” along the coast of his state, with waves reaching as high as eight metres (26 feet). On Sunday, he also shared video on social media of the storm surge crashing onto sidewalks and flooding waterways. “Here is the current state of Jalisco’s beaches this morning — from Barra de Navidad to Puerto Vallarta — as Hurricane Simon passes through,” he wrote in the video’s caption. “I ask everyone to heed official instructions, take precautions and avoid putting themselves at risk. The safety of Jalisco’s families is the top priority.”

events.title: Republican senator says Trump diesel agreement with Russia may be illegal
events.summary: US President Trump’s bid to bring down diesel prices by easing sanctions on Russia has prompted rare Republican criticism. United States Senator Thom Tillis has questioned the legality of President Donald Trump’s decision to temporarily relax sanctions on Russian diesel , in an effort to bring down record-high fuel prices caused by the US-Israel war against Iran. During a Sunday interview on the NBC News television show Meet the Press, Tillis argued that the sanctions relief could violate congressional law. list 1 of 3 Trump says Ukraine and Russia agree to ‘energy ceasefire’ list 2 of 3 Oval Office spat to public rebukes: A timeline of Trump-Zelenskyy ties list 3 of 3 Trump calls on Ukraine to replace Zelenskyy amid tensions over Russia deal “I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law,” said Tillis. Trump’s decision has unsettled some Republican lawmakers who continue to support Ukraine in its war with Russia, which began in February 2022, after Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of the eastern European country. Tillis warned that his vote in support of Trump’s legislative priorities would be contingent on the White House reversing course. “If the president wants my support, which I believe he should get for funding military operations and year-end funding beyond baseline funding, I think the president needs to understand this is a problem, and I’m not the only Republican concerned with this,” Tillis said. Tillis has become a critical voice within the Republican Party, denouncing what he sees as overreach from the Trump administration. But his time as a senator is nearly at a close. In June 2025, Tillis announced he would not be seeking re-election in the November 3 midterm elections, after Trump threatened him with a primary challenge in his home state of North Carolina. His term ends in January. Separately on Sunday, Tillis joined a bipartisan group of senators in issuing a letter to denounce the sanctions relief for Russia. The group included Republicans like Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and John Curtis of Utah, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen and Richard Blumenthal. “The United States should not provide [Russian President Vladimir] Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” the senators wrote. Another retiring Republican lawmaker, Representative Don Bacon, also said on Friday that “propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities”. The pushback points to schisms within the Republican Party over Russia’s invasion. Figures from the party’s establishment wing have generally pressed for robust support for Kyiv , while other party members have been sceptical of continued US support for Ukraine. Trump himself has been critical of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy , accusing the government in Kyiv of impeding a US-negotiated ceasefire. “I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals, and for some reason, he never does,” Trump said on Saturday. “That’s a war that should have never started, and I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.” A day earlier, Trump had announced that a call with Putin had concluded with an agreement to provide 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the global marketplace, with a further 500,000 tonnes to be delivered in November. In an interview with Fox and Friends on Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued that the administration’s decision to ease some sanctions on Moscow was necessary to obtain relief from surging diesel prices . “We’re going to do it with all the legal authorities we have,” Bessent said. Analysts have said that the decision is unlikely to bring prices down in the long term. Critics like Tillis have also pointed to previous law barring the importation of Russian fuel, including a 2022 executive order. A law signed last month — named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham — also prohibits US investment in the Russian energy sector. This year’s rise in global fuel prices has largely been attributed to the US-Israel war against Iran, which began in February. As a result of that war, Iran has limited commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for the fuel trade. Tillis pointed to those circumstances in his remarks to Meet the Press. “ If President Trump wants to end the strain on energy supplies, number one, get things right in Iran, and number two, recognise that it was Vladimir Putin, not Zelenskyy, that started this war,” Tillis said. “It’s Vladimir Putin who owns the responsibility for energy prices to the extent that they come from that part of the world.” Trump’s decision also garnered international criticism, with the office of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney issuing a statement in support of Ukraine.

events.title: Justice Department opens antitrust probe as White House press-access fight escalates
events.summary: The Justice Department is investigating whether ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC violated antitrust law by jointly suspending pooled television coverage of Trump. The networks paused pooled video coverage after the White House barred CNN, MS NOW, and Politico; they later resumed coverage. A federal judge temporarily restored access to the White House on due-process grounds, but that order did not cover later Air Force One travel exclusions. The U.S. Department of Justice launched an investigation into whether the White House television press pool's decision to suspend coverage of President Donald Trump violated antitrust laws. The Justice Department said in a statement that it is examining whether the White House TV press pool — a group of broadcasters including CNN, Fox News, ABC, CBS and NBC — violated the Sherman Act by temporarily halting pooled TV coverage of Trump. The Sherman Act is a federal law that prohibits certain agreements that unreasonably restrain trade. Introduced in the 1890s, the law has rarely been applied to media organizations, particularly regarding their coverage. Members of the press pool did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment sent outside of normal business hours. The DOJ investigation follows the White House television press pool ceased its coverage of Trump on Sept. 21, shortly after he prohibited CNN, MS NOW and Politico from accessing the White House. In a Truth Social post , the president said then that those outlets "shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America." A judge lifted restrictions on those reporters on Sept. 24, several days after White House staff confiscated their press passes. Despite the ruling, reporters from CNN and Politico were barred from traveling with the president on Air Force One, the New York Times reported . The Trump administration now faces a lawsuit from CNN, MS NOW and Politico over its ban of their reporters from the White House grounds. Television pool coverage of the White House has also resumed. The DOJ investigation marks another escalation in an ongoing dispute between Trump and the media over press rights. The Trump administration has moved to restrict news agencies that have produced critical coverage of its policies. Last year, Trump moved to rescind about $1.1 billion previously approved for the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, federal funding earmarked for public broadcasters NPR and PBS. Trump and his allies have also sued several media organizations, including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and BBC News, over alleged biases or inaccuracies in their reporting. Seth Stern, chief of advocacy for the Freedom of the Press Foundation, called the DOJ investigation "nonsense." "Depriving Trump of the attention he craves is not a competitive harm and in any case, antitrust law has long recognized First Amendment exceptions even when there is anticompetitive impact," he said. "After all his 'fake news' rhetoric, Trump is weaponizing the DOJ to pressure the networks he calls the 'enemy of the people' to stay at the White House. It's a weird way of telling the press how much he missed them." The White House Correspondents' Association did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Disclosure: CNBC and MS NOW are divisions of Versant Media.

events.title: War and high debt to dominate IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok
events.summary: The US-Israel war on Iran and its inflationary impact will dominate the agenda. Finance officials from around the world will gather in Bangkok this week under the shadow of a widening war in the Middle East, the biggest-ever energy supply shock and rising interest rates that together pose daunting risks to already-sluggish global economic growth. The US-Israel war on Iran, now in its eighth month, and its inflationary impact are slated to dominate the agenda and sideline conversations during the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank, held outside Washington for the first time in three years. list 1 of 4 US stocks slide as oil prices fluctuate over renewed Iran war fears list 2 of 4 Trump says US will not strike Iran before midterm elections list 3 of 4 What the Iran war has done to the world’s energy supply, in charts list 4 of 4 Trump says Ukraine and Russia agree to ‘energy ceasefire’ IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva told Reuters News Agency that 18,000 people were registered to attend the meetings, 4,000 more than the last off-site meetings held in Morocco in October 2023. Notably absent will be United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who dispatched two senior officials in his stead while he handles some “domestic engagements”, a US official said. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh will attend and is slated to participate in a public event with Georgieva on October 16. Several other finance ministers were also staying home due to domestic budget and election duties, but most central bankers would attend, Georgieva said. Bessent’s decision to skip the high-profile gathering and a meeting of the Group of 20 (G20) major economies, which the US leads this year, may frustrate counterparts amid rising tensions over the Iran war, Ukraine’s battle against Russia’s invasion, and the US move to impose sanctions on the International Criminal Court. The Group of Seven (G7) countries have agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves under pressure from US President Donald Trump, who is keen to see lower petrol prices before November elections that could see his Republican Party lose control of Congress. Trump on Friday announced a deal with Russia that would provide even more diesel to global markets and a temporary waiver of US sanctions designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its ‌‌war on Ukraine. The move drew swift criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. More than one billion barrels of oil have been released, mainly from onshore commercial inventories, since the start of the war on February 28. But industry executives say the amount of oil in storage that is accessible to the global market is running low, making the market more fragile and fuelling pressure on prices. The IMF has signalled little change in its forecast for three percent global growth in 2026, and may edge its forecast for next year slightly higher. But some countries will see downgrades, including Ukraine, now in its fifth year of war against Russia’s invasion, and Gulf countries hit by Iranian strikes and sharply reduced energy exports. IMF research released on Tuesday showed that sharp spikes in food and energy prices are an increasingly common source of crises that drive inflation expectations higher for longer, worsen poverty and threaten economic stability. One headache for policymakers is the growing public debt burden that is sapping growth and adding inflationary pressures. The IMF says public debt is at the highest level since World War II and will exceed 100 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) before 2030. Advanced economies, led by the US, have the highest debt-to-GDP ratios, but emerging markets and low-income countries are particularly vulnerable, given a perfect storm of challenges: capital outflows in search of higher US rates, weather extremes triggered by the El Nino climate phenomenon, and a lack of investment in artificial intelligence (AI), which has mitigated negative supply shocks in the US and other rich countries. Developing countries are particularly vulnerable given high public debt levels that will have to be renegotiated at higher interest rates. Together, they face $400bn in debt payments to external creditors in 2026, and interest payments already exceed 10 percent of revenue on average. Many lower-income countries are worried about new IMF recommendations for loan programmes that call for fewer but deeper reforms as a condition for approving lending, a change that many fear will lead to painful austerity measures.

events.title: 'SNL' takes aim at Kevin O’Leary and his Utah data center: 'I'm going to make the future go away’
events.summary: James Austin Johnson portrayed Kevin O'Leary on "Saturday Night Live." Will Heath/NBC via Getty Images "Saturday Night Live" took on Kevin O'Leary and his data center. "These things shouldn't be anywhere. That's why I'm building one in Utah," Johnson's O'Leary said. The real O'Leary is backing a giant data center project spanning over 20,000 acres. AI data centers got the "Weekend Update" treatment on "Saturday Night Live" this week. Comedian James Austin Johnson portrayed "Shark Tank" investor Kevin O'Leary on the sketch comedy show, during which he addressed the dispute over the real O'Leary's proposed data center in Utah, known as the Stratos Project . "It's very simple. All I want is to buy up 40,000 acres of God's untouched splendor and replace it with a very loud computer that steals your job," Johnson's O'Leary said. "Is it going to take up precious water? Absolutely. Is it going to provide a necessary service? Who's to say? But on the flip side, it's going to make me a tremendous amount of money, and I think that's great." The "SNL" version of O'Leary said he understood that some Americans were concerned about data centers near their homes. (An actual May Gallup poll found that over half of American surveyors opposed constructing AI data centers in their local area.) "These things are terrible and shouldn't be anywhere. That's why I'm building one in Utah," he said. Data centers are a contentious issue in the United States. Leading tech companies rely on AI data centers to power their systems and products. Supporters say they'll create new jobs , bolster the economy, and help the US defeat China in the race to control the global AI market. Residents in the places where they are being built, however, are often much less excited about them. The Utah project, backed by O'Leary Digital, has drawn criticism from many local residents over concerns that the data center could strain local resources and worsen the environment. Some residents are also upset over what they consider a lack of transparency from O'Leary and local leaders. Critics of the Stratos Project have staged protests, created petitions, and taken legal action to stop its construction. O'Leary scaled back the data center's size from about 40,000 to just over 20,000 acres after public pushback. He has said he remains undeterred, though. "There are bumps in the road. There's litigation. There's misinformation. There's propaganda. You name it. But if you know what you're doing is right, you make it, you get there," O'Leary told Business Insider in June. "Persevere." During a May interview on Fox News, O'Leary said said some critics of the project have ties to the Chinese Communist Party, a claim he later walked back. A Utah advocacy group that has publicly opposed the project filed a defamation lawsuit against Fox News and O'Leary in July. On "Saturday Night Live," Johnson's O'Leary acknowledged the incident. "I made the mildly inflammatory claim that every single person in Utah who opposes me is a paid communist super agent from China. Was I wrong? Perhaps. But just because they're not, doesn't mean they aren't," he said. He added, "I'm going to make the future go away. And we're doing just that in Utah." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Critics warn of 'Santos-sized loopholes' in gas reservation plan
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Critics say 'Santos-sized loopholes' will make gas reservation a joke Liquefied natural gas ships from Curtis Island in Queensland. ( Supplied: Photopia Studio ) Gas market players say the federal government's draft gas reservation scheme has been weakened by loopholes. They argue that changes to the policy favour the Santos-led GLNG venture, which has been blamed for rising prices on the east coast. The government is expected to release legislation for the scheme in the coming weeks. A giant LNG plant blamed by critics for driving up east coast gas prices could largely or totally escape a federal scheme designed to protect local buyers, observers have warned. The Albanese government last month released a draft plan to force gas exporters to set aside up to 20 per cent of their production for the domestic market in a bid to force prices lower. But analysts and industry players say the draft is full of loopholes that will allow some exporters to reduce or even eliminate their exposure. They point to the Gladstone LNG project, a plant on Curtis Island in Queensland that is operated by Adelaide-based Santos, as the exporter most likely to benefit. An investigation by the ABC revealed GLNG had sucked up and exported the equivalent of 20 per cent of eastern Australia's domestic gas demand over the past 10 years. This was because the venture built an LNG plant with a capacity of 7.8 million tonnes a year despite not having nearly enough gas of its own to fill it. By contrast, the other two LNG projects in Queensland — run by global super-major Shell and Australian company Origin along with US firm ConocoPhillips — had overwhelmingly been supplying the local market in net terms. Paul Farrow from the Australian Workers Union is unsympathetic to Santos. ( ABC News: Kit Mochan ) Paul Farrow, the national secretary of the Australian Workers Union, said "Santos-sized loopholes" threatened to turn the government's reservation plans into a joke. Mr Farrow said that, compared with earlier iterations of the plan, the draft had been watered down in significant ways that appeared to favour GLNG above all others. "Australian industry and Australian consumers deserve to derive an advantage from Australia's gas because it's our sovereign wealth," Mr Farrow said. "The government is so close to getting it right. "But the exposure draft, as it stands, contains a bunch of Santos-sized loopholes. Curtis Island in Gladstone is home to three gas plants that export Australian gas. ( Supplied: Nearmap ) Under the draft policy, the Australian Energy Regulator would be able to reduce an exporter's supply obligation below 20 per cent, while the minister could cut it to zero. But critics say a raft of other provisions in the bill could enable Santos and its GLNG partners to slip the net themselves. They say the draft, unlike earlier iterations, effectively allows GLNG to count contract extensions as "existing contracts" that are exempt from consideration. Crucially, this would allow GLNG to extend for five years from 2030 a supply agreement with South Korea's KOGAS. The current deal is for 3.5 million tonnes of LNG a year, an amount equivalent to about 40 per cent of annual east coast gas demand. Observers also say the draft will give rise to "take-or-pay" deals that allow Santos to generate paper sales to the domestic market without actually supplying any gas. And they argue the government has given too much ground to Santos over questions about whether the company can "reasonably" find enough gas without breaking export contracts. Mr Farrow said the provision should require Santos to explore all practical options such as buying gas from other providers in the local market, substituting LNG cargoes from its international operations or using flexibility in its contracts to reduce overseas sales. Instead, he said the draft appeared to allow Santos itself to set those terms, which he argued the company would do so however it liked. "If a massive project like GLNG wants to claim that it simply doesn't have enough gas to share with the Australian market, it should have to prove it's actually explored all practical options to get hold of that gas," Mr Farrow said. "These options might incur a small cost for Santos' shareholders. The government hopes its reservation plans can encourage more gas wells. ( ABC News: Hamish Harty ) As well as these provisions, Mr Farrow said the draft contained other clauses that would allow GLNG off the hook. Among them was a so-called "additional gas" test.

events.title: Man City beat 10-man Liverpool 3-0 in first game after guilty verdict
events.summary: Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki score second half goals after Ryan Gravenberch sent off. Manchester City shrugged off the threat of swingeing sanctions to beat 10-man Liverpool 3-0 in their first game since being found guilty on more than 100 charges of breaking Premier League financial rules. Second half goals from Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki on Sunday extended City’s flawless start under Enzo Maresca after Ryan Gravenberch had been sent -off for two yellow cards. Victory reestablishes City’s three-point lead at the top of the table, but the future of any title challenge rests on the outcome of the club’s appeal against widespread financial impropriety. An independent commission found City and their Emirati owners arranged “sham” deals to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs by more than 900 million pounds ($1.2bn) between 2009 and 2018. No sanction has yet been handed down, but a severe points deduction or even expulsion from the English top-flight is on the table unless City overturns the decision. There has even been speculation that there could be retrospective action to strip City’s titles. The multiple breaches of Premier League laws came during a period in which City won three titles and a clutch of other trophies. City’s rivals believe, however, that the illegal spending during that period also built the foundations for a golden era under former boss Pep Guardiola, who left at the end of last season. Liverpool were one of the clubs most affected, having finished second to City three times in the past 12 years. “There are so many moments and memories we can’t get back,” Liverpool fan Martin Reilly, 23, told the AFP news agency. “They have to throw the book at them.” City arrived under the protection of a police escort with a hostile Anfield welcome expected, but there was no repeat of the violent scenes when their team bus was pelted with bottles ahead of a Champions League clash in 2018. Liverpool fans lined the streets to greet the visitors with chants of “cheats” and “going down”, while merchandise stalls were littered with flags and scarves mocking City’s financial scandal. In the iconic Kop end behind one goal, a banner read “a generation of supporters cheated”. The battles between Guardiola’s City and Jurgen Klopp’s Liverpool in recent years became the Premier League’s marquee event. But with the eyes of the world watching today, Liverpool failed to rise to the occasion on the field. New Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola’s options were blunted without the injured Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo as the Spaniard suffered his first defeat since taking charge of the Reds. The home side briefly flickered into life at the start of the second half when Lewis Koumas was denied a goal on his first Premier League start by Gianluigi Donnarumma. The Abu Dhabi-backed takeover in 2008 transformed City from mid-table mediocrity into the dominant force of the English game. City’s economic might was on full display to help turn the game, as Maresca could turn to Jeremy Doku off the bench early in the second half. Within minutes the Belgian winger had been chopped down by Gravenberch, who was shown a second yellow card and Liverpool never recovered. Doku’s deflected shot was then smashed home by Haaland to break the deadlock 25 minutes from time and open the floodgates. Three minutes later Doku curled a sensational strike into the top corner himself. Cherki then exchanged a slick one-two with Josko Gvardiol before slotting under Alisson Becker to rub salt in Liverpool’s wounds. City midfielder Elliot Anderson told reporters after the game that his side had shown “courage” as they got the win in a hostile atmosphere. “We have shown togetherness and fight, this is tough place to come and we have shown courage,” he said. “It [the noise from the Anfield crowd] was more than normal … Arriving and the first 10 minutes of the first half, but we quietened the crowd and improved in the second half. “During the game you can feel it, and it is a game where you have to stick together and we did.”

events.title: For the first time ever, 10-year bond yields track diesel prices more closely than crude, and Trump’s fuel deal with Putin may be too little too late
events.summary: Diesel prices have come off their all-time highs in recent weeks, but the key industrial fuel has already moved the needle across the economy and financial markets, making affordability a more potent issue in the midterm elections. The national average for diesel is about $6.277 per gallon, according to AAA , down from its $6.528 high but still 71% above year-ago levels. By contrast, U.S. crude oil is up 56% from a year earlier as damage to refining capacity in the Middle East and Russia has produced a sharper crunch in fuel markets. Because diesel is a critical input in manufacturing, agriculture and logistics, the recent price surge has been felt broadly. The latest consumer and producer price indexes showed jumps in transportation costs, while purchasing manager surveys signaled big spikes in prices businesses are paying. “This is why products have been trading at double the price of crude during the past few months, something that has never happened before. Ultimately, diesel and gasoline drive inflation, not crude oil,” Amrita Sen, director of market intelligence and co-founder at Energy Aspects, wrote in the Financial Times on Wednesday. And as higher fuel costs keep inflation forecasts elevated, markets are pricing in a more hawkish Federal Reserve that’s ready to hike rates further. Bond yields have risen in anticipation of tighter monetary policy, raising borrowing costs for consumers. Crude prices had previously moved in tandem with prices for refined products and had long been a proxy for those costs, but that relationship has broken down, according to Sen. “In fact, since May, 10-year US Treasury yields have correlated more closely with diesel prices than crude prices, for the first time ever,” she added. That’s why the Trump administration has started paying more attention lately to bringing down diesel prices, Sen said. Over the past week alone, President Donald Trump has taken steps to ease the cost burden. On Monday, he signed an executive order to defer the 24-cent federal tax per gallon on diesel until the end of the year, though most states have separate levies on diesel. And on Friday, he said he reached a deal with Vladimir Putin to obtain diesel from Russia , a stunning reversal from years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine. Russia will supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel now, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter,” according to Trump. Russia will deliver another 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that. The surprise announcement was more shocking considering that Trump signed a sweeping sanctions law  last month that imposes steep tariffs on the top buyers of Russian energy. Diesel prices are displayed above $8 per gallon at a gas station in Los Angeles on September 17, 2026. Frederic J. BROWN / AFP via Getty Images But Trump’s efforts to lower diesels costs are unlikely to improve affordability significantly. Farmers and truckers have said his executive order on the diesel tax will offer little relief , especially given that per-gallon prices are $2.60 higher than a year ago while the federal tax is just 24 cents a gallon. Similarly, energy experts said the deal for Russian diesel is also unlikely to make much of a dent. “It’s kind of shuffling deck chairs on the Titanic,” Michael Lynch, distinguished fellow at Energy Policy Research Foundation, told the Associated Press . “If we get diesel from Russia, basically it means that their existing customers are not going to get it and they’ll have to go somewhere else, and that will keep the price basically where it is now.” And even if Trump somehow managed to end his Iran war or bring fuel prices down sharply, Republicans may not see a lift with voters in November. According to a new Politico Poll , just 10% of undecided voters said they would be more likely to vote for a Republican if gas prices went down by $1 a gallon versus 29% who said it would have no impact and 57% who didn’t know. The results were similar when asked about how an end to the Iran war and a sharp drop in inflation might affect their midterm choices. “There’s nothing that Trump can do, and frankly, even if he did something, no one would believe it anyway at this point,” one GOP operative working on battleground races told Politico. events.title: From BJ’s to Lululemon, retailers are trimming assortments to boost business
events.summary: Dollar General, BJ's Wholesale Club, Lululemon and Under Armour have said in earnings calls that they have already cut or plan to cut assortments. Analysts said that after trimming product lines, brands may focus on raising prices to get back to healthy growth. Box retailers can offer thousands of individual brands, so product cuts can help streamline assortments and stabilize their businesses. Trimming assortments comes with challenges, as retailers risk losing customers and have to answer to investors as their revenue base shrinks in the short term. Retailers are trimming assortments in an effort to clean up their balance sheets. As shoppers cut spending in the face of high gas and food prices, businesses have pulled more levers to boost profitability and appease investors. During earnings calls this year, a range of retailers have highlighted efforts to reduce the number of items they sell, commonly tracked as stock keeping units, or SKUs. In March, Dollar General said it trimmed 1,500 SKUs. In August, Under Armour said it shrunk SKUs by 25% over the past few years and plans to cut another 25%, while BJ's Wholesale Club said it plans to reduce roughly 20% of SKUs . In September, Lululemon said it cut North America SKUs by 15%. Trimming inventory can help a business stabilize its sales or even get back to growth, and can reduce the chances a company gets stuck with unwanted inventory. But the move can also leave consumers with less choice — a trade-off many retailers have been willing to make. When a brand struggles to sell certain products, it can lead to discounting, which hurts profitability. Some markdowns are expected when businesses roll the dice on new products that don't end up selling well, but too many promotions can cause problems. "If you have zero discounting, you're not taking enough fashion risk," said Guggenheim Securities senior retail analyst Simeon Siegel. "But discounting needs to be fixing mistakes. It needs to be done quickly." Under Armour and Lululemon are both facing repercussions from what investors see as too many markdowns. Under Armour's operating income, which illustrates its underlying profitability, turned negative in fiscal 2025 and 2026. The company said its problems would not be solved by chasing unhealthy sales volume or short-term revenue. "Today, we're managing for quality. Fewer products with greater purpose, tighter execution and a clear reason to buy," said Under Armour CEO Kevin Plank on the company's fiscal first-quarter earnings call in August. "We will sell so much more of so many less products at a much higher full retail price." Siegel said that when a retailer acknowledges it wants to shrink revenue, the goal is to regain pricing power. Lululemon grew its sales by more than $500 million from fiscal 2024 to 2025. Yet its operating profit fell by about $300 million in the same time span. Shares are down around 65% over the past two years. "Selling fewer options is not the same as selling fewer things," said Siegel. "Lulu has a long way to go, and simply cutting SKUs, simply saying we need to have better product is not the answer." Siegel said too much of even the best product can dilute the value of a brand. Lululemon reported $6.3 billion in U.S. sales in fiscal 2025. Siegel said $3 billion to $4 billion in domestic revenue is where companies typically hit a healthy saturation level. "It's a level where they can be large and still cool. Above that, they start cheapening what they stand for, literally cheapening the product, but also cheapening the perception," said Siegel. He noted that Nike is an exception to this rule, after posting $20 billion in North American sales in fiscal 2026. Still, the apparel and footwear giant, which has seen shares crater around 45% this year, said it is "rebalancing" its portfolio, having reduced revenue from classic footwear franchises by more than $2 billion in fiscal 2026, according to its fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter earnings call in June. For small-box stores such as Dollar General and big-box retailers like BJ's, cutting down the assortment doesn't necessarily give them the ability to raise prices. Rather, for those stores carrying thousands of brands, removing certain products can help them better manage inventory and refine their offerings to help stabilize the business. "When you shrink a box ... and say, I'm going to focus more on curation, you're getting smaller, but you're trying to reestablish why someone's walking into your box in the first place. And so it does get better, but it doesn't necessarily help your bottom line as much," said Siegel. BJ's CEO Robert Eddy said reducing choice, such as cutting the number of scents of body wash, pushes sales into the remaining products on shelves and then makes room for more product categories that weren't previously offered.

events.title: Citroen revives the 2CV for an electric age
events.summary: French carmaker Citroen has brought back its 2CV brand in a bid to boost sales of electric cars in a difficult market. The new model, unveiled at the Paris Motor Show, is a small city runabout with retro styling which harks back to one of the company's most famous designs. As a "concept car" intended to show Citroen's direction of travel, it is not yet ready to go on sale but the plan is to have a version in showrooms by 2028. As they face mounting competition from Chinese manufacturers, Citroen and other European brands are exploiting their heritage as a means of selling modern motors. Citroen chief executive Xavier Chardon described the new car as "a modern, ingenious and refreshing response to the mobility challenges of tomorrow". The original Citroen 2CV was launched in 1948, as Europe was recovering from the ravages of World War Two. It was designed as a cheap, robust way for French farmers and country folk to get around. The car had high wheel arches and soft suspension, letting it travel across a ploughed field or rough roads - as legend would have it, without breaking a tray of duck eggs. Its high roof let drivers wear a hat at the wheel. It was easy to drive and simple to repair. The car was so popular, it remained in production for more than 40 years. Over time, it went from being a utilitarian tool for the countryside to a cult classic, and a favourite of hippies and counter-culturalists. Fans of Citroën's 2CV hold annual meet-ups such as this muddy gathering in Switzerland Now, Citroen wants to draw on that heritage to sell an electric, small city car that is expected to sell for about £13,000. The look of the new 2CV may well evolve as Citroen develops its design. But as it stands, it shares plenty of styling features with its famous predecessor. The high, flared wheel arches, the tall, curved roof and the eye-like headlights are all reminders of the original "deux chevaux" or "two horses". By using memories of an old car to sell a new one, Citroen is following a well-travelled road. VW notoriously brought back the Beetle in the late 1990s, with limited success. BMW's Minis have always carried styling designed to hark back to the very British original. Fiat has been selling a retro-styled Fiat 500 for the past two decades. But the retro-nostalgia trend has accelerated recently, as carmakers have looked for ways to sell electric cars to sceptical consumers. Citroen's French rival, Renault, has led the charge. It started with the Renault 5 E-Tech, which visually echoed the distinctive boxy styling of the original Renault 5, once an ever-present sight on French streets. It has since revived the Renault 4 and Twingo brands as well. VW has the distinctive ID-Buzz minivan, a throwback to the classic T2 Transporter, while Ford is working on a new EV which is widely expected to be called the Fiesta. Rachel Burgess, senior editor of Autocar magazine, thinks it is a strategy that makes perfect sense. "It's a brilliant differentiator from all-new car brands", she says. "An older audience might remember the originals and feel warmly towards them, and a younger audience might find an appeal in the retro aspect." Finding new ways to make cars appealing has become more important than ever, at a time when European manufacturers are facing growing competition from Chinese brands. "Many in the industry believe the big automotive players in Europe…face a very serious existential threat from aggressive Chinese manufacturers," says David Leggett, automotive editor at Global Data. Back to the future: VW looked to the past when designing its ID-Buzz minivan In this hostile business environment, heritage and nostalgia could prove to be powerful weapons for more established brands, thinks automotive researcher and author Dr Paul Nieuwenhuis. "In a world where a wave of credible decent quality Chinese EVs are hitting Europe, linking European designs back to their history while using the latest powertrain technology is something the Chinese cannot do," he says. "The Chinese can establish new design trends, but there is limited history there." But Leggett thinks Citroen will need more than a heady whiff of nostalgia to turn its new car into a best-seller. "A reimagined Citroën 2CV should give a big nod to its ancestor - especially on price and design simplicity as well as visual cues," he says. "But it also needs to be a credible modern electric car in terms of functionality and features, with widespread appeal." events.title: Volkswagen boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic European industry
events.summary: Oliver Blume says ‘Made in Europe’ rules to counter rapid rise of lower-price Chinese brands ‘must reward real value creation’ The boss of Volkswagen has backed EU proposals to boost its domestic industry, arguing European carmakers need to be able to “compete under comparable conditions” with Chinese rivals. Oliver Blume said “Made in Europe” rules from the EU “must reward real value creation in Europe”, speaking in Paris before the motor show this week. The rules are aimed at countering the rapid rise of Chinese brands in Europe in the automotive sector and other important manufacturing industries. Lower-priced Chinese manufacturers have prompted a crisis in several industries. Volkswagen is among the most-affected European companies. Germany’s biggest carmaker has launched a brutal plan to cut as many as 100,000 jobs . Blume said it was the “largest transformation programme in its history”. The proposals for the Made in Europe rules, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act, would limit subsidies and public procurement to products with a large proportion of their materials and manufacturing coming from within the EU. Blume listed a litany of challenges facing European carmakers, saying: “Europe is under enormous competitive pressure.” These included: high energy costs; lower demand as consumers struggle with high inflation; the need to be quicker to develop cars; and intense competition from China . On Friday, the EU said it had reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry. Blume said Germany’s carmakers were happy to compete with Chinese rivals, but said the EU should try to reward businesses with significant European footprints. “Companies that invest and develop in Europe must see a clear benefit,” he said. Referring to Chinese companies, he added: “Those who sell here should compete under comparable conditions and create jobs and value here in Europe, too. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Blume added: “We believe in open markets, but openness also means standing up for our own interests in Europe. Because a strong industrial base means more than economic success. It protects technological independence.” Volkswagen is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years. Blume emphasised the “close ties between France and Germany”, while hosting the French industry minister, Sébastian Martin. Arno Antlitz, VW’s chief financial officer, said the job cuts were necessary to “increase our economic power” by increasing profitability and allowing it to defend its “home turf”. The company is cutting the number of models it offers worldwide from 150 to 75 across brands including Audi and Škoda. It hopes the move will reduce complexity in its factories and for dealers, cutting the cost of each vehicle it makes. On Sunday, it revealed the production version of its ID Tiguan, an electric edition of its bestselling family SUV.

events.title: Can the AI industry persuade data center opponents by getting rid of NDAs?
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Amazon recently followed Microsoft’s lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centers. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Sean O’Kane, Rebeccan Bellan and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities. Rebecca was a bit skeptical that the recent spate of data center moratoriums will have a lasting effect, especially since the moratoriums only last for a year or two and “these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years,” though I countered that data center backers definitely seem worried. Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication. “We’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Sean O’Kane: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon’s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren’t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular. There are so many things that could be said about whether or not people should be worried about the effect that data centers have on their property values, on their electricity bills, on their water usage in the area, and whether or not those things are real problems, inflated problems, etc. etc. I think so much of that just really goes back to the fact that a lot of these projects are being negotiated essentially in secret. Sometimes they’re being negotiated [with the public knowing] that it’s a data center, but just not knowing who’s actually going to use it or occupy it at any point. This is a long-standing issue with the tech industry. I always go back to the mid-2010s when Uber was expanding really fast. Uber was one of the companies that really used this tactic a ton when it came to working with local governments. In particular, I remember I was working at The Verge at the time and we had a freelancer write a story about a city outside of Orlando where Uber was trying to negotiate tax subsidies to subsidize rides for people to use public transit after the Uber trip. The whole thing was negotiated in secret. And not only that, which was frustrating on its face, but also, because of the secrecy, you could just see Uber getting really comfortable with asking for a lot of other stuff, too. So there needs to be more of this. I’m glad Amazon’s doing this. We’ll see if it actually does have any positive effect, but people are pretty entrenched right now. Rebecca Bellan: Yeah, I’m curious about what effect this will have and whether it will lead to communities successfully delaying or or killing any infrastructure that the companies need to build. What I’ve heard from some people I’ve spoken to, who deal with data centers every day, a lot of these moratoriums that are getting passed — and there are a significant number of them, including one recently in San Francisco , which is pretty ironic — but they’re only for like a year or two years. But these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years. All of the buildouts are going to be massively delayed for a number of reasons from zoning to funding. Of course, if the pushback keeps going, then it might have an effect, but I often wonder just how much of an effect this political pushback is having on this. Anthony Ha: The moratorium I’m most familiar with is the one in New York . I believe it’s a one year moratorium, and that’s on permits for large projects. [Technically, it’s until the state finalizes an environmental review process, which is expected to take a year.] So already, there’s some wiggle room within that. And often, they’re framed as: “It’s not like we think [data centers are] bad, let’s not do this. It’s [that] we need to take the time to study this.” Which gives them a lot of room to say later on, “Actually, we’ve decided this is great. We love it.” But you can tell that the people trying to build these data centers are worried, which is why you have these unhinged tweets from people like Trump or David Sacks. Only time will tell in terms how long and how deep that [community] resistance is, but I do think they are worried.

events.title: Alexandr Wang wanted to make Meta 'cool again' — and memes were part of his plan
events.summary: Alexandr Wang's wild X feed seemed to lack any rhyme or reason, but the 29-year-old said it helped serve a broader purpose. Bloomberg/Getty Images Alexandr Wang said his prolific X posting is part of a broader effort to make Meta cool again. The 29-year-old has filled his feed with memes about Muse, the company's AI agent. Wang said his posts "made an impact" on the growth of Muse. Alexandr Wang said he had trouble focusing during recent Meta meetings. On his mind: New memes to post about the company's popular new AI assistant. "I would just like think of a meme and I'd be like 'Oh God, I have to get this out,'" Wang said in a recent interview with podcaster David Senra, adding that his coworkers were "somewhat surprised" at the buzz his posts were generating. "It actually made an impact on growth," he said of the posts, "which is kind of hilarious." Much has been said about Meta's chief AI officer and his chaotic X feed, which the 29-year-old has crammed with occasionally off-color yet invariably eccentric references to Muse, Meta's personal AI assistant that sent the company's stock soaring and redefined the market for AI tools. https://t.co/TXOR8iI4MK pic.twitter.com/NnBHKMdj8X — Alexandr Wang (@alexandr_wang) October 9, 2026 In his interview with Senra, though, Wang said that his often spur-of-the-moment posts served a broader goal — to make Meta "cool again." "Despite having like these incredible pieces of cultural software like Instagram and Facebook, historically, Meta was not cool," he said. "I remembered that the internet rewards risk." After launching on September 8, Muse shot to the top of Apple's app store 10 days later, surpassing ChatGPT. Meta says Muse can help users research , fill out forms, buy items online, book restaurant reservations, find a dog sitter, and connect with services such as email, calendars, Spotify, Instagram, and OpenTable. The app marked Meta's first successful breakthrough in AI tech, after its Llama and Spark LLM models failed to find niches already filled by widely used models from OpenAI and Anthropic. With Muse, Meta found a largely untapped gold mine — though competing AI agents from OpenClaw and Instinct already existed in Silicon Valley circles. Muse, however, had the advantage of coming from a popular company with several billion potential customers already signed up on Instagram and Facebook. And the internet, weary of staid pronouncements from CEOs who were perhaps once cool but are now entering their 40s (Mark Zuckerberg is 42), welcomed the boundless energy of a young executive newly endowed with power in the AI era . "It was a lot of fun," Wang said. "There were like a few tweets where I just didn't think that much about it and just said, 'Fuck it, post.'" President Donald Trump said he is considering joining Saudi Arabia in its retaliation against Tehran-backed Houthis in Yemen after a deadly attack on Riyadh's main airport, a move that could draw the U.S. further into a second front in the Iran war . "We may. We're going to look at it," Trump told reporters outside the White House on Saturday when asked if the U.S. would back Saudi Arabian strikes. "We just found out about the recent attack. So, we'll make a decision. We move very quickly." Two Saudi Arabian government officials told MS NOW that the kingdom is requesting "urgent defense support" from the U.S. following the attacks. The officials, including a senior member of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, did not want to be identified because of the matter's sensitivity. They added that the U.S. needs to intervene "as soon as possible" to help the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen fight the Houthis. The White House did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment. On Sunday, a projectile struck a passenger terminal at the Riyadh airport, one day after a missile struck the same terminal, the Associated Press reported. No immediate details were available about the latest strike on the King Khalid International Airport complex for terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, AP said. The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said Saturday's attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed 12 people and injured 309 others, the country's official Saudi Gazette media outlet reported . Colonel Turki Al-Maliki, the spokesman for the Saudi-led Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen, which has been leading the fight against the Houthis, described the attack as a "war crime." "Therefore, the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will respond decisively to this terrorist attack in accordance with the Customary International Humanitarian Law," Al-Maliki said in a post on X. It was the second deadly assault on Riyadh's airport in less than a week. Three Saudi nationals, including a pilot , were killed in attacks on the facility by Iran-backed Houthi militants on Thursday. Following Saturday's attack, the Houthis renewed their warning against using Saudi airports. "We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using ⁠Saudi ‌airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become ⁠a theatre of operations for our forces, with the exception of the airports in (the holy cities of) Mecca and Medina," the Houthis said in a post on X. Saudi Arabia, a key U.S. ally in the Middle East, intervened in Yemen's civil war between the Houthis and its internationally recognized government after the group seized the Yemeni capital Sanaa in 2014. Last month, the Trump administration approved the potential $24.3 billion sale of nearly 50 F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia in what was seen as a major boost for the kingdom as it faces intensifying attacks from the Houthis. The sale is under congressional review. International energy conference still on The Saudi energy ministry said a long-planned international energy conference will still take place in Riyadh on Sunday, Reuters reported. The five-day WPC Energy Congress ⁠is taking place at a convention center near King Khalid airport. State television told Reuters that more than 70 ministers, ⁠300 company executives and representatives of more than 25 international energy organizations have confirmed their attendance, though it was not clear ⁠whether the participants would attend in person or virtually. Reuters said a ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum is also set to take place, with its plenary session to be held behind closed doors.
