events.title: I'm a top auto industry analyst. Improv taught me to scare myself in public.
events.summary: Erin Keating took five seasons of improv classes. It taught her about how to really listen to coworkers and family. Erin Keating Erin Keating spoke too fast during her first big presentation. She also felt kinda sweaty. In her mid-40s, she took an improv class to get better onstage. It's taught her lessons about listening to others that have helped at work and at home. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Erin Keating, an executive analyst for Cox Automotive. It has been edited for length and clarity. People should scare themselves. In public. I tested that theory out in my mid-40s by taking five seasons of improv classes at the DC Improv Comedy Club. My goal was not to become a comedian — I wanted to take on a challenge that I could easily fail at. And to add to the pressure, I had to perform in front of my family. I work as an executive analyst in the auto industry at Cox Automotive. I distill data to explain the industry's market dynamics to automakers, dealership groups, lenders, and journalists . The material I cover can quickly get boring if I'm not careful. Some of those conversations happen in small rooms, others happen in high-pressure settings: on stages in front of hundreds or thousands of people, on live television, at product unveilings, in podcasts, you name it. I also consider myself an introvert . I didn't always feel so comfortable in front of people — and I certainly haven't always been the funniest person in the room. Getting on the stage At my first major corporate presentation, I couldn't stop sweating. My colleagues said I was good, but I was talking too fast. Their feedback was basically, "You did fine. Slow down." I improved over time and got less sweaty when talking in front of people. There was still more I could learn. I decided to take the improv classes in 2018 because, honestly, I was a little bit bored. I had just left a marketing communications job and was trying to figure out what to do next. I knew I liked talking: I was hosting a successful podcast about books, but I wanted to be better at having conversations. Loving to talk is definitely not the same as being a good conversationalist. The classes with a cast of characters… So, I joined my first class. I was there with a biology teacher, a German woman who was really funny, an older woman who had done a ton of onstage acting, and a handful of people (like me) who were nervous about participating. The majority of us stuck it out for our five consecutive seasons. At the beginning, I fought against my preconception that I had to be funny. I remember playing a game called "Die, not today," where we had to mime throwing a hammer or a spear at each other. If the object was heading your way, you had to come up with how you'd survive the attack on the spot. Most people just tried to shield themselves, but one woman staged a dramatic scene where a spear nearly struck her nose. She grabbed it at the last second, saving her (improv-ed) life. It was amazing. … And their lessons Improv is really about paying attention to what another person is giving you. You have to build upon the scenario they set up, a principle called "yes, and." You accept the premise someone introduces, and add something to it. You also learn about status. In a scene, you might be the character driving the action. In your next, you could be supporting the other person's arc. Scenes are most interesting when you watch people respond to each other and create together through those statuses. Some of the worst scenes are when two people are just trying to compete to be the funniest. All of that applies to work and your life more than you might realize. Before I speak at big conferences, I talk to people in the audience to understand the energy in the room and what is on their minds. I don't like working from a script. It can get too prescriptive and keep you from responding to the people in front of you. I'm listening for the thought that is begging for a "yes, and." The same goes for one-on-one conversations. When someone talks, improv has taught me to follow the unexpected and respond to what was actually said. Those skills also matter a lot for office politics. Those classes taught me to recognize an awkward moment, assess the reaction, and apologize if I misread it. I am now comfortable saying, "Thank you for receiving that with the intent it was given," when I know I don't express myself well. The final big lesson was authenticity. Near the end of my third improv season, I jumped into a scene and used the New York Jewish-grandmother voice I'd always been able to pull off (do not ask me to do other accents — even when I think I sound like a señorita, I always revert back to that Eastern European drawl.) I'd avoided that voice because I thought, "This is not acting, I'm not supposed to do that." But for that scene, it was exactly what my partner needed. My classmate asked me why I had never done it. That voice was a breakthrough for me. I realized I could bring my whole self to that stage. Onto the next challenges Human skills are becoming more important , especially as AI changes how we work . Sure, technical skills will remain important. But I think people who can listen, relate to others, read a room, and recover gracefully from an uncomfortable moment will have a real advantage. Those are human skills that you can't fake by memorizing a script. So, I suggest doing the thing that scares you: get onstage, take a class, give the speech. You may sweat, and you may talk too fast. But you'll get through it — and learn something about how you show up for the people around you. I plan to keep testing that theory myself. My first stand-up comedy class starts on Tuesday. And I'm terrified. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: As youth sports booms, churches compete for American families' Sundays
events.summary: America's youth sports boom is quietly rewriting Sunday mornings, turning the family calendar into a competition between the pews and the playing fields. Why it matters: For generations, churches helped organize American family life around a shared weekly ritual. Youth sports are increasingly filling that role on Sundays — reshaping what families treat as sacred time. The U.S. has undergone one of its fastest religious shifts in modern history, marked by a rapid increase in the religiously unaffiliated and in church closures . Youth sports are one of the less visible forces driving that broader cultural change. As it's boomed into a multi-billion-dollar industry , more games are moving to Sundays, something less common a generation ago. "The idea of missing church for sports is just assumed," Linda Flanagan, author of " Take Back the Game : How Money and Mania Are Ruining Kids' Sports — and Why It Matters," tells Axios. "It's just not even a consideration anymore." By the numbers: Among parents of children ages 5-17, Sunday religious participation fell from 26.8% in 2003-07 to 16.7% in 2021-24, an Axios analysis of American Time Use Survey data found. Meanwhile, youth sports participation climbed to 58% in 2024, up from 53.8% in 2022 and marking a third consecutive annual increase, according to the Aspen Institute's Project Play . Another measure found 65% tried a sport at least once — the highest share in Sports & Fitness Industry Association data dating to at least 2012, the Aspen Institute's Project Play found. State of play: The youth-sports industrial complex is rapidly commercializing, fueled by private equity , massive tournament complexes and the normalization of out-of-state travel teams. Parents are increasingly treating sports not just as recreation, but as a primary identity and community anchor. How it works: Youth sports often start in local rec leagues, then move into club and travel teams that play weekend tournaments across a wider region. Across basketball, baseball, softball, volleyball and soccer, many weekend tournaments use Saturday for pool or preliminary play and Sunday for elimination rounds and championships. That fuels cities' and towns' investments in sports complexes built to draw traveling families and their hotel and restaurant spending. Zoom in: The average sports parent spends 3 hours, 23 minutes every day their child has a practice or game, including driving, attending activities, washing uniforms, preparing meals and communicating with coaches. Families are spending heavily, too: The average sports family spent an average of $1,016 on a child's primary sport in 2024, up 46% from 2019, Aspen found. What they're saying: Tim Morey, lead pastor at Life Covenant Church in Torrance, Calif., tells Axios that sports don't necessarily sever families from church, but they make attendance "more spotty" at times. "If we inadvertently teach our kids that sports (are) more important than weekly worship, then everything is more important than weekly worship." Yes, but: Religious institutions are attempting to adapt rather than surrender. Morey said some families "divide and conquer," sending one parent to church and the other to the field. Others have kids attend the first 10 minutes of service in their sports uniforms or stream services live from team hotels. Between the lines: Youth sports can create the same sense of community that mirrors what church did — to a point, Flanagan said. Parents form tight bonds because they spend so much time together, but competition for positions and playing time can also strain those relationships, Flanagan said. The bottom line: For generations, Sunday was about getting the family closer to heaven. For many families today, Sunday can also be about getting a daughter closer to UCLA's softball team.

events.title: HPE's networking boss says AI will handle all trouble tickets without humans in two years
events.summary: HPE is extending its AI-powered networking automation across its hybrid cloud portfolio. That news came from Rami Rahim, formerly CEO of Juniper Networks and now president and general manager of HPE's networking business, whom The Register met last week when he visited Australia. Rahim champions what HPE calls "self-driving networks" – AI-assisted monitoring and automated remediation, part of the broader field known as AIOps. The networking boss thinks AIOps will mean human network administrators soon won't need to work on any trouble tickets. "I think we're now at probably around 70 to 80 percent of all tickets don't require human intervention," Rahim said. "Within two to three years, we'll have no issues that require humans." He allows that hardware swaps will be the exception to that rule, but even for that job he thinks skilled network administrators shouldn't be involved. "The technology should, without your knowledge, order a new part. It comes in the mail and you don't need an IT person, just an intern can come and take this thing, attach it to where the failed device is, and everything else just happens automatically." Why you'll trust your career to a machine The Register asked why net admins should trust AIOps, given that following bad advice issued by a machine is unlikely to improve anyone's career prospects. Rahim responded by pointing out that self-driving taxis have quickly become widely accepted in the Bay Area, and that first-time riders draw on their past experience of adopting cars with automatic transmissions, then cars with cruise control, lane assist, and self-driving capabilities. Each successive experience of automation working safely, he suggested, imparts confidence to try new forms of automation. "And so what we do is we give the operators the ability to turn on actions, automated actions, feature by feature, and capability by capability," he said. Simple jobs like allowing AI to reboot a port on a switch is a fine place to start, he suggested. The metrics he uses to measure the success of automation are the number of tickets lodged about poor Wi-Fi performance and the speed with which they are fixed. "I think if you look at the number one trouble ticket that is filed in a typical enterprise environment, it is 'the Wi-Fi sucks.'" "Regardless of what the actual problem is – it could be an application going down, or a WAN issue, or a cloud provider issue – the experience is first felt through Wi-Fi and therefore it's as simple as 'The Wi-Fi sucks.'" Rahim thinks AI will figure out why Wi-Fi isn't at its best quicker than a human can do the job and also use agents to fix it faster. Those agents, he suggested, make automation even more important because they represent a new class of users that are dependent on networks. "We're quickly approaching a realm in which every enterprise has way more agents working than humans working, and they need a reliable network connection to do their work," he said. Organizations can't scale their human teams to a size at which they solve problems fast enough to manage all those connections. And because agents make so much traffic, buyers will need to add more networking hardware, which will further scale networks to a size no human can hope to manage alone. Only AI, Rahim believes, will make it possible to use AI. A 'networking company'? Of course he would say that, given that he claims HPE's networking portfolio and AI capabilities are second to none since it closed the acquisition of Juniper in July 2025. The Register covered that moment with the headline "HPE-Juniper deal closes, integration questions remain." Rahim assured us it's going swimmingly, pointing to the fact that HPE continues to sell Wi-Fi access points that started life as products from Aruba and Juniper – but that users can now drive them with management tools from either vendor. He proudly pointed to that becoming possible within 18 months of the acquisition closing, then made a sharp reference to certain other vendors taking far longer to achieve the same thing. The Register mentioned Cisco and Meraki: Rahim didn't show any signs of disagreement. Asked about HPE CEO Antonio Neri's statement on the company's last earnings call that "we are at the core becoming a networking company," Rahim emphasized networking's importance across workloads. "When you look at the AI datacenter, it's become as much a networking problem as it is a compute problem. So I just believe that networking is becoming more important in general for the industry, and it's certainly becoming more important for HPE as a company," he said. Which is why HPE is now bringing the self-driving network tech that started life at Juniper to the rest of its portfolio. "We've already, for example, integrated our network fabric management capabilities with OpsRamp, which is the observability software for the hybrid cloud stack," Rahim said. "So that would be an example of something that's now done. But more and more pieces will come along the way." ®

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Korean boffins use oxygen to stop crystals forming in the wrong places, aiming to get tech to commercial sector by 2030 TSMC taps GlobalFoundries to bolster US silicon interposer production in $2B deal 3 days ago Altman-backed Volantis reveals plan to vault the memory wall by baking photonics into AI accelerators 6 days ago America is planning more AI datacenters than its chip supply can fill 11 days ago Marvell pushes GlobalFoundries to light up wafer production 23 days ago ASML and TSMC want bigger masks for smaller chips September 8, 2026 Researchers have demonstrated a way to control where 2D semiconductor crystals begin growing, potentially addressing an obstacle to manufacturing next-generation chips at scale, according to a study published in Nature. The paper, " Spatially deterministic nucleation of 2D semiconductors by etching flux ," was authored by a team including researchers at KAIST and South Korean startup TDS Innovation and published on October 7. The technique uses an etching flux to suppress the formation of new crystals everywhere within each patterned growth region except at its geometric center. Two-dimensional materials are atomically thin rather than literally two-dimensional. Graphene, perhaps the best-known example, is a single layer of carbon atoms, but its lack of an intrinsic band gap makes it unsuitable for conventional switching transistors. Monolayers of some transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), such as molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂), do have a band gap and are being investigated as materials for future transistors and other nanoscale devices. When grown on a wafer, however, 2D semiconductor crystals typically start forming at random points, or "nucleation events occur stochastically at random sites within the growth region," as the paper puts it. This means that multiple crystals form, and as they grow and meet, they create boundaries between them that degrade electrical performance and make devices less uniform. To encourage a single crystal to form in each patterned region, the researchers developed what they call an etching-flux-mediated single-centred nucleation (EF-SCN) process. Oxygen released from an oxide barrier creates a lateral etching flux that suppresses nucleation except at the pattern's geometric center. The researchers used the process to build working field-effect transistors (FETs), the basic building blocks of modern chips. They reported higher charge-carrier mobility – a measure of how readily charge moves through the material – than previously reported for selectively grown MoS₂ transistors. In a separate test across a two-centimeter substrate, the process produced single crystals at 397 of 400 patterned sites – a yield of 99.3 percent. That is promising for scaling up, although it is not yet a demonstration of commercial chip production. Paper co-author Kibum Kang is co-CEO of TDS Innovation, which develops equipment and materials for 2D semiconductor devices. The firm says stacking 2D semiconductor devices on silicon chips could bring logic and memory closer together, fitting more functions into a given area and reducing the time and energy spent moving data between them. Two-dimensional semiconductor materials are also being investigated for CFETs (complementary field-effect transistors), which stack n-type and p-type transistors vertically rather than placing them side by side. This kind of 3D stacking has been shown off by IBM and Intel . "Building on this ability to control where crystal growth begins, we will form high-quality 2D single crystals uniformly where we want them and develop it into a next-generation semiconductor process that brings logic and memory closer together," Kang states. The paper doesn't say when we can expect to see 2D semiconductors made this way in production chips, TDS's Jony Jung told us: "We are aiming to enable commercial use of 2D semiconductors around 2030.

events.title: Musk vows affordable Starlink in India days before Ambani’s record Jio IPO
events.summary: Elon Musk has previously accused India of stalling Starlink’s entrance into the country’s market. Musk said Starlink will be priced affordably in India to challenge Reliance Jio, as Jio’s parent prepares for India’s biggest-ever IPO. He said competition would help Indian users, while Ambani’s profits would fall. He did not give prices, but noted India’s data costs are already very low. Musk accused Modi’s government and Ambani of delaying Starlink’s entry. India denied bias, saying Starlink and Jio satellite ventures still await final security clearance. BENGALURU, India – Elon Musk said he would price Starlink’s satellite internet service affordably in India to take on Mukesh Ambani’s low-cost Reliance Jio, escalating his attacks on the rival billionaire days before Jio’s parent launches India’s largest-ever initial public offering. Jio Platforms, which owns the telecom arm, is targeting a valuation of US$106 billion ( S$135.62 billion ) in the offering. Much like SpaceX-owned Starlink , Jio’s own satellite venture is also awaiting final security clearance to launch. Cheap data is the playbook that built Jio in India, and the one Musk has used in markets like Kenya to unsettle local telecom players. SpaceX now plans to enter the mobile carrier market itself, starting in the US. Musk did not specify prices for India, where mobile data costs about eight cents per gigabyte, among the lowest in the world. “Obviously, if Starlink is too expensive in India, no one will buy it, so SpaceX will need to make pricing affordable,” he said in a post on his social media platform X on Oct 10 . “The reality is that competition would greatly benefit the average citizen in India by giving them more choices, as it always does. Ambani’s profits will be lower, but he is not going out of business,” Musk added. The billionaire’s remarks were the latest in a series of X posts where he accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government and Ambani of stalling Starlink’s entry into one of the world’s biggest internet markets to favour market leader Jio . The posts have marked a sharp turn for Musk, who has long enjoyed a warm public rapport with Modi. India’s government has denied any bias in its approval process, noting that the three satellite ventures seeking to launch, including Starlink’s and Jio’s, are all awaiting final security clearance. Late on Oct 9 , Musk taunted Ambani directly, addressing him as “Prime Minister Ambani” and asking whether he would “consider allowing Starlink to compete”. Reliance has not responded to requests for comment on Musk’s remarks. REUTERS

events.title: Saudi Arabia presses on with global energy summit after deadly Riyadh airport attack
events.summary: Saudi Arabia pressed ahead with a major gathering of global energy ministers and industry executives on Sunday, hours after an attack by Yemen's Houthis on Riyadh's international airport killed 12 people and injured 309. The International Energy Forum's 17th ministerial meeting, hosted by Saudi Arabia and co-hosted by Italy and Nigeria, is being held alongside the WPC Energy Congress, bringing together policymakers and industry leaders. Media access to the ministerial meeting will be restricted, with only journalists invited directly by the IEF permitted to cover the opening remarks, according to a Saudi Energy Ministry spokeswoman. “As you are aware, the ministerial plenary will be held behind closed doors,” she said. No live broadcast pool arrangements were in place, she added. The event is proceeding despite mounting security concerns after repeated attacks on King Khalid International Airport , which have forced airlines to cancel flights and complicated travel arrangements for delegates. Italian Energy Minister Gilberto Pichetto Fratin said on Friday that he would participate in the IEF meeting by video link rather than travel to Riyadh. The WPC Energy Congress, which runs from Sunday until Thursday, is also proceeding as scheduled. Organisers have directed delegates to alternative routes into the Saudi capital, including by road from Dammam on the kingdom's east coast. A projectile landed near King Fahd Airport in Dammam on Saturday, a representative for the Saudi coalition said. Saturday's strike was the third on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport in a week and the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack, which killed four Saudis and eight foreign citizens, including one from the US. Two attacks on the airport this week killed four people and caused extensive damage to a Saudi commercial aircraft parked on the tarmac. The latest strike caused widespread disruption to aviation, with about 260 flights cancelled and another 219 delayed on Saturday, according to flight-tracking data from Flightradar24. The attacks have heightened security concerns, as Saudi Arabia seeks to maintain its calendar of high-profile international gatherings despite the war's growing regional spillover. Riyadh is scheduled to host the Future Investment Initiative from October 26 to 29, with organisers saying the event will proceed as planned, with additional security arrangements put in place.

events.title: ‘Halloweenmas’: how the spooky one-nighter turned into a month-long spectacular
events.summary: Welcome to Halloweenmas, weeks of themed fun and gifts – from costume parties to decorating trees – without the stress, rules or cost of Christmas The tree is up, the wreath is hanging on the front door and you’ve just opened your advent calendar . All told, it’s beginning to feel a lot like … Halloween . If it sounds like the stuff of nightmares then that’s the point: Britons are increasingly decorating their homes with ghoulish versions of Christmas traditions. Think of it as Halloweenmas. “What was traditionally a single-night celebration has turned into a month-long event mirroring many of Christmas’s traditions, but without the same level of expectation,” said Charlotte Broadbent, the UK general manager for the online wholesale platform Faire. Analysis of thousands of sales transactions on the platform revealed a huge rise in the number of Halloweenmas products available – up more than 500% in the past four years, from 425 in 2021 to 2,632 in 2025. The biggest areas of growth are trees, wreaths and ornaments. According to the budget retailer Wilko, Halloween trees are one of the biggest decorating trends of 2026. It said sales of artificial trees were 200% higher in September than a year ago. “There really aren’t any rules with a Halloween tree,” says Wilko. “You can go all-out or keep it simple with a smaller tree and a few spooky accessories.” The lack of rules is clear from social media, where the looks span student party – black tinsel tree shaped like a witch’s hat – to child-friendly cuteness. The arts and crafts retailer Hobbycraft’s website offers “five ways to decorate a twig tree” that include DIY spiderwebs made out of lolly sticks and felt pumpkins. Libby Ewart, who runs the online partyware and gift retailer The Box Party, has bought 40% more stock this year. “Houses are decorated earlier and with way more thought than before,” she said. “Also, this year it falls on a Saturday, so there has never been a better excuse for a party.” Emily Viberg, a senior retail analyst at the research group Mintel, said Halloween was “no longer just about costumes and sweets, it’s about a full season of engagement, gifting and themed activities”. Mintel’s research shows young Britons, in particular, see it as an opportunity to express themselves and experiment with fashion and makeup, with 16- to 34-year-olds over-indexing in purchases of fancy dress, cosmetics and decorations. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “Consumers are increasingly buying into the atmosphere and social moments Halloween creates,” Viberg said. “Younger adults are at the heart of this shift, transforming Halloween from a one-night celebration into a broader season of self-expression and experience-led spending.” Viberg said social media had accelerated this shift, with 40% of Halloween buyers using the platforms to buy products directly. “Viral costume trends, makeup tutorials, home decor inspiration and content tapping into popular culture are shaping consumer spending and helping to extend the season well beyond October,” she said. While some people might complain it is all over the top, Broadbent said: “What we’re seeing is people investing into Halloween as a reason to share quality time together ahead of Christmas, with lots of fun and creativity at its heart and without the need to spend big.”

events.title: Charities and businesses wrestle with diesel cost
events.summary: Cancer charity Daft as a Brush's Scott Jobson said funds raised by donations were being lost at the pump Published 11 October 2026, 07:23 BST Charities and businesses across the North East have said they are struggling with the rising cost of diesel. The average price of diesel has risen above £2 a litre in the UK for the first time, according to the RAC motoring group . Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil and refined products from the region, causing prices to surge worldwide. The North East cancer charity Daft as a Brush said it could no longer afford to upgrade its diesel vehicles to electric as they grappled with filling them up, whilst Teesside Minibus Hire said soaring prices were "not sustainable". Daft as a Brush, which provides cancer patients with transport to their hospital appointments, said it was shelling out £15,000 a month on diesel - £5,000 more than last year. The Newcastle-based charity - which drives 600,000 miles every year in its 30 vans - said it had planned on replacing them with electric vehicles, but now could not afford to because the money was being swallowed up at the pump. Volunteer driver Davey Hall said: "Before the big hikes, we used to maybe fill up and it would take £40-45. "Last week, it was £94 to fill the tank from half full." Head of income generation Scott Jobson said the money was being taken from funds raised by donations, and they were not eligible for any kind of discount. "At the pump, what you see is what we pay," he said. "It stunts our growth and development." In Middlesbrough, Teesside Minibus Hire director Billy Johnson said they often signed contracts with schools and businesses which could span multiple years - and were based on the cost of fuel when they were written. "We're not running at a loss yet, but we're running close it to it not being worthwhile or sustainable," he said. Johnson said they were having to pass the cost on to customers using services such as day hires, but because those customers were struggling with inflation themselves, they were not always prepared to pay the increased price. Instead, people were turning towards cheaper, unlicensed hire services which did not pay the same overheads, he said. Asked whether the business could survive if fuel prices did not drop, he said: "Long term, probably not." In May , the government announced it would extend a fuel duty (tax) freeze until the end of the year. It caps the tax at 5p per litre for petrol and diesel, and was introduced by the previous Conservative government after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine pushed prices up in 2022. The government has stressed that there is no cause for concern about potential diesel shortages over the Iran War and has said the country has a "diverse and resilient supply". events.title: ‘You have a meeting’: the calendar phishing scam growing exponentially
events.summary: Appointment or renewal reminder appears in victims’ calendar to lure them into logging in to fake Google, Microsoft or PayPal page Y ou’re preparing for the week ahead and take a look at your Google calendar. There’s an entry for a meeting that you must have completely forgotten. The note that pops up when you click on it says you’ll be reviewing a project and includes a link to more details. Confused, you follow it to find out more; the website you land on asks for logon details, and you provide them. Unfortunately, this was not a failure of your memory but a calendar phishing scam. You have handed your name and password to fraudsters who will sell it on in a batch with other people’s details, use it to break into your work email, or to persuade you that they are contacting you from your bank , or another institution. Luke Wescott, a threat detection engineer at Sublime Security, says calendar phishing is still relatively new but the company has seen “exponential growth”. The scam takes several forms, including a fake meeting, or a prompt to renew a service you pay for. In all, an entry appears in your electronic calendar. It ends up there after scammers send an email to your work, or personal address, with a calendar request. It doesn’t matter if you miss it, or it ends up in your spam folder. “Calendar apps, such as Google Calendar, can add invitations automatically without users even accepting them,” Wescott says. “So scammers don’t even need you to open an email.” And while you may not look twice at one from someone whose name you do not recognise, when something turns up in your calendar you may treat it differently. “It can create a borrowed credibility by showing up in the same place as your dentist appointment or a weekly 1:1 with your boss,” he says. Max Gannon, an intelligence analysis manager at the cybersecurity company Cofense, says some scammers are using legitimate platforms such as Zoom to send the invitations, making them look more convincing to the recipients, and to security software. “That makes it really hard to block,” he says. “Even AI-backed blockers struggle.” If you set up something to filter out invitations from these platforms, he says “that would also block any legitimate meeting invitations”. You will receive an email and see an entry in your calendar. The titles vary: examples seen by the Guardian include fake meetings, notifications of voicemail messages, and software renewals. Wescott says this is standard. “We typically see stuff like ‘New voicemail received’, ‘Payment receipt confirmation – $298.99’, ‘PayPal unusual activity’ warnings, ‘Your auto-payment will be processed within 24 hours’, and invitations to bid on a contract,” he says. Gannon says the invitation could look like it has come from within your company. “If they want to they could make it look like an internal invitation,” he says. “They can customise the content, may be adding the logo of your company.” The event description will typically contain a link, or a phone number. Wescott adds: “Either they want you to click a link to a fake login page like Microsoft, Google or PayPal, and enter your password, or to call a ‘support’ number to cancel a charge that never actually happened.” Until you click on this, or make a call, you are not compromised. The scammers do not have access to everything in your calendar – they are just trying to lure you to a place where you will hand over your details. As Wescott says, “it sounds familiar to typical phishing, it’s the same technique, just using a different delivery method”. Don’t panic if you see an unexpected meeting or reminder in your calendar. Treat it as you would an unexpected email and don’t click on the link. “My number one advice is people just need to be paranoid,” Gannon says. “It doesn’t matter if the invitation has come from someone two desks down, you’ve got to be suspicious of everything.” Wescott advises turning off automatic accepting. In Google Calendar you can go into settings and opt to only accept invitations from known senders, or when you have accepted. He adds: “Don’t click ‘decline’ on suspicious invites as it can tell the sender that your address is ‘live’. Instead, delete or report it as spam/junk.”

events.title: ‘We need less point scoring’: What party conference season taught us about UK climate action
events.summary: Tories plan to scrap low-carbon housebuilding, Greens back new nuclear reactors, and Labour put oil-drilling decisions on hold New homes could be built without solar panels, heat pumps and high-grade insulation, leading to higher household bills if the Conservative party wins the next general election. Kemi Badenoch made scrapping the future homes standard (FHS) one of the central planks of her bid to become the next prime minister at the Tory party conference this week. The announcement gained little attention compared to her inheritance tax bombshell , but it would have more far-reaching impacts on a greater number of people. The UK is in need of approximately 6m new homes and failing to equip them with efficient and low-carbon energy sources would doom households to higher bills for decades to come . The Tories quoted estimates of £30,000 for new-build houses, but the real cost is likely to be much less. Installing heat pumps, solar panels, batteries and insulation costs about £5,000 to £8,000 at the point of building – a figure estimated in 2024 when energy prices were much lower – to save more than £1,300 a year on bills , a saving likely to be substantially higher now. To retrofit homes after building would cost more than £20,000. Jan Rosenow, a professor of climate and energy policy at the University of Oxford, said: “Every home constructed today that runs on fossil fuels is a liability for the occupants. It also results in investor uncertainty and disrupts the supply chain that has been gearing up for this. What we need is less political point scoring and more long-term clarity.” Housebuilders have been among the biggest donors to the Conservative party , though this has fallen off in recent years. And according to the UK Green Building Council (UKGBC), the construction industry is well prepared for the FHS and will have to implement the policy before the next general election, so scrapping it is of little benefit. Simon McWhirter, the chief executive of UKGBC, said: “The housebuilding industry has spent years preparing for the introduction of the FHS, investing in skills, supply chains and new products. Reversing course would … risk slowing progress towards building the homes that people want and need.” Badenoch’s housebuilding plans are only part of a torching of the Tories’ green policies. Despite the crisis of sewage and farm pollution in the UK’s rivers and beaches, and the dramatic drop in wildlife, the party would abolish the Environment Agency and Natural England. The party’s U-turn on environmental issues and net zero was contrary to what voters wanted, said Robbie MacPherson, Kennedy scholar at Harvard University and the former head of the UK’s all-party parliamentary group on climate. “No winning political strategy, after years of fossil fuel-driven energy price spikes and a summer of climate breakdown, can include environmental regression. “Voters won’t reward politicians who want to kill employment opportunities, spurn economic growth and fail to keep Britain safe.” While the Conservatives spent their party conference burning their green credentials, an equally unexpected U-turn came from the Green party, which resolved last weekend to abandon its long-held opposition to nuclear power . Although the party would still prioritise renewable energy, Green MPs could now support new reactors, in recognition of their potential role in low-carbon generation. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Paul Dorfman, Bennett scholar at the University of Sussex and the chair of the Nuclear Consulting Group thinktank, said: “The Green party has taken a wrong turn on nuclear and this will lose them significant grassroot support and votes. “With 20-plus-year construction times, repeated delays and huge cost overruns, new nuclear diverts scarce resources from faster options. Renewables, storage, efficiency and stronger grids can deliver much more for every pound spent.” The battle between the Green party and the Labour party in this week’s Holborn and St Pancras byelection is likely to be repeated during the general election, where the Greens could be the main challengers in urban Labour strongholds. Responding to Sagal Abdi-Wali’s win for Labour, Greenpeace UK’s head of politics, Ami McCarthy, said: “Abdi-Wali has shown that voters are putting their trust in Labour, but the Green party increased its share of the vote and remains a serious challenger. As extreme heat becomes a regular threat and droughts extend for much of the year, concern about climate change is on the rise and cannot be ignored.” At Labour’s conference, Andy Burnham made only passing references to the climate, pollution crises and nature. He announced a publicly owned body to invest in the energy grid , alongside the privatised National Grid, which has been criticised for slow progress on upgrades.

events.title: UAE IPOs and credit markets primed for growth once war ends, Morgan Stanley executive says
events.summary: The UAE is expected to see a rebound in initial public offerings once the US-Iran conflict ends, and the country’s credit market is also set to boom, according to a senior Morgan Stanley executive. While there have been no listings in the UAE so far this year, the investment bank is bullish about the capital market prospects despite the uncertainty caused by the war. UAE companies raised a total of $1.1 billion through three IPOs in 2025, Dealogic data shows. “I think long term, as the conflicts get resolved or hits some level of stabilisation, you will definitely see a rebound in the IPO marketplace in the UAE,” Dan Simkowitz, co-president of Morgan Stanley told The National . “So, we are investing in and have high confidence in that. And we've been so impressed with the leadership on the sort of financial infrastructure in the country all the way around,” he said. The Iran war, which began on February 28, has led to increased uncertainty across the Middle East. After the US-Israeli bombing of Iran and Tehran’s retaliatory strikes on its Arab neighbours halted in early April, peace in the region has teetered on a fragile ceasefire. A report from the World Bank released last week said Gulf economies will contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downward revision of 5.7 percentage points from its April forecast. While the International Monetary Fund also anticipates that the Gulf economy will contract this year, the region is expected to face a strong recovery next year, conditional on the normalisation of shipping, the fund’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, said. "I think it [the war] clearly creates a slightly higher and hopefully temporary risk premium in the region, but not so much that it changes long-term investment perspectives and investor interest," Mr Simkowitz said. The investment bank's commitment to the region is "as strong as it's ever been". "We continue to be thinking about how to invest in growth. Our corporate clients, FDI clients, are still very focused on the demographics in the region, the potential for GDP growth, the diversification that is coming in the marketplace,” he added. There is extreme resilience that has been built in the region, the Morgan Stanley executive said. “There is also real capital strength in the region, and so as they need to either rebuild or redirect energy infrastructure, for example, there is the capability to do so. And … there is international capital ready to help do that,” he explained. Morgan Stanley, which is headquartered in the US and has more than $10 trillion in assets, has been present in the region for the past 20 years. It also opened a new office in Abu Dhabi in 2024. [The war] creates a higher and temporary risk premium, but not so much that it changes long-term investment perspectives and investor interest Dan Simkowitz, co-president of Morgan Stanley The bank currently has well over 100 employees in the region and it plans to expand its operations further. "We're going to stay very committed to growing that. I think wealth and asset management will be a part of that,” Mr Simkowitz said. The company's current pipeline of deals in the region is still active, he said. "Some element is on pause, and I think it would change a little bit in that people will have to re-underwrite maybe some of their resiliency supply chain and diversification. But I would argue most of it that was on is underway." Credit market boom The Morgan Stanley executive is also bullish about growth in credit markets in the UAE and across the region, with global trends also positive. Credit markets cover bonds, government debt, private credit and bank loans. Globally, asset managers and owners, including sovereign wealth funds and pension funds, are playing a key role in the credit market, he said. “The credit market has become more important because we're entering into a period where high capex manufacturing is back ... and in that context, you need to spend money, and you need to bridge this ‘build to revenue, build to profitability’ gap … and it is not just banks or governments.” Economic tailwinds from the AI buildout and "surprisingly enduring demand" have bolstered credit conditions in many major economies this year, S&P Global Ratings said in a report this month. But the positive momentum of overall credit stability seen over the past few years will become more difficult to sustain, it said. Heading into the fourth quarter, "risks are building amid the sharp rise in benchmark borrowing costs, including yields on government debt, as investors bet that major central banks have a complex challenge in their fight against inflation", the ratings agency said. In the UAE and the Gulf, the credit market “is coming, and I think that's encouraging”, Mr Simkowitz said. Gulf debt capital markets reached $1.2 trillion outstanding at the end of the first half of this year, according to Fitch Ratings. Even in mature markets like the US, the credit market is evolving and building, Mr Simkowitz said, adding that the growth of a fixed income market or a bond market is "incredibly important”. “Over the last several years, the conversations we've had throughout the Gulf with finance ministries, stock exchanges, and other leadership … has been skewing more and more towards bond markets and credit markets, as we've had some great success with ADX [Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange] and with other exchanges in the Gulf around equities, it's a natural progression,” he said. More than $100 billion has been raised in debt markets in the region this year, he said. "That is really important to continue to satisfy the growth, diversification and resiliency ambitions, it can't all be done with equity, and so you need some element of credit and bond markets.” AI, midterms and outlook The big economic theme is AI, which is "incredibly transformational", Mr Simkowitz said. "It's going to require a lot of capital today to drive an immense amount of productivity in the future. "Certainly, the UAE has been at the centre of that. events.title: Mary Chia admits disclosure lapses over CPF arrears at four subsidiaries after SGX queries
events.summary: Mary Chia Holdings has admitted that it failed to disclose CPF arrears and court proceedings involving four of its five subsidiaries. Mary Chia admitted it failed to disclose CPF arrears and court cases at four subsidiaries. SGX RegCo queried the Sept 11 filing, and the group blamed weak internal checks. The CPF Board revised total arrears to $103,727, down from about $153,000. The company said its chief executive knew of the notices, while independent directors learnt later. Mary Chia is reviewing reporting controls and plans instalment payments for the debts. The disclosure issue comes as it faces loan disputes, weak cash flow, and a planned $1 million share issue. SINGAPORE – Cash-strapped beauty and wellness group Mary Chia Holdings has admitted that it failed to disclose CPF arrears and court proceedings involving four of its five subsidiaries, despite its chief executive being aware of the court notices earlier on. The admission came in an Oct 9 response to queries from Singapore Exchange Regulation (SGX RegCo), which questioned why the four subsidiaries and their involvement in court proceedings were not disclosed in the company’s Sept 11 announcement, and when the company first became aware of these matters. Mary Chia’s Sept 11 announcement disclosed $50,208 in outstanding CPF contributions at one subsidiary but omitted arrears and court proceedings involving four others. All five subsidiaries’ cases had already been heard together on Sept 10, and the CEO knew of their court notices. The Catalist-listed company attributed this omission to shortcomings in its internal information consolidation and disclosure assessment processes, saying it failed to sufficiently consolidate information across its human resources, finance and management functions when preparing its Sept 11 announcement. The group said its earlier disclosure assessment had focused primarily on Mary Chia Beauty & Slimming Specialist, whose CPF arrears and court appearance were the subject of SGX RegCo’s initial query. It said it had not undertaken a comprehensive assessment of similar issues involving other group entities, resulting in the omission of four other subsidiaries from the announcement. These were Masego, Organica International Holdings, Spa Menu and Urban Homme Face & Body Studio for Men. Mary Chia also revealed that the outstanding CPF contributions across the five subsidiaries had been revised to $103,727 as at Oct 9, down from approximately $153,000 stated during a court hearing a day earlier. The revised figure was provided by the CPF Board following a reconciliation of outstanding contributions, taking into account payments made by the subsidiaries towards their arrears. The latest filing also shed light on when the group’s management and independent directors became aware of the CPF issues. Mary Chia said its CEO Ho Yow Ping and the group’s human resources manager were aware of the respective notices to attend court upon receiving them. Ho also attended an interview with the CPF Board on July 22 concerning the outstanding contributions of the five subsidiaries. The group’s independent directors, meanwhile, first became aware of CPF contribution discrepancies within the group at an internal audit meeting on May 25. At that meeting, management informed them of the discrepancies uncovered through an internal review, rectification reports submitted to the CPF Board and efforts to settle the arrears. However, the court notices and related proceedings were not brought to their attention. Mary Chia said its two current independent directors, Chay Yiowmin and Foo Say Tun, learnt of the outstanding contributions and court proceedings involving the four other subsidiaries only on Oct 8, when management updated the board following that day’s hearing. The company disclosed that nine separate notices to attend court had been issued by the CPF Board across the five subsidiaries. Although the matters were initially handled separately, the CPF Board requested in August that the court mentions be consolidated. All five companies subsequently appeared together in court on Sept 10 and Oct 8, with their cases adjourned to Nov 12. According to the CPF Board’s updated computation provided on Oct 9, Mary Chia Beauty & Slimming Specialist owed the largest amount, at $52,266, for outstanding contributions covering November 2025 to May. Organica International Holdings owed $25,248 for contributions covering November 2025 to May 2026, while Masego had $11,341 outstanding for the period from November 2025 to April. Urban Homme Face & Body Studio for Men owed $9,847 for contributions covering September 2025 to March, while Spa Menu had $5,025 outstanding for February. The periods refer only to months for which CPF contributions remain unpaid, rather than every month within the stated date ranges. The revised aggregate amount of $103,727 excludes late-payment interest and composition sums.

events.title: Shares of S’pore banks stabilise after recent decline; SGX cuts board lots: Markets this week
events.summary: In this column, ST’s business correspondents unpack the latest developments in Singapore and global markets during the week – and explain what they mean for investors. Analysts expect further volatility in bank shares amid earnings concerns and global bond market risks. SINGAPORE – Shares of Singapore’s three local banks stabilised at the end of the week after two consecutive sessions of losses , as investors took profit following their recent rally. UOB shares declined 0.29% to $39.96, taking their weekly losses to 7.71%, while OCBC shares closed flat at $29, having fallen 8.63% over the week. The volatility comes after Citi on Oct 7 cited softer than expected third-quarter earnings expectations for OCBC and downgraded the stock to “sell”. Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, said the continued weakness in Singapore bank shares appears to reflect profit-taking, concerns over earnings expectations and broader volatility in global bond markets. She said the downgrade also raised questions about whether market expectations for Singapore-dollar interest rates are too optimistic, and whether the banks can sustain their strong wealth-related income from the first half of 2026. Higher global bond yields are also adding pressure, as they could weigh on credit demand, bond portfolios and investor appetite for dividend stocks. Still, the recent declines are not expected to be the start of a prolonged downturn across the banking sector, given the lenders’ strong capital positions and dividend support. “In the near term, further volatility is possible as investors reassess earnings expectations and valuations,” said Chanana. Citi also cut its price target on shares of Singapore Exchange and placed it on a 90-day “negative catalyst watch”, according to an Oct 2 note. It maintained a “sell” rating. SGX closed the week at $20.73, down 0.86 per cent for the week and more than 16 per cent from one month ago. That could make the stock even more palatable for some investors, who will now find it more affordable to buy the pricier stocks on the local bourse, after the board lot size reduction for an initial 11 stocks kicked in on Oct 5. These are DBS, Great Eastern Holdings, Haw Par Corporation, Jardine Cycle & Carriage, Jardine Matheson Holdings, Keppel, OCBC, Prudential, SGX, UOB and Venture Corporation. These stocks accounted for 35% of trading activity on SGX in the first six months of 2026. For stocks priced between $10 and $100 a share, the minimum trading quantity was cut to 10 units from 100. For stocks trading on the bourse with a price above $100, the minimum trading size is now just one unit. SGX said the board lot size reductions will remain even if the stock prices fall below the $10 or $100 thresholds. According to the exchange, 10-share lots were traded substantially more frequently than the traditional 100-share lots on Oct 5, while around 55% of trades on the day were executed in trade sizes below the previous 100-share board lot. Among the 11 stocks, the three banks, SGX and Jardine Matheson saw the highest trades. IOI Properties and CapitaLand Investment are conducting exclusive due diligence for the proposed acquisition of One Raffles Place, after jointly submitting a 50-50 bid to owners OUE Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT) and UOB, the Malaysia developer said. If completed, the deal would broaden IOI’s exposure to the Downtown Core. One Raffles Place, which comprises two office towers of 62 and 38 storeys respectively, as well as a six-storey retail podium, also sits on an exceptionally long 841-year lease. The development has an indicative value of between $2.3 billion and $2.4 billion. IOI also confirmed that it is in the process of listing a REIT each in Malaysia and Singapore, and will also have a separate private fund through which it plans to monetise its assets and bring down its debt. IOI Central Boulevard Towers and the South Beach have been identified as seed assets for the fund. The Bursa Malaysia-listed company also told the media here that it is in talks to do a secondary listing on the SGX. The company on Oct 16 proposed issuing 100 million new shares at one cent each to four investors, which would allow it to raise $1 million to strengthen its financial position and fund overseas expansion plans. The move will bring in new investors but significantly dilute the shareholdings of Mary Chia’s existing investors. Mary Chia expects to receive net proceeds of about $946,570 from the proposed share issue, after estimated expenses of about $53,430. Of the amount raised, $750,000, or 79.2%, will be used for working capital, including manpower costs, professional fees, compliance and continuing listing expenses, and administrative and head office costs, the company said. The remaining $196,570, or 20.8 per cent, will fund the expansion of its operations in China and Thailand.

events.title: The Inside Brief: Menzies chief on aviation’s recovery and a lifetime of navigating crises
events.summary: When you look out of the aircraft window on the apron, the people turning your flight around probably work for Menzies . Its chief executive, Hassan El Houry, manages 65,000 of them across 65 countries and joined me for the launch edition of season two of The Inside Brief . This was days after the security incident on flydubai flight FZ1073 , which diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia on September 30 and is now under investigation by UAE authorities. He said the industry's next task is clear. “Airlines need to reinstall confidence in the general public,” he said. What most people do not know, he explained, is how thoroughly staff are screened. “After September 11, airports and airlines introduced an array of security measures for passengers,” Mr El Houry said. “While there are security measures for people that work at airports and airlines, they’re not so much in the spotlight like taking off your shoes and your belt.” That is about to change. “I think what we’ll end up seeing is that a lot of the security measures that are applied to pilots, to cabin crew, to our staff, to airport staff ... will come to the spotlight because it is quite thorough actually.” Every Menzies employee is background-checked and passes through “the same security measures that a passenger does”. And no new bill is coming. “All those security measures are already there,” he said. The bigger pressure is cost. Impact of a deal on the Strait of Hormuz Jet fuel has risen by 50 per cent or more since the war began, and ticket prices are “two, three, four times more expensive than they were pre-crisis”, Mr El Houry said. Asked whether fuel prices would fall straight away if a lasting peace reopens the Strait of Hormuz, he replied: “Every time there’s been an aviation crisis, we’ve recovered fairly quickly”. After September 11, “it was just a year and a half or two years, and aviation recovered”. Covid-19, the longest crisis, took “about three and a half years”, he said. “When there is some sort of peace and more clarity, I think we’ll recover fairly quickly.” The reason is demand. “Every airline that I’ve been talking to has been telling us that there isn’t a demand problem," he said. “Passengers are still flying. There’s a cost problem.” About five billion passengers will fly this year. “Five billion, that’s a record,” Mr El Houry said. Yet airline profits are expected to halve, from $50 billion last year “to about 25 billion this year”. ‘Quitting is permanent’ Mr El Houry learnt about risk early. His privileged childhood in Kuwait ended with the Iraqi invasion in 1990. “We were made refugees literally overnight,” he said. The family drove to Baghdad, then Amman, and spent two years in Cyprus. “At any moment you can have a black swan event. You can have a binary event from one to zero literally overnight, and you just have to be resilient enough to overcome it.” Compulsory military service in Lebanon followed. “I would spend 10, 12, 14 hours a day on my feet, and the one idea that kept going through my mind was the pain, the discomfort is temporary, but quitting is permanent.” His tolerance for complaining today? “It’s very low. It’s very low.” The fork in the road Wharton had been his dream since he was 19. It taught him to ask when he does not know. “You have to be humble. You’re not expected to know everything about everything.” Then came the choice: a New York investment bank, with the draw of “walking down Wall Street every day, going up to the 50th floor”, or Agility in Kuwait. “It wasn’t a cash decision,” he said. He chose Agility. “It was probably one of the best decisions I’ve made in my life.” At 28, he was running National Aviation Services, with 200 employees in one country. “Leadership is not a right that you have. You have to earn it.” Today, the combined business is the largest of its kind in the world, and Mr El Houry has the Gulf in his sights. “We don’t need to IPO,” he said. “The barriers to entry in the region are pretty high, but our resolve is much higher.” The Inside Brief with Manus Cranny is available on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Spotify and other major platforms.

events.title: Hawkish sentiment returns to IMF and World Bank meetings
events.summary: The world’s finance ministers and central bankers are set to gather for this year’s IMF and World Bank annual meetings as a new set of inflationary drivers descends on the global economy. This year, representatives from the IMF and World Bank member countries will meet in Bangkok, Thailand, from Monday. The meetings are typically held in Washington for two consecutive years and in another member country every third year. The 2029 annual meetings will be held in Abu Dhabi . During the meetings, the Bretton Woods institutions’ board of governors hold discussions on how international monetary issues should be addressed, while other talks are held on emerging economic trends and regional programmes. This year's meetings come amid a renewed threat of inflation. Supply disruptions from the Iran war are pushing up energy prices, with the Strait of Hormuz’s prolonged partial closure driving the price for Brent crude roughly 30 per cent higher than prewar levels. The expansion of artificial intelligence is placing additional pressure on electricity demand, and the massive debt issuance it requires partially accounts for the recent rise in bond yields , also driven by the US national debt reaching $40 trillion. The global economy is still grappling with the inflationary after-effects of the Covid-19 pandemic and Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Inflation has remained above 2 per cent in the US for more than five years. “While this rise in inflation pales in comparison with what we saw in the immediate wake of the pandemic, it is large enough to be of real concern to central banks, many of whom hadn't wrestled inflation back to its target before this episode had begun,” Karen Dynan, non-resident senior fellow at the Peterson Institute, said during a round-table discussion on Tuesday in Washington. Speaking in Singapore on Tuesday, IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva said the environment was right for most countries to adopt a “prudently hawkish” posture. The US Federal Reserve , the world’s most influential central bank, entered a new tightening cycle in September after it raised interest rates by a quarter point. The European Central Bank and Bank of Japan have also recently raised rates due to rising inflation. The Bank of England is expected to hike rates next month. Meanwhile, US government borrowing costs have reached multi-decade highs. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury, a benchmark for global borrowing costs, recorded a 24-year high this week. Bond yields in Germany, the UK and Japan are also on the rise. Against this backdrop, Ms Georgieva suggested austerity was back on the menu for advanced economies. “After a succession of shocks where, each time, fiscal policy has had to step in to cushion the impact, populations have grown accustomed to state support. Some very tough political choices stare us in the face,” she said. Meeting the moment? The question persists whether the IMF and World Bank have done enough to support low-income and conflict-afflicted countries facing higher funding costs, slower growth and shrinking aid flows. “We are living a perfect storm at this moment, especially for low-income countries,” said Marina Zucker-Marques, a senior academic researcher at Boston University's Global Economic Governance Initiative. We are living a perfect storm at this moment, especially for low-income countries Senior academic researcher at Boston University's Global Economic Governance Initiative Since the Iran war broke out at the end of February, the World Bank has pledged up to $60 billion in financing to help countries absorb the impact of the conflict's energy shock. The African Development Bank Group has launched a $5.1 billion framework to offset the impact of the war's energy and fertiliser crisis on the continent. The Asian Development Bank said it is mobilising $4 billion in financing to help countries withstand the war's impact. The IMF last week said it would provide non-financial support to war-torn Yemen, and reached a staff-level agreement with Pakistan that would unlock $1.21 billion for the country that is dependent on Gulf energy imports. Bangladesh has also requested a programme due to the war's impact. “The international financial institutions are weathering these crises remarkably well compared to other multilaterals,” Rachel Glennerster, president of the Centre for Global Development, said during a webinar. However, Ms Zucker-Marques questioned how eager low-income countries might be for more funding from the IMF, citing the fund's conditionality for programmes. Ms Georgieva said in April that the fund expected at least a dozen countries, including several in sub-Saharan Africa, to seek new loan programmes to respond to the war's impact on energy prices and supply chain disruptions. The US central bank's new tightening cycle is also expected to lead to higher borrowing costs for low-income countries seeking loans. The Federal Reserve's rate-setting activity directly influences borrowing costs from the IMF, World Bank and other multi-development banks. Traders anticipate the Fed will raise interest rates three more times by July 2027, according to CME Group data. “A lot of people are talking about the bond yields, which is quite important for countries that have access to markets, but also we need to pay attention that the interest rate hike in the US is actually increasing the tide to all types of lending,” Ms Zucker-Marques said.

events.title: Nvidia discusses boosting Reflection investment, computing deal
events.summary: Nvidia has been using its financial might to cultivate the broader AI industry in recent months. Nvidia is in early talks to boost its stake in Reflection AI or give it computing power, but no deal terms have been agreed. Reflection AI launched its open-weight model Beam, aimed at business users and developers, and says it is cheaper than many rivals while matching strong reasoning results. The possible tie-up fits Nvidia's wider AI push and US efforts to back open-weight models against cheaper Chinese rivals, with President Donald Trump calling them possible global standards. Nvidia is in talks to boost its investment in Reflection AI or offer the start-up computing power, a move that would strengthen ties with a key developer of open-weight models, according to a person familiar with the matter. The discussions are at an early stage, and no terms have been reached, said the person, who asked not to be identified because the matter is private. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment, while Reflection declined to comment. The Financial Times previously reported on the talks, saying they could lead to an acquisition offer. Possible deal structures include an “acqui-hire”, in which Nvidia would hire staff and license technology, an agreement to provide the start-up with more chips, or an increase in Nvidia’s equity investment, the newspaper said. The start-up debuted its first open-weight model , Beam, earlier in October , pushing into a market where Chinese start-ups have a strong presence. With such software, developers release the model’s parameters or weights, allowing others to freely use and modify the technology. Beam is designed to perform well for business customers and developers on coding and AI agent tasks while costing less than many competitors’ products, Reflection said on Oct 5 . It said Beam scores comparably on advanced reasoning benchmarks to GLM-5.2, a flagship open model from China’s Z.AI. The start-up, which was founded by two former Google DeepMind researchers, has held talks to raise US$2.5 billion ( S$3.2 billion ) at a valuation of US$25 billion, the Wall Street Journal previously reported. Reflection has also struck billion-dollar deals with Elon Musk’s SpaceX and cloud provider Nebius Group NV to secure computing power to develop its models. A Reflection tie-up would add to a frenzy of transactions by Nvidia in recent months. The chipmaker, which is the world’s most valuable company, has used its financial might to cultivate the broader AI industry. The deals have included a US$13 billion agreement to buy AI model company Hugging Face in September and a roughly US$20 billion licensing pact with the chip startup Groq. Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang is also a major proponent of open-weight models. The hope is that US development of the technology could curb startups’ use of Chinese open-weight models, which are much cheaper to use than those from American companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, while not far behind in intelligence. The US government is also encouraging the development of such models. “We need to ensure America has leading open models founded on American values,” reads President Donald Trump’s July 2025 AI action plan. “Open-source and open-weight models could become global standards in some areas of business and in academic research worldwide.” BLOOMBERG

events.title: House Republican, invoking Reagan, moves to block Trump's Russia oil deal
events.summary: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed Saturday to force a House vote to block Russian oil purchases, challenging President Trump's diesel deal with President Vladimir Putin. Why it matters: Trump has touted the deal as a way to lower fuel prices, but it could also provide revenue for Russia's war in Ukraine. Driving the news: Fitzpatrick, co-chair of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, said he would introduce the "Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act" and force a vote through a discharge petition. "It will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly," Fitzpatrick wrote on X . Retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) tells Axios he has "already agreed" to sign the petition. Catch up quick: Trump said Friday Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to U.S. and global markets, with more shipments to follow. Energy analysts are skeptical the additional diesel will meaningfully lower prices. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal "not fair and not honest," telling Axios it amounted to a gift to Putin. Trump called Saturday for Ukraine to replace Zelensky with a leader willing to reach a deal with Russia. The White House has not yet responded to Axios' request for comment about Fitzpatrick's bill. The big picture: Fitzpatrick is the latest Republican lawmaker to break with Trump in a high-profile way, as the party fights to keep control of Congress amid mounting disapproval of the president. Zoom out: Fitzpatrick is turning to a tactic lawmakers have increasingly used to bypass Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.): a discharge petition, which requires 218 signatures to bring legislation up for a vote without House leadership's approval. Fitzpatrick and Bacon forced a House vote on Ukraine aid and Russia sanctions earlier this year; it passed the House but stalled in the Senate. Reality check: Fitzpatrick has little time to pass the bill before this Congress ends in January. The House isn't scheduled to vote again until after the Nov. 3 midterm. Any legislation that passes the House would still need Senate approval and could face Trump's veto pen. What they're saying: Another House Republican, speaking anonymously to offer their candid thoughts, tells Axios: "Being that Congress won't be in session for another four weeks, any prudent lawmaker would probably not make a commitment to this prematurely." One House Democrat tells Axios that they will personally sign the petition and that "most" of their colleagues probably would as well, but unanimous support from Democrats is not guaranteed. "Leadership may not want people to help him," the Democrat said, though they added that may change after the midterms. Ben Geman contributed.

events.title: Attacks on Riyadh threaten Saudi confidence
events.summary: The News Several people were wounded in another likely Houthi attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday, the third strike this week on the gateway to Saudi Arabia’s capital. Earlier attacks killed four people. Flights were canceled or diverted, and airport operations were suspended. Hours of silence and speculation in the aftermath added to a sense of fear in Saudi Arabia and across the region. Rumors of injuries circulated in the afternoon, flights were canceled, Canada’s embassy warned citizens to avoid the airport at 5:34 p.m. The US followed at 8:03 p.m. Al Arabiya TV, which usually switches to breaking news if firecrackers are heard in other countries, was airing reruns. Saudi authorities finally acknowledged the incident at 8:34 p.m. There are definitely security considerations to withhold information during an attack. But the insistence on projecting calm is starting to backfire. Firms in Riyadh were telling their employees to work from home tomorrow, and people have been spooked for weeks. Since the US-Iran war began on Feb 28, Gulf governments have restricted media coverage and criminalized social media posts, even as everyone living here could see and hear explosions themselves. For months, Riyadh seemed relatively insulated from the war (sorry, “conflict,” as many officials in the region prefer to call it). Its airport remained open as travelers fled attacks elsewhere in the Gulf, and Saudis rallied around the flag, deeming any expressions of concern as unpatriotic. The messaging also seemed coordinated, with official statements followed by a flood of pledges of allegiance on social media. Now this confidence appears to be fraying. And in a war that is as much about economics as explosives, this may be the vulnerability that the Houthis, and Iran, are banking on. Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces had pushed back the Houthi advances around Bab el-Mandeb, the Red Sea shipping chokepoint this week. But in a similar move to the substantial losses that Iran had been dealt by the US and Israel earlier in the war, the Houthis chose asymmetric targets. The Iran-backed group has escalated attacks on Saudi oil facilities and civilian aviation, declaring Saudi airspace a military operations zone. The timing matters. Riyadh hosts the World Petroleum Congress this week, with CEOs from ExxonMobil, Shell, TotalEnergies, and BP expected, followed later this month by the Future Investment Initiative and Wall Street’s billionaire financiers. Organizers insist both events will proceed , according to Reuters. But it’s certain that some of these executives — or their boards — will have second thoughts. Some US officials who were planning to attend the events in Riyadh this month are reconsidering. At stake is not just some meetings, but a questioning of the kingdom’s pitch as a safe home for trillions in financial assets, data centers, and new industries. The repeated airport attacks provide a sense that a major escalation is close. President Donald Trump said on Saturday that the US may join strikes on the Houthis and will decide quickly. If that happens, it’s likely the region will remain the punching bag for any Houthi or Iranian response. Notable Ambulances and helicopters were sent to collect the wounded from Saturday’s attacks. The kingdom may be short on missile interceptors or are “struggling” to take out the Houthis’ rockets, The Wall Street Journal reported .
