events.title: Attending a programme in secondary school turned him into a serial entrepreneur at 28
events.summary: Xavier Tan was inspired by an entrepreneur programme run by Halogen Singapore and is now setting up businesses in London. SINGAPORE – Xavier Tan was 16 and had no clear idea of what his future would look like. But everything changed when his secondary school signed him up for the Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship programme. Tan, now 28, has started four companies, including a private members’ club he co-founded in London, the Rive Gauche Club London. “For a 16-year-old, that exposure was life-changing. It showed me that the world was much bigger than what I knew at the time, and more importantly, that I could build something of my own. “It gave me confidence, hunger and direction,” he recalled. The programme was run by Halogen Singapore, a non-profit organisation created to inspire youth and empower them to make a change in their community. Tan said: “Through the programme, I learnt how to put together a business proposal and present to industry partners, and visited corporate offices such as LinkedIn and Google. “I was later given the opportunity to represent Singapore in New York, where I presented in front of industry professionals from organisations such as Citi and EY.” When Tan returned from New York, he found himself bitten by the entrepreneurial bug. He started his first business – in shirt-printing – at age 17. A year later, he founded a fashion platform for young people to express themselves through art and design. In 2020, he moved to London to intern with a fashion public relations company. “That experience gave me my first real exposure to the pace, scale and possibilities of the London market,” he said. He has been based in the English capital since. In 2022, he started Enchante Communication, a London-based marketing and communications agency focused on supporting emerging brands with public relations, media visibility and brand positioning. Just a year later, he co-founded Rive Gauche Club London, which brought together his experience across marketing, events, hospitality and community-building. “Looking back, many of the opportunities I’ve pursued since then can be traced back to that first experience with the programme,” said Tan, an only child whose mother is a waitress and father works as a masseur. “It was where I first realised that entrepreneurship was not just about building businesses, but also about creating opportunities and shaping your own path.” In a full-circle moment, Tan has returned to Halogen as a speaker and mentor to pay it forward by helping other students develop themselves professionally. Tan also said that living and working abroad has taught him many life lessons. “One of the biggest lessons I have learnt is that you have to show up, regardless of whether the opportunity seems big or small. You have to show up with sincerity, consistency and a genuine interest in people,” he said . Tan is single and holds a diploma in product design and innovation from Ngee Ann Polytechnic. For me, growing money starts with investing in myself first. I believe you make better financial and business decisions when you are in the right state of mind. Beyond that, I invest in my businesses where I see potential for growth. That could mean improving the quality of our club events, increasing member engagement, hiring the right people, or building better systems so the company can operate more efficiently. When there is disposable income, I believe in taking a long-term and researched approach to financial investments, such as broad market funds like the S&P 500. I am quite cautious by nature. Q: What has been your biggest financial mistake? One of my biggest financial mistakes was not hiring quickly enough when I needed help. At the time, I was stubborn and thought I could do everything myself. In reality, it consumed a lot of my time, energy and creativity. It eventually led to burnout and limited how much I could grow the business. As a founder, your job is not to do everything yourself. Your job is to build the vision, lead the team and make sure the business is moving towards the next milestone. Q: What has been your best financial decision? My best financial decision was investing in skills and tools early, especially when I bought my first MacBook and taught myself design for my shirt-printing business. The investment was a stretch at the time, but it helped me secure client work and generate many times that amount over the years. Q: What were your growing-up years like? Growing up with limited resources shaped the way I look at money. It also taught me not to take opportunities for granted. I am ambitious, but I am also aware of the importance of financial discipline. I think when you grow up understanding what it feels like not to have much, you become very conscious of how money can create security, but also how it should be used with purpose. My childhood dream was to own a home – not necessarily a very grand one, but a place that felt safe.

( ABC News: Simon Amery ) NSW small businesses are looking at how to cover the cost of merchant fees after the ban on card payment surcharges took effect on October 1. Some owners have increased the price of items, while others have opted to absorb the cost. The consumer watchdog says businesses have the option of offering "discounts to consumers, who pay using a particular payment method, such as cash or PayID." Small businesses across New South Wales are grappling with how they will cover the cost of merchant fees. The Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) last week introduced a ban on business owners adding extra fees for credit or debit card payments on EFTPOS, Mastercard, Visa and American Express. The changes, according to the RBA, are in the "public interest", and designed to make the system more transparent and less confusing for both businesses and customers. The Reserve Bank of Australia says the changes are in the "public interest". ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) Sydney cafe owner Philip Barbaro said he had been forced to put prices up for some items, as his fees to the bank must still be paid for the use of cards. Mr Barbaro said the cafe business was tough in the Sydney market. "In my very competitive market in the city we have not touched the price of our coffee, but there were other items on the menu we had to increase this week, to offset the bank surcharge." Specialist baker and owner of the Jamaican Patty Bakehouse in Sydney's inner west, Chris Skuce, said he opened his shop a year ago as a nod to his Jamaican heritage. Mr Skuce says he will, at some stage, have to increase prices. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) Mr Skuce said he had been absorbing the cost of the bank fee in order to keep making the patties that were part of his childhood. "I haven't passed the cost on yet, but I will increase my prices at some stage probably in the new year," he said. Businesses 'need to cover their cost' Executive director of advocacy group Business Sydney, Paul Nicolaou, said people were struggling. "There have been rising interest rates, energy costs and the subsequent drop in discretionary spending affecting both households and business," he said. Price rises were now being introduced across the board, he added. "Business owners need to cover their costs, and unfortunately someone has to pay, and it is going to be the consumer." Coffee prices at some cafes rise by 10pc The unintended consequence of the Reserve Bank's card surcharge ban, which was intended to lower prices for consumers. Mr Nicolaou said the banks should be doing something about merchant fees, along with other payment platforms. "It is all electronic now, does it require a fee?" A spokesperson for the Australian Competition & Consumer Commission (ACCC) said that while businesses were able to build the fee into their pricing structure, they "must not mislead consumers about their prices or the reasons for any price changes". "Businesses can also offer discounts to consumers, who pay using a particular payment method, such as cash or PayID," the spokesperson added in a statement. "Where a business offers a discount for a particular payment method, this should be clearly disclosed before consumers choose to book, order or pay. "Businesses should not display only the discounted price or make the discounted price more prominent than the full price." Mr Barbaro said he was now looking at alternatives for customers. The removal of card payment surcharges took effect on October 1. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) Mr Barbaro said that could be an incentive. "There is the old saying that cash is king." Mr Skuce said, however, he was not looking at cash discounts. "Most people want to pay by card. It is just a hassle to handle cash." Mr Skuce said he did not see any net benefits to the consumer, as prices would increase. "I am befuddled with the change. Another hit to the bottom line and completely unnecessary in my opinion.

Apple revealed in a regulatory filing that it has reached an agreement to bring on team members and technology from personalized audio startup Huxe, in what’s commonly known as a reverse acqui-hire deal. As first reported in MacRumors , Apple disclosed to the European Commission that it has agreed to make employment offers to “certain employees of Huxe AI,” and to “receive a non-exclusive license to Huxe’s intellectual property rights.” Reverse acqui-hires emerged in recent years as a way for larger companies to hire key team members and license technology from startups without acquiring the startups outright — presumably allowing them to build up AI talent and tech without drawing as much antitrust scrutiny. (Confusingly, these deals have both been referred to as “reverse acqui-hires” and as plain old “acqui-hires.” ) In the case of Huxe, the startup was founded by developers who’d previously worked on the AI-generated podcast features in NotebookLM (recently renamed Gemini Notebook ). But Huxe announced on May 21 that it was shutting down , with the team posting on the Huxe website that the company would be removing its app from the Apple and Google stores, halting service, and deleting user data. “The team is moving on to new things, and we won’t be continuing development of the product,” the company said. It also thanked its users, saying, “The fact that you used it, told friends about it, sent us your suggestions and your ideas, made it feel like we built it together.” On June 9, shortly after Huxe’s announcement, Apple notified the European Commission of its deal. The filing does not say who received employment offers or if they accepted. Nor does it disclose anything about Apple’s plans. Possibly related: Huxe’s shutdown announcement came just a day after Spotify unveiled AI-powered podcast generation features of its own , so Apple could be hoping to add similar functionality to its Podcasts app. Tech executives seem enamored with the idea that personalized audio can replace regular podcasts (and maybe even parent-child interaction ?), though it’s not clear how many normal listeners agree. events.title: Why we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-rich | Jonathan Wilson
events.summary: Why we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-rich There’s little prospect of the model changing in a country that welcomes wealthy international owners with open arms F ootball, the world’s most popular sport, played by laws drawn up in London in 1863. The Premier League is the UK’s greatest soft power export. Premier League clubs are owned by a deputy prime minister of Abu Dhabi, the public investment fund of Saudi Arabia, a billionaire based in Monaco for tax reasons and a disappointing assortment of investors and private equity funds. And what, really, could be more British than that? Football truly is the national game. What the Manchester City case has exposed is just how difficult it is to regulate some of the richest and most powerful bodies in the world. While the wait for the verdict was frustrating, it was perhaps unavoidable given the possibility of legal objection at every turn when a leaked email from City’s in-house lawyer during Uefa’s action against the club had threatened to “ spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyers in the world to sue them for the next 10 years”. You didn’t get that with Albert Alexander Sr or Peter Swales. Football clubs in England and Wales still represent their communities, a relationship that may be strained in certain cases by the pressures of a globalised entertainment economy, but remains broadly true. Arsenal can feel like the club of choice for the nouveau fan from across the world, but the scenes of celebration when they ended their 22-year wait for the league title last season were an undeniable expression of local pride. The idea that there was ever an idyll when clubs were run by benevolent potentates for the good of those communities is romantic nonsense. But just because there was no golden age is not to say that the situation has always been as bleak as this. How did we get into a situation in which clubs are flotsam on the swirling currents of geopolitics and the world economy? Chelsea alone in the past four years have had a Russian oligarch forced to sell the club after falling under UK government sanctions, while a subsequent American co-owner has been forced to sell his minority stake after his insurance business came under federal investigation in the US. It’s a curious world in which the professional gamblers feel like a welcome breath of fresh air. The days of the local businessmen, the owners of mines, shipyards and factories, the hauliers and scrap-metal dealers, are gone. Some invested because they genuinely wanted to give back to their communities or liked the sport. Others did so because it was easier to fund a local football club than to improve working conditions or pay a proper wage. And some did so because, wrongly in most cases, they thought there may be money to be made. But no one should think those were days of purity. The decrepitude of English stadiums in the 1980s should caution anyone who thinks football was uncomplicatedly better then. The contradiction has always lain at the heart of English football. Clubs represent their communities and for fans support becomes an aspect of identity, a link to family and place and past, a role that has only become more significant as the influence of traditional institutions – the church, the workplace, the social club – has faded. Yet fans in England have almost never owned their clubs, which in part underlies the present crisis. That is not to say fan ownership is a panacea. There is much to be admired about the German 50+1 model which, to oversimplify, ensures outside investors can never own a majority of the club. But it has not prevented Bayern Munich from winning 13 of the past 14 Bundesliga titles. Some sort of recognition that a club is not just a business, that it has a community function might, though, have prevented the free-for-all that has led to this mess. At least when most owners were local, there was some understanding of what the club meant to its area, and a recognition that exploitation or neglect could have direct consequences. No owner wanted demonstrations at the directors’ entrance, or to be jeered as he drove the streets in his Rolls-Royce, or to have his car showroom boycotted because he put up ticket prices then sold a popular centre-forward at a knockdown price. The distant majority shareholder in his boardroom in Los Angeles, his penthouse in Monte Carlo or his luxury villa on the Gulf feels the sting less keenly. Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Richard Scudamore, the former chief executive of the Premier League who did more to shape the modern competition, for good and for ill, than any other individual, always spoke of being “neutral about ownership models”. Essentially that meant taking the money without worrying too much about where it came from. The current Premier League is the consequence: a gleaming, world-leading edifice, but built on what?

events.title: Captains offered $US100,000 a month in the Strait of Hormuz
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Shipping companies offering captains $US100k a month to transit Strait of Hormuz Before the US-Israel attacks on Iran, well over 100 commercial ships passed through the strait each day. ( Reuters ) Oil tanker captains in the Persian Gulf are being paid up to $US100,000 (about $143,000) a month to navigate the Strait of Hormuz, industry insiders and maritime unions say, as Iran and the United States continue to impose separate blockades of the critical waterway. Gulf oil producers are increasingly desperate to get their oil out of the region and onto market after a recent step-up in attacks from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on tankers attempting to pass the dangerous choke-point. The new wave of assaults on vessels followed reports last month that crude shipments were edging back toward prewar levels, indicating Middle Eastern oil exports were recovering. Facebook ads seen by the ABC show some seafarers in Asia have been offered double or triple their pay as well as "danger money" bonuses worth tens of thousands to work in the Gulf. The vast sums of money are being used to persuade them to stay on vessels and continue running the strait despite the risk of attack. "Right now [the captains] are getting paid crazy," Indian marine engineer Harshal Singh told a podcast in late September. "A ship captain usually get 15 lakh Rupees per month (about $22,000). Right now in Strait of Hormuz they can make 1 crore rupees (about $143,000) in a month." The commercial tankers struck as they transited the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks were "highly, highly targeted", according to marine traffic watchers. Captains receive pay increases while they are in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Oman, and again during each Hormuz transit, according to Indian union representatives. But the journeys come with substantial risk, with at least 24 seafarers killed in 100 confirmed incidents since the war began, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization. In this month alone, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) has recorded nine incidents of attacks on tankers within the Strait of Hormuz. For many shipowners, the risks are being outweighed by revenues reaching levels rarely seen in the industry's recent history. "They are offering [seafarers] double, sometimes even five times the wages they will get during the transit of Hormuz," Manoj Yadav, the general secretary of the Mumbai-based Forward Seamen's Union of India, told the ABC. In India, where the vast majority of the world's seafarers are from, the salary bump is a huge draw. But unions have warned seafarers are at risk of being exploited and some have very little choice in performing a job that could cost them their lives. The strait's significance has been in the spotlight since Iran placed an effective chokehold on the shipping route, used for 20 per cent of the world's oil and gas trade, at the end of February. After months of gridlock, the US responded by implementing its own blockade on Iranian shipments through the critical energy artery. Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war. ( Reuters ) Sailing into the Gulf, loading and coming out again now carries great risk. While the US intercepts vessels attempting to trade with Iran, the IRGC targets ships sailing in the strait and harasses them, including through drone overflights and surveillance, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center said last weekend. It means fewer operators are willing to make the voyage, and transit remains below typical prewar traffic levels, when more than 100 commercial vessels crossed the strait each day. "I think the issue is less [to do with] insurance and more availability of crews that are willing to make that hazardous transit because of a significant amount of attacks," former Australian naval officer Jennifer Parker told the ABC. An increasing number of ships have attempted to get around Iranian controls by taking the south corridor route, which hugs the Omani coast, rather than the north corridor route, which sails close to Iran. Ships navigating the strait also take "dark journeys" by travelling at night with their GPS signalling equipment switched off. Marine intelligence companies previously told the ABC some of these dark transits have occurred with the knowledge and permission of Iran via diplomatic-level negotiations. Others have not.

events.title: Richard Morecroft had a furry studio companion viewers never knew about
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Late veteran presenter Richard Morecroft's foster journey with grey-headed flying fox Archie Late veteran presenter Richard Morecroft is best known for his decades of news reading, but unbeknownst to viewers, he was sometimes joined at the desk by a furry companion. Morecroft, who died this week aged 70, was a familiar presence as an ABC 7PM NSW anchor, BTN presenter and host of Letters and Numbers on SBS. But if you were to peek under his shirt as he read particular news bulletins in late 1987, you would find another passion. Wrapped inside a handkerchief was a baby grey-headed flying fox. Morecroft adjusting Archie before presenting the NSW 7PM news bulletin. ( ABC News ) Archie was considered well-versed in current affairs. ( ABC News ) Morecroft originally thought it was a boy and named it Archie. "I think probably of its species, that little flying fox ... was probably the best educated in terms of knowledge of news and current affairs," he said in late December, 2001. "Thousands of people watching at home wouldn't have known that there was a small furry animal wrapped in a handkerchief stuffed inside my shirt." The presenter said the handkerchief was used to keep the pup warm. Morecroft fostered two-week-old Archie, who he believed belonged to the Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park colony, after completing a Wildlife Information and Rescue Service (WIRES) training course in the late 1980s. Archie and Morecroft recorded their journey together in a 30-minute Wildscreen episode with ABC TV's natural history unit, titled Raising Archie. "This is a young grey-headed flying fox which came from a colony not very far from Sydney," he explained during the program. "His mother died and so I'm the new foster parent for a few months. "What we're hoping is that eventually he will be able to rejoin the colony and get back into the wild." Morecroft encouraging Archie to fly. ( ABC News ) He said pups needed lots of attention. "They have to have nappies changed, their fur cleaned and be wrapped up as they would be in their mother's wings." At one point, Morecroft encouraged an older Archie to fly. The documentary also highlighted threats facing colonies, including overdevelopment and the impact of flying foxes raiding orchards. Morecroft also interviewed iconic naturalist, David Attenborough, with an older bat named Gollum. A letter Morecroft sent to his trainer in November 1987 reveals more about how he cared for Archie. "It's been a delight (and occasionally quite a challenge) to have the opportunity to raise a young flying fox," he wrote. "According to weight and forearm measurements (90 grams and 60 millimetres) a couple of days after receiving her, she must have been very young when orphaned. "However, she seems to be progressing well (now 107g and forearm 71mm) and is enjoying exercise sessions." Baby Archie, the grey-headed flying fox. ( ABC News ) He said Archie "took particular delight" in being groomed. "Warm, damp cotton buds are great for the armpits and the 'hip pits!'" the letter read. "And a soft baby's toothbrush grooming the fur produces either a relaxed ecstasy or a vigorous cooperative effort with tongue and one foot." John George, whose late wife Helen trained hundreds of people to care for native animals, including Morecroft, said the presenter was "totally committed". "She loved it, loved him and she could rely on him totally," he said. Morecroft was an active member of the wildlife rescue, as seen here with the founder Mikla Lewis (centre) at the 1991 Christmas party. ( Supplied: WIRES ) WIRES founder Mikla Lewis still remembers being surprised by Morecroft's call. "One day I picked up the phone and this voice on the other end said, 'Hello, I'm Richard Morecroft and I'd like to join'," she said. She said he was "really besotted" with Archie. WIRES bat unit coordinator Storm Stanford said bats these days did not stay with carers as long, and incubators were used for warmth to reduce disease risks. "Back when Richard was doing it, we didn't know about lyssavirus or, I think it just came in the year after or a few months after he was doing the caring," Ms Stanford said. Archie was fostered at two weeks old. ( ABC News ) She said the disease was spread by saliva through a cut or a bite, which could cause a fever, fatigue and seizures. There is a vaccine, but people are told not to handle bats, even while wearing gloves. Ms Stanford said caring for a pup could take at least four or five hours a day. Archie was eventually sent to a creche to socialise with other bats away from their carers, before being released back into the colony.

events.title: Decades-old exemption tweaked to give cruise ship workers more rights
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Cruise ship crews still vulnerable to exploitation as government announces updated protections A decades-old exemption to Australian labour law for cruise ships has been extended with some new protections for workers. ( ABC News: Jasper Wells ) A legal exemption for cruise ships from Australian labour law has been altered to allow some new protections for crew. Critics say the legal loophole that left them vulnerable shouldn't have existed in the first place and allows for worker exploitation. The exemption was due to expire at the end of the year but has been extended to 2028. The union that represents cruise ship workers has warned that the exploitation of staff will become "embedded" in the industry after the federal government extended a decades-old exemption that allowed cruise ships to circumvent Australian labour law. The government has announced new protections for cruise workers following an ABC News investigation that revealed allegations of shocking conditions among the crew on some Carnival Cruise vessels. It includes the ability to collectively bargain and make complaints to the maritime safety regulator. Punishing conditions face Carnival crew Passengers boarding a Carnival cruise ship are promised a world of endless food, relaxation and oceanic luxury. But for the crew, life is vastly different. But the government has decided to continue the practice of allowing cruise ships an exemption to labour laws, extending the long-standing exemption until 2028. The ABC revealed in August that workers were accusing the company of 12-hour work days for seven days a week, medical neglect, not providing safe drinking water and wages less than $3 an hour. Carnival denied the allegations. Transport Minister Catherine King called the allegations "horrifying". Catherine King said the new conditions on the exemption would help draw tourists as well as protect workers. ( ABC News ) In response to the investigation Australia's anti-slavery commissioner said: "I think some change in this area is long overdue." Exemption should never have existed: union Maritime Union of Australia national secretary Jake Field said the exemption should never have existed in the first place and did so at the expense of Australian jobs. Introduced in 1998, the exemption lets cruise ships avoid Australian labour law and instead follow the looser international Maritime Labour Convention. The new obligations are the first time cruise operators have had conditions attached to their exemption. Originally expiring at the end of this year, it was extended until 2028 with the new conditions that ship operators cannot restrict crews rights to collective bargaining, and complaints about working conditions must to be reported to the maritime regulator, the Australian Maritime Safety Authority. Under the new conditions, cruise operators can no longer restrict crews' rights to collective bargaining. The ABC has seen letters from Carnival that warned crew against the presence of Maritime Union of Australia representatives at ports and reminded staff that they were under no obligation to stop. Carnival corporation operates over 90 ships globally, with around 100,000 crew on their ships at any one time. ( ABC New: Pete Garnish ) Transport Minister Catherine King said in a statement that the changes would protect workers while supporting Australia's maritime industry. Carnival and Royal Caribbean Cruises did not comment when asked if they would begin bargaining with crews. Carnival said it was considering the details of the announcement. Carnival operates three ships full-time in Australia: Adventure, Encounter and Splendor. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) Regulator to have more oversight of complaints The changes also mean that all crew complaints regarding the Maritime Labor Convention must be reported to the Australian regulator. It is intended to give the government a better understanding of the types of complaints being made about conditions and how they are managed. The government has said it will be the last time the exemption is renewed and it is considering a review of the laws, the findings of which are not yet public. Carnival operates three ships full-time from Australia, with roughly 1,000 crew on each, mostly flown in from South-East Asian and African countries. In a previous statement to the ABC, Carnival rejected the allegations made by crew and said the maritime authority had carried out "surprise inspections of our three ships in recent weeks and cleared Carnival on each occasion". It said that the company followed international standards.

events.title: Anthropic's Claude AI submits a false tip on a Philadelphia unsolved homicide case
events.summary: An Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a false tip to Philadelphia police about an unsolved homicide case, authorities and Anthropic said NEW YORK -- An Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a false tip to a Philadelphia police website about an unsolved homicide case, authorities and Anthropic said. It's the latest example of AI models acting in unintended ways and manipulating government and other websites during tests. In a report Friday , Anthropic also disclosed a separate incident when its AI model submitted forms to an undisclosed government website instead of stopping before submission. The incident in Philadelphia occurred on July 18 when the AI model Claude Haiku 4.5 was tasked with generating and performing example tasks on randomly selected webpages, Anthropic said. Claude filled out a form on police site PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com indicating it might have information regarding an unsolved murder listed on the site. Philadelphia Police said in a statement they were unaware of the incident until Anthropic notified them on Wednesday. Then they found the submission in the website’s tip records and confirmed it was marked spam and never forwarded to police. There are rising concerns about AI companies’ unchecked AI agents meddling with everything from U.S. government websites to healthcare data. Critics have been calling for more regulation. In September, another AI company, OpenAI, disclosed six reports of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in artificial-intelligence models. events.summary: President Trump called Saturday for Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky with someone willing to make a deal with Russia to end the war. Why it matters: Trump's attack on Zelensky came after the Ukrainian president criticized his diesel deal with Russia and signals the most serious crisis between the two leaders since their February 2025 meeting exploded in front of cameras. Driving the news: Trump announced Friday he had reached a deal with Russia to lift sanctions to allow Russian diesel exports to the U.S. and the global energy market. Zelensky, who was surprised by the deal made behind Ukraine's back, attacked the move and told Axios it was "not fair and not honest" and was a "sign of weakness" by Trump and a "birthday gift" to Putin. A U.S. official told Axios later that Trump struck the diesel fuel deal after Zelensky ignored half a dozen U.S. requests to stop attacking Russian oil refineries. What he is saying: Trump said Zelensky could have reached a deal with Russia many times "but chooses not to." "I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal," Trump told reporters Saturday. "… And I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president." He said he asked Zelensky to stop attacking Russian oil refineries and claimed Zelensky's actions harmed American farmers. "He better damn well stop," Trump said.

events.title: Petra Power looks to modernize energy for data centers and defense vehicles
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. As AI gobbles up an ever larger amount of energy, the hunt is on for efficient and cost-effective power sources. One of the companies leading the charge is Petra Power . Petra, which was founded in 2017, sells solid oxide fuel cells — ceramic devices that convert fuel, like natural gas, into electric power without burning it. The company markets them as a more efficient and environmentally friendly way to operate data centers and large vehicles. Petra’s founder, Aaron Goodman, told TechCrunch that his company’s product has significantly lower fuel costs and emissions than traditional power sources, and that they have much less of a physical footprint, too, because they’re more compact and lightweight. The efficiency, and the cost savings that come with it, is what makes the fuel cells attractive. “Combustion takes fuel and creates explosions,” Goodman said, describing how traditional power generation works. “Those explosions create heat. That heat creates motion. The motion powers an electromotive force, which eventually creates electricity. It’s a lot of steps, and they all have so much loss in them that you end up with a really inefficient system.” Petra’s fuel cells skip most of these steps. “What fuel cells do is they take the electrons directly off of the fuel, so they strip the fuel of its electrons, which creates electricity,” he explained. “It’s one step, no loss, and subsequently, in theory, at least, they’re much, much more efficient.” As a result, companies that run off fuel cells stand to save a significant amount on fuel costs, Goodman said. Although it may offer an innovative product, the customer base is still emerging for Petra. Goodman said that his company is targeting two different types of customers: data centers and the Defense Department. Goodman doesn’t want to reveal specific agreements just yet, but said Petra is currently working with neoclouds and other infrastructure providers that were a few steps down from the hyperscaler crowd. The target for first deployment with these customers is 2028, with full-scale production for the company hopefully set for 2029, Goodman said. “Hyperscalers are an ICP [ideal customer profile] for us, and we talk a lot to them, but we don’t have anything firm with them yet,” said Goodman. “We’re still kind of working in that direction. Obviously, they’re the largest consumers of power. They’re the ones that we can make the biggest impact with, so that’s where we’d like to go.” The other customer — the government — is also still taking shape. The idea is that Petra’s fuel cells will be able to provide auxiliary power for land vehicles, meaning electricity for onboard equipment when the main engine is off. But Petra’s product has not actually deployed on a live vehicle yet, Goodman clarified. Instead, the fuel cells are in the testing phase, during which the government is deciding whether to move forward, he said. Petra is a small team — some 15 people — but the company is growing, Goodman said. Petra has so far received nearly $9 million in contracts from the Defense Department, and the hope is to scale that work significantly in the coming years, he said. Petra Power was selected for this year’s TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 200 , a group of 200 startups chosen for the program. events.title: Christa Pike left the hospital and returned to Tennessee prison after failed lethal injection
events.summary: Tennessee inmate Christa Pike was released from the hospital and is back in prison more than a week after she survived the state's attempt to execute her by lethal injection , her attorneys said Saturday. The big picture: The failed execution was unprecedented. Pike, 50, got two doses of the deadly drug pentobarbital on Sept. 30 and was still breathing. The state called an ambulance and Pike got life-saving care at a local hospital. Pike's attorneys said they believed she was "brain dead" and on life support. It shocked them and her doctors when she woke up and began talking earlier this week . What they're saying: Pike's attorneys said she had returned to Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she had been housed for decades. "She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," the attorneys said in a statement. "She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery." Catch up quick: Gov. Bill Lee ordered an independent review to determine how Pike was able to survive the attempted lethal injection. Another execution set for December was called off while that investigation plays out. Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.

events.title: JPMorgan makes bullish call in fixed income space, suggests it's a once in a generation opportunity
events.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management is making a bullish call on an underinvested market group: high-quality fixed income. Priya Misra, a portfolio manager at the firm, sees a once in a generation opportunity for investors. "You can actually take credit risk in the highest quality companies and still get [a] 6.5% [yield], Misra told CNBC's "ETF Edge" this week. "So, you actually don't have to go down in credit [quality]." She suggested the strategy is particularly well suited for investors concerned about having too much exposure to artificial intelligence stocks. "There's a huge AI exposure," Misra said. "What fixed income gives you is this diversified set of returns. It's not just an AI trade or a tech trade. You have the Treasury trade. You have credit outside of AI." Misra co-manages the JPMorgan Core Plus Bond Fund ETF (JCPB) . The fund has almost $16 billion in assets under management, with just over three-quarters of its holdings in BBB-rated debt and above, according to the firm's website as of Aug. 31. "We've actually been increasing some of the double-B [and] single-B exposure because there has been a widening in high yield spread," she said. "We like some investment grade. And now, we've started in the last few days to increase some duration as well, thinking we may be nearing the end of that rate move." The JPMorgan Core Plus Bond Fund ETF is down more than 5% so far this year as of Friday's close, according to FactSet. "You want to be looking bond by bond and sort of sector by sector to see where the macro and you have to do the bottom up as well to make sure that companies are not over levered," noted Misra, who's concerned about how higher rates could hurt the housing market. BondBloxx co-founder Joanna Gallegos is also advising investors to take advantage of "historically attractive" yields across debt markets. "You want to really consider getting some corporate debt into your portfolio," Gallegos said in the same interview. "It's really in the investor's best interest to start looking at the income that's back in fixed income. It can offset the volatility in your portfolio." Part of her bull case: Base rates are high, and they're stable. "The fundamentals of these corporations are so strong, and the economy continues to grow," added Gallegos. "We really think that's being lost in the narrative around Treasury rates." Her firm BondBloxx is known for fixed-income exchange-traded funds in sectors including Treasury, corporate, private credit and emerging markets. One of its funds includes the BondBloxx Private Credit CLO ETF (PCMM) . As of Friday's close, it's down 0.6% so far this year, according to FactSet.

events.title: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to Putin
events.summary: Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met in Alaska last year Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has condemned Donald Trump's announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel into the US. Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged", a position quickly backed by Ukraine's European allies. Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and a further one million after that. It is understood that the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen. Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that a further three million tonnes of Russian diesel would be delivered "within a short period", dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine. Putin later said that Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products, but his statement did not specify amounts. Zelensky said Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror". "We count on America's fair support for our defence of life, for our defence of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one," he wrote. He later pointed to deadly overnight strikes on Zaporizhzhia and Kyiv as Russia expressing "its thanks" for the agreement. Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers. Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices Published 1 day ago Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 15 people Published 23 hours ago Tim Armitage, an investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot, said the numbers mentioned by Trump were "relatively small". He said the first tranche equated to approximately 2.25 million barrels, and daily US consumption was around 3.8 million barrels, "so it won't make a material difference to pump prices in the US". "Granted, there are then two more releases to come, but it does appear to be a slightly desperate move by President Trump to try to lower inflation ahead of the midterms," he said. Paul Johnson, former director of the Institute of Fiscal Studies think tank and provost of The Queen's College, Oxford, said: "What would make a difference, of course, is sorting out what's happening with Iran. "Let's be clear, President Trump has created this problem himself," he told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg. "This is a problem not created because of Ukraine and Russia in terms of diesel prices at the moment, this is created by the war in the Middle East." The BBC has asked the White House what Russia will get from the US in return for the commitment. The agreement with Russia also opens Trump up to criticism from European allies and pro-Ukraine politicians in the US that the American president is now helping to fund Moscow's war machine. The EU's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said suspending sanctions "provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war", adding: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't." She said European foreign ministers intended to approve the biggest set of sanctions on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion on Monday. Meanwhile, a UK government spokesperson said its position "could not be clearer" and that it would continue working with international partners to support Ukraine and bring about sustained peace. "We will also maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by the UK, increasing the cost of Putin's aggression and supporting efforts to secure a just and lasting peace." Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war. That conflict, which began in February, has sent the cost of petrol and in particular diesel skyrocketing, which has soured his standing with the American public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation. Ukraine's President Volodymr Zelensky said Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror" The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September. Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel into the market.

events.title: Vance says Microsoft replaced laid-off workers with foreign hires. Here’s what the visa data shows
events.summary: The Trump administration suspended Microsoft, Adobe and six IT services firms from PERM, the Labor Department program that lets employers sponsor foreign workers for green cards. Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of replacing laid-off American workers with foreign hires. Data shows two-thirds of Microsoft's H-1B approvals went to people already working at the company. Amazon and Meta, the nation's two largest H-1B work visa sponsors, were not suspended. As the Trump administration announced Thursday that it suspended eight tech companies from sponsoring foreign workers for green cards, Vice President JD Vance singled out Microsoft , claiming it replaced the 6,000 workers it laid off in 2025 with people on H-1B work visas. The suspension of the Labor Department's PERM program for green cards, which grant permanent residency to immigrants, doesn't affect H-1Bs, which are temporary work permits, but H-1B approval data shows how heavily these companies rely on foreign workers. Data from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services' H-1B Employer Data Hub also shows that Amazon and Meta were the biggest sponsors of H-1B visas, and neither was suspended. The crackdown went beyond tech. At the same news conference Thursday, the Labor Department's inspector general, Anthony D'Esposito, announced an investigation into alleged J-1 visa fraud involving nine major American universities. Trump supporters have long argued that these programs undercut American workers by incentivizing employers to hire from abroad. All eight suspended companies rank among the nation's top 50 H-1B sponsors. Most are IT services and consulting firms. Adobe is the smallest, at No. 45. The biggest sponsor wasn't suspended Amazon, with 19,178 H-1B approvals in fiscal 2025, and Meta, with 6,294, were the top two sponsors, and neither was suspended. Microsoft was a close third with 6,258, according to the USCIS data hub. Microsoft out-sponsored Amazon for years. Amazon passed Microsoft in 2017 and now gets about three times as many approvals. The numbers cut both ways. Microsoft did receive more than 6,000 H-1B approvals last year, as Vance said. But 2 in 3 went to people already working there. Amazon, which brought in nearly four times as many H-1B workers new to the company, was not on the suspension list.

events.title: How de-extincting dire wolves and woolly mammoths may extend human life
events.summary: To join the CNBC Technology Executive Council, go to cnbccouncils.com/tec Colossal Biosciences is on a mission to revive extinct species. The company has created three genetically engineered dire wolf pups and is working on the woolly mammoth. The science of de-extinction has implications for the environment, medicine and research on evolution. Colossal Biosciences' efforts to bring back extinct animals like the woolly mammoth and dire wolves have drawn comparisons to Jurassic Park. CEO and co-founder Ben Lamm told CNBC's Julia Boorstin at the CNBC AI Forum last week that he understands those comparisons. "I think anyone that saw Jurassic Park in the 90s and didn't say it was cool, like I don't think they're probably very fun at parties," Lamm joked. "But yes, I saw the movies. I love them. They entertained us. They scared us." However, Lamm said, "I constantly have to remind people on X that, you know, they were movies," he said. "I don't think Jurassic Park had any conservation or general human benefit models to it, so we've tried to take a slightly different perspective." Since viable dinosaur DNA is no longer available, bringing back dinosaurs is, in fact, impossible. But what is underway at Colossal, besides the dire wolf and woolly mammoth projects, is work to genetically engineer the dodo bird, the Tasmanian tiger, and a giant bird called a moa, among others. "It's highly likely in the next coming year or two, people will continue to see us deliver extinct species back to Earth, and we could even have more dire wolves, too," Lamm told Boorstin. The process of creating the wolf pups involved taking genetic material from a skull and a tooth that were tens of hundreds of years old. Using AI models, Colossal used the ancient DNA to reconstruct the dire wolf genome and map it to its closest living relative, the gray wolf. The team then created embryos by editing the cells of modern gray wolves. Three pups, named Romulus, Remus, and Khaleesi, have been born to domestic dogs used as surrogate mothers. Skeptics, Boorstin pointed out, say that they didn't really de-extinct a dire wolf, rather, they created a genetically modified gray wolf. Lamm called this a "semantic argument" that "misses the forest for the trees." "Gray wolves are just genetically modified dire wolves. They were just done by nature or God or however you want to classify it," he said. Colossal is undertaking a similar process in their woolly mammoth project – that involves genetically modifying an Asian elephant. Lamm told Time in August that the company is aiming to have a woolly mammoth birth in the 2030s. "We call it a woolly mammoth," he said. "Because if it looks like a duck, it quacks like a duck, it serves ecological functions of a duck, it's a duck, in our perspective." Lamm became interested in this work after a 2019 meeting with renowned Harvard geneticist George Church, who Lamm called "arguably the father of synthetic biology." Church, who initiated the Personal Genome Project, had been dreaming about bringing back the woolly mammoth for decades, he told CNBC in 2021. However, the vision to revive animals like the woolly mammoth goes far beyond creating a real-life Jurassic Park with previously extinct creatures. "[Church] had this vision that we could leverage CRISPR and all these tools and technologies to bring back extinct species, use some of those technologies for human healthcare, and then build this programmable life model that we could apply to so many different use cases on Earth," Lamm said. Those use cases include those aforementioned conservation-focused benefits that de-extinction promises. For example, the engineered woolly mammoths could help fight climate change by stomping down snow cover in high-altitude arctic regions, which keeps soil frozen, and knocking down trees, thereby converting heat-absorbing forests into grasslands. But the processes around de-extinction are also opening new doors in genome engineering and developmental biology, Lamm said. That could have implications on "everything from microbes to plastic in the oceans to gene therapies and targeted delivery for humans to eradicating genetic diseases," he said. Lamm theorized that these efforts around DNA synthesis could even lead to developing crops or trees that grow faster. "We're pushing the bounds of DNA synthesis to synthesize the largest cargos of DNA," he said. "That will be massively transformative for how we think about programmable life." A company spun off from Colossal, called Astromech, is pushing into what Lamm called "convergent evolution," studying what causes species that are similar in nearly every way to have different immunities or other health issues, such as why elephants get cancer at a fraction of the rate humans do. That research could be leveraged to solve human healthcare challengers or pandemic responses, Lamm said. Astromech was valued at $2 billion in March, according to D Magazine .

events.title: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished. Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps. It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls. Comma is free to start and open source. Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future. The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription. Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations. One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally. Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background. Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account.

events.title: United Auto Workers president Shawn Fain easily wins re-election
events.summary: Fain was dogged by investigation but still decisively beat challenger Rich Boyer, who received just 13% of vote The president of the United Auto Workers, Shawn Fain, has easily won his re-election bid after an campaign period marred by accusations of corruption and election interference. The union’s election of leadership for a four-year term began with mail-in ballots being sent out in late August 2026, with vote tabulating commencing on 6 October. Fain won with over 68% of the vote as of Friday evening, with additional 13 candidates on his slate, United UAW, winning their elections. The closest opponent to Fain, Rich Boyer, received just over 13% of the vote. “The membership has spoken. UAW members are united and want us to keep fighting and building on what we’ve done,” said Shawn Fain in a statement on his re-election win, citing upcoming contract negotiations at John Deere, Volvo and General Dynamics Land Systems in 2027, and the big three automaker contracts expiring on May Day in 2028. “These results are about taking on corporate America and reversing the worst out-of-control wealth inequality in America’s history,” added Fain. “We are fighting for the entire working class, whether that’s at the bargaining table, organizing new members or in the political arena.” In July 2026, the Department of Justice announced it was investigating Fain over allegations he pressured Boyer, another union official, to provide benefits to his fiancee and sister and then retaliated against him when Broyer refused to cooperate. Fain denied the allegations and characterized them as an attempt to interfere in the election. Fain won his first election to serve as the union’s president as a reform candidate in March 2023. He has clashed with the union’s independent monitor, Neil Barofsky, claiming the monitor was weaponized by his re-election opponent. The monitor was also accused of pressuring Fain over the UAW’s passing of a resolution calling for a ceasefire in Gaza. Fain led the union during a roughly six-week strike in September 2023 through October 2023 at the big three automakers, General Motors, Ford and Stellantis, highlighting corporate greed through the strike and citing the companies’ stock buy-backs and record profits. Joe Biden joined the union on the picket line, the first sitting president to ever join a strike picket line.

events.title: Putin relayed Iran war proposal to Trump, Kremlin says
events.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin conveyed Tehran's view on a possible resolution of the Iran conflict to U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian state media reported. The report comes a day after Trump said Russia will supply diesel to the global market amid a surge in energy prices caused by the wars in Iran and Ukraine. Trump said Russia will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under an arrangement Trump said he agreed with Putin. Russian President Vladimir Putin conveyed Tehran's vision for a possible end to the war in Iran to U.S. President Donald Trump , Russian state media reported Saturday. Russia's Interfax news agency quoted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying Putin sent the message to Trump "in agreement with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian," according to a Google translation. Other Russian media reports said Putin spoke to Trump by phone after the Russian leader met Pezeshkian on the sidelines of a summit in Turkmenistan. Interfax didn't elaborate on the specifics of how Iran sees the war — which began on Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iranian targets — coming to an end. The White House didn't immediately respond to CNBC's emailed request to confirm the reported conversation between Putin and Trump. Trump said Friday that Russia will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under an arrangement the U.S. president said he agreed with Putin during a phone call. Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons immediately thereafter, Trump said in a post on Truth Social . Moscow will then deliver another 3 million tons of diesel based on the condition of Russia's refineries, Trump said. The Treasury Department temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel through April 2027 under a general license issued Friday. Iran has stepped up its attacks on oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, with vessels coming under fire almost daily as Tehran tries to choke off a rebound in crude exports. A senior Iranian Revolutionary Guard official said Wednesday that Iran will block all "illicit routes" through Hormuz, according to the Fars News Agency , an outlet considered close to the Guard. The surge in attacks on tankers comes as crude oil exports from the Middle East rebounded in September to prewar levels, largely because the U.S. military escorted ships through Hormuz along Oman's coast. An interim deal signed in June between the U.S. and Iran to pause hostilities to allow for negotiations quickly broke down. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy immediately condemned Trump's diesel deal with Putin. Ukraine's leader warned that easing sanctions without a commitment from Russia to de-escalate the war will only prolong it. "Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," Zelenskyy said in a social media post . "Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged." Diesel prices have surged worldwide as Ukraine has pounded Russian refineries, forcing Moscow to ban diesel exports to global markets. Iran and its Houthi allies have also attacked refineries in the Middle East, further constraining fuel supplies. Trump is under growing political pressure to lower fuel prices ahead of the November midterm elections. Republicans face competitive elections in conservative strongholds like Iowa, where farmers feel the pinch of high diesel prices.

events.title: UAW tries to reassert political power in Michigan despite internal divisions
events.summary: Membership is divided over which party best represents working-class interests. SHELBY TOWNSHIP, Mich. -- Walter Usakowski was mowing his lawn in a northern suburb of Detroit when three canvassers from the United Auto Workers approached. “I don’t even need to talk to you,” Usakowski said. As a retired member, he was already supporting the union’s slate of Democratic candidates in the Nov. 3 midterms. But he is not sure how many of the other “guys in the shop” will vote for Democrats. He worked at Ford Motor Co.’s Sterling Axle Plant for more than 45 years, and he knows many members who backed Republican President Donald Trump . The election-year canvassing was one part of the UAW’s efforts to reassert its political power in Michigan, a premier political battleground. Although the union generally backs Democrats, its membership is more divided over which party best represents working-class interests. It also is reckoning with past corruption scandals , a drop in membership and a lack of transparency that has eroded trust within its ranks. “It’s not going to be an overnight thing,” said JJ Jewell, who is part of the UAW’s Community Action Program executive committee. “Even if this election goes fantastically, that’s not mission accomplished. That means we’re 1% of the way done.” Jewell and others made the rounds on a recent sunny Saturday in Macomb County, where Trump won by nearly 14 percentage points in 2024. Many of the union members they met in a neighborhood of well-kept suburban houses were retirees, and while most said the cost of living was their top concern , they did not agree on whether Democrats or Republicans would better address it . One resident, who said she blamed billionaires for the country’s problems, planned to vote for Democrats. Another street over, a couple said they both supported Trump and declined to take a flyer of the UAW-endorsed candidates. In a microcosm of broader political rifts , union voters remain politically divided. Union voters have traditionally been seen as a Democratic-leaning constituency, but Trump made direct appeals to them with his anti-elite rhetoric and promises to overhaul international trade agreements that sapped factory jobs. In 2024, voters who were union members or were in a household with a union member split between Trump and Democratic nominee Kamala Harris , with more than half voting for the then-vice president and 44% for Trump. Betty Anderson, a UAW member, thinks the organization is on the right track, but she is not confident about bridging internal political divisions. She said she is angry with members who voted for Trump, whom she sees as selling out the working class. “I don’t think those people are ever going to be on our side,” Anderson said. “They think they have an opportunity to be in an elite class.” Since 2017, more than 10 UAW officials have pleaded guilty in a corruption investigation that found millions of dollars of union dues were stolen. Members also faulted leaders for closed-door contract negotiations that they said destroyed trust in the UAW. Shawn Fain was elected UAW president in 2023 on a platform of transparency, and victories in labor disputes with Detroit's three major automakers bolstered member support. Leaders hope this will translate into votes for its candidates. “I think the UAW members now are starting to fall a little more in line,” said Usakowski, the retired axle plant worker. On Friday, Fain said he won reelection to lead the union for four more years. The results have not yet been certified. Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Fort Hood survivors speak out on Pentagon's decision to livestream Hasan's execution Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Mark DePaoli, director for one of the UAW’s southeast Michigan regions, said the union hosted forums with candidates where any member could ask questions. The UAW endorsed progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the U.S. Senate primary even though rival Haley Stevens , a four-term congresswoman, worked as chief of staff on an auto bailout task force during the Great Recession, a position she frequently cited while campaigning. “I don’t think anybody expected us to endorse him,” DePaoli said. In its announcement, the union referenced El-Sayed’s support for universal healthcare and criticism of corporate money in politics. El-Sayed wore a UAW pin during the first Senate debate with his Republican opponent, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers . “The UAW’s backing of Abdul was critical in winning a historic primary despite being outspent by tens of millions of dollars, and will be just as critical in winning" next month, El-Sayed spokesperson Cole Wozniak said in a statement. Rogers is emphasizing his opposition to controversial federal regulations under Democratic President Joe Biden that would have required automakers to ramp up production of electric vehicles, which some feared would lead to factory closures.

events.title: Pokémon card values are soaring. What collectors should know before buying or selling
events.summary: What is driving interest? Pokémon and other trading-card games are drawing strong collector demand, while sources say high sports-card prices are pushing some buyers toward non-sports cards. What determines value? Authenticity, condition, graded population, liquidity and verified transaction history can sharply affect what a card sells for. What is the biggest risk? Counterfeits are rising, especially in Pokémon submissions, making authentication and careful price research critical before buying. In 2022, a rare Topps 1952 Mickey Mantle baseball card — one of sports-card collectors' holiest grails — sold for $12.6 million. Wow, you say, that's a lot of dough for a thin piece of cardboard, slab of bubblegum not included. Well, what do you say about a 1998 Pikachu Illustrator Pokémon card going for $16.5 million earlier this year? If you're pro wrestler and social media influencer Logan Paul, seller of the item, you say, Not a bad return on the $5.3 million (plus a trade) I paid for it in 2021. Those are extreme examples, but a vivid illustration of how TCGs — shorthand for competitive trading card games, led by Pokémon, Magic: The Gathering and Yu-Gi-Oh! — are encroaching on an over-saturated sports-card market as an enticing investment opportunity. Throw in vintage and modern-day non-sports trading cards, depicting historical events and fictional characters ranging from the Civil War to Luke Skywalker, and it's a whole new ballgame. The record $16.5 million Pokémon card sale is drawing fresh attention to a collectibles market where grading, scarcity and authentication can determine whether a card is worth dollars or hundreds of thousands. "It is one of our fastest-growing categories that we've seen and one of the largest contributors to [our] growth over the last number of quarters," said Adam Ireland, vice president and general manager of collectibles at online marketplace eBay , which also provides authentication and price guides for TCGs and non-sports cards. "From an investment point of view, you start with Pokémon," he said. "It was the most searchable term within the eBay collectibles environment through the first half of the year." Heritage Auctions, which deals in art, jewelry, coins and many other collectibles, launched a dedicated TCG department six years ago. "Now it's a $50-million category," said executive vice president Joe Maddalena. "That's just TCGs. I'm not talking about Star Wars and any of that stuff," he said, though he added that non-sports stuff contributed around $10 million to Heritage's overall sales in 2025, which topped $2.1 billion. While buyers can find myriad non-sports cards for less than $10 — almost like investing in penny stocks in hopes of eventually striking gold — Maddalena and Ireland cited some eye-popping sales on their respective platforms. A first-edition Pokémon Charizard card worth $20,000 pre-Covid is now valued by Heritage at $500,000. A Tyler the Great Warrior Yu-Gi-Oh! card shattered records when it was auctioned on eBay for $311,211, while Magic's Black Lotus card has gone for $500,000 on the site. Heritage sold a 1977 Luke Skywalker card for $687,500 in May. Whereas collectability, value and investability of sports cards can rise and fall on the real-world performance of athletes, both trading-card genres share common factors. For instance, rookie cards of superstar athletes are highly coveted; the non-sports counterpart is referred to as first appearance. Especially critical are the authenticity, physical condition, total graded population, liquidity and pricing of specific cards, criteria determined by professional grading services such as PSA and CGC Cards. How cards are graded for monetary value PSA (Professional Sports Authenticator), founded in 1991, is the most recognizable grading service. Its process begins when a trained grader examines a card to verify its originality or genuineness, then assesses the quality and condition of the card using PSA's grading scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the most pristine, aka gem mint. There generally are very limited populations of PSA 10s of highly sought-after cards, thus their astronomical values. PSA has been grading non-sports cards since its inception, "but with more people viewing it as a potential asset class or thing they want to potentially invest in or speculate in, you're seeing more demand for grading services in the last seven years," said PSA president Ryan Hoge. Indeed, PSA graded more than 19 million cards in 2025, up from two million in 2020. The company had already graded more than eight million cards as of last May, with output from January through April up 39% year-over-year. Much of that uptick, Hoge said, is attributable to TCGs. "Collectively, TCGs [account for] 50% of our current business, more than all the sports cards combined.
