Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Anthropic said its models exploited websites on the internet, including some run by U.S. government agencies, and it will turn off live internet access for all of its internal evaluations until the frontier lab is sure it can monitor and control its AI agents. The incidents, disclosed in a blog post , involved AI agents tasked to solve problems seeking resources on the internet. In the process, they exploited software flaws, accessed databases without paying fees, used URL shortening services to smuggle information past restrictions, and even submitted a false murder tip to the Philadelphia police. Anthropic said it discovered these new issues in a review of its model’s activities that began in July, demonstrating the lab’s lack of awareness of its software’s behavior in real time. Notably, the company said that alignment training was not yet sufficient for skills like search and computer use that are central to its pitch that AI agents will be used by any professional who relies on digital tools. The behaviors Anthropic disclosed are similar to incidents involving OpenAI agents that collaborated to break into various websites in search of information, including some run by the Australian government. Anthropic previously disclosed that its models had broken into external systems. The frontier lab said it considered today’s disclosures “significantly less severe from an alignment and security perspective” than those it announced before. However, the lab still said it had “turned off live internet access” for “all our internal evaluations” until it is certain it can monitor and control its agents. It’s not clear what that means. Sydney Von Arx, the founder of Nightingale, an AI safety organization, told TechCrunch in an interview before this disclosure that developing models on a data center cut off from the open internet would be very challenging for researchers, and hinder the progress of the models, which benefit from internet access. “You have to align them at some point,” Von Arx said. “If the AIs are released to production and never have access to the internet, that’s not a very useful tool.” Anthropic said the behavior was a result of flaws in the lab’s training environments, which led the models to believe they would be rewarded for finding loopholes or avoiding restrictions, a behavior called “reward hacking.” The company said it would stop running some of its evaluations or move them offline, and has built tooling to detect and block this behavior. This tooling was tested against the kind of incidents disclosed today and blocked them; it’s not clear what evidence will prompt Anthropic to return live internet access to its internal evaluations. Anthropic also said it would migrate its internal AI agents to “centrally managed infrastructure with strong containment,” and is beginning to using safety classifiers more frequently to monitor those agents. “It’s encouraging that Anthropic voluntarily disclosed more recent incidents, including where their agents targeted U.S. government websites,” Conrad Stosz, an official at AI oversight lab Transluce and former head of the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation, said in a statement. “But it just underscores the need for independent, credible, third-party verification of Al systems. Trust in this technology needs to be built through science-backed oversight and governance with meaningful access — not by relying on researchers to find these things in the wild or on companies to voluntarily disclose.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: FBI Arrests Executive at Ransomware Negotiation Firm
events.summary: Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity. The New York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel . One source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity the Canadian person arrested this week was visiting Pennsylvania for a cyber insurance conference, and that the suspect’s company specialized in handling ransomware negotiations with cybercrime groups. Another shared that control over the ShinyHunters investigation has been centralized at an FBI field office in Texas. An online search reveals the Cyber Risk Summit was held at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel between Oct. 5 and Oct. 7. The conference had several sponsors, but according to the summit’s website its biggest sponsor was a Canadian security company called Cypfer . According to LinkedIn, one of Cypfer’s “ex-founders” was Edward Dubrovsky , who is now associated with another Canadian security firm and sponsor called CyberSteward . In a post to LinkedIn approximately one month ago, Dubrovsky said he had plans to attend the Cyber Risk Summit with the rest of the CyberSteward team. [ Update: Oct. 10, 9:58 a.m. ET: A spokesperson for Cypfer said Dubrovsky was not a founder or co-founder as his LinkedIn profile claims, but instead served as a managing director before resigning in November 2025]. Edward Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile. “Looking forward to continuing conversations around strategy & compliant driven coercive (ransomware, extortion) advisory, negotiations and settlement services that are global and truly agnostic,” Dubrovsky wrote. Federal court records show that on October 8, an Edward Dobrovsky (note the slight misspelling of the last name) was arrested in Pennsylvania on cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. Several of those documents — including the core complaint — are now sealed. But a handful of them were indexed at Courtlistener.com , including a summary of the complaint, which charges the defendant with “conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money,” and “interference with commerce by threats.” Image: Courtlistener.com The inmate locator at the U.S. Bureau of Prisons website reports that a 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky is currently being held at a federal facility in Philadelphia. But the court records indexed by CourtListener include a notice filed on October 9 that moved the case to the Eastern District of Texas, which sources say is now the epicenter of the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation. The FBI declined to comment for this story. Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile states he is the author of Cyber Extortion Strategic Response , a 252-page book that promises to “take readers beyond the ransom note and into the decisions that determine how an organization responds, recovers, and protects what matters.” Edward Dubrovsky’s book, which centers on the intricacies of ransomware negotiations. “At the heart of the book is a critical distinction: communicating with a criminal is not the same as negotiating a payment, and negotiating is not a commitment to pay,” reads an excerpt from the book’s listing on Amazon. “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.” Mr. Dubrovsky could not be immediately reached for comment. KrebsOnSecurity also sought comment from other executives at CyberSteward, and will update this post in the event they respond. The available court records in Dubrovsky’s case show that he does not currently have an attorney and has yet to be appointed a public defender by the courts. ShinyHunters typically uses phishing and stolen credentials to siphon data from corporate accounts at software-as-a-service companies, and then threatens to publish the stolen data online unless a ransom demand is paid. According to the FBI, the group has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year. Sources tell KrebsOnSecurity the FBI has been poring over devices that were seized last month when the Dutch police arrested the convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation, and that charges against principals at other companies that specialize in ransomware negotiation may be forthcoming. Immediately after Van der Stap’s arrest, another member of ShinyHunters named “ Rey ” assumed control over the group and began taunting the FBI over data the group stole from the agency’s online recruitment portal, which included each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records. Last week, Reuters reported that Rey — identified as a teenager named Saif Al-din Khader — had been detained and was cooperating with FBI investigators. On October 7, we detailed how Rey was apprehended as the cybercrime group allegedly sought to extort a navigation and digital aviation unit that was divested by Boeing in late 2025. This is likely to be a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted along with timestamps.

events.title: 'FishTok' trend creates fishing boom among young Victorians
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Teens in Victoria are taking up a new hobby. ( ABC News: Harrison Tippet ) If they were not standing on Geelong's Cunningham Pier, Ivy Renouf, Zane Winterton and Xavier Clair say they would either be hanging out in the shopping centre, playing video games, or scrolling their phones. Instead, this trio of 16-year-olds are enjoying a day in the sun, as they try to catch some fish. Ivy Renouf, Xavier Clair and Zane Winterton are a new breed of anglers in Geelong. ( ABC News: Harrison Tippet ) "I didn't want to be in bed at home, or in town because I do that all the time, so I just wanted to get outdoors with my mates." These Geelong teens are part of a new generation of Victorians getting hooked on fishing, sparking a surge of interest in the recreational activity. Zane remembers when he was the only kid he knew who was into fishing, regularly heading out on trips with his dad. The teenagers use an old tackle box, bait and fishing knives. ( ABC News: Harrison Tippet ) Now, he has plenty of mates who want to come along. "When I was in primary school, before COVID, no-one fished," he says. "It was just me, like, in the whole school. All three of these teens say more young Victorians have been taking up fishing in the past few years, lured by both the challenge and the urge to get outside with friends. "It's a good way to get some good memories with your friends, to be honest," Xavier says. "Getting outside and maybe catching a fish or maybe not but, like, just hanging out with your friends and having a good time." The trio catch little more than a pufferfish from the pier, before heading to a new spot. At the foot of the pier they pass a group of six other young teens, who cheer each other along as they reel in a bream. Teens carrying fishing gear through towns like Geelong has become a common sight. ( ABC News: Harrison Tippet ) It is hard to put a number on the increasing popularity of fishing with younger Victorians. Victorians under 18 years old do not need a licence, and the handful of fishing clubs the ABC spoke to say they may have seen slightly more younger members signing up, but have few useful statistics to back up a boom. Instead, they say it is an increase most visible on Victorian waterways. Teens and young anglers throughout the state are often seen walking around clutching rods or setting up at popular fishing spots. Anthony McGrath says it is impossible to miss the jump in fishing's popularity with young Victorians. ( ABC News: Harrison Tippet ) Anthony McGrath, executive officer at VRFish, the state's peak body for recreational fishing, says the increase in younger Victorians fishing is irrefutable. "It's been incredible," Mr McGrath says. "There's definitely been a massive increase in kids fishing." "We see it here every day. The buses arrive back from schools, and the kids are walking past in school uniforms with fishing rods in hand or sticking out of their bags. On the other side of the bay, Jet Reef Worsteling has spent much of his 19 years fishing. He is the son of one of Australia's most famous anglers, Paul Worsteling, and is a big name on social media, counting 2.3 million followers on TikTok alone. Jet Reef Worsteling is already a big name in fishing, particularly on social media. ( ABC News: Billy Draper ) "When I was in primary school and then going into high school, fishing was more of, like, was an older person's activity … it just wasn't cool like surfing or skating or any of that," Mr Worsteling says. "I could never have pictured it in a million years, but I think the last year and a half, two years, fishing is now one of the cool things for young people to go do when they've got free time." Who wins your vote for the 2026 ABC Australian Insect of the Year? Family day care shrinks as parents opt for centre-based care Victorians say 'lazy planning' leading to poor social housing outcomes Licence granted for controversial mineral sands mine What's behind fishing's increasing popularity? Those in the fishing industry point to a handful of factors behind the activity's increasing popularity with young Victorians: social media, a post-COVID desire to get outdoors, and a program handing out free fishing rods to 180,000 Victorian kids. Mr Worsteling says there has been a clear increase in younger users getting active on "FishTok" and other platforms. "There's definitely a lot more kids posting videos, liking videos, reacting with videos, all that sort of stuff," he says.

events.title: Boots has a new owner: Three ways it could affect you
events.summary: If you have been looking to buy a health or beauty product, the chances are you will have shopped at a Boots somewhere in the UK. The pharmacy and retailer is a stalwart of Britain's high streets, where it has served generations of customers for decades. But now it is set to enter its 178th year under new ownership after an £7bn deal was agreed this week - here's three ways it could affect your shopping experience. Upgrading its portfolio of 1,800 stores is high on the list of Boots' new owners, Wittington Investments. This is the holding company of the Westons - a wealthy and retail-steeped Canadian family who used to own Selfridges and currently own several large retailers across the Atlantic. The UK branch of the family also controls the owner of Primark, Associated British Foods (ABF). What Boots stores might look like in the future has not been disclosed. Business has been good for Boots in recent years, and new-look beauty areas in some of its bigger shops have given shoppers more of a department store experience, according to Sofie Willmott, an associate director and analyst at GlobalData Retail. Since the opening of its first beauty-only store in 2023 in the Battersea Power Station development, it says it has redesigned over 180 beauty halls, while also opening its first fragrance concept store and an Opticians dedicated to luxury eyewear. "They should invest in the rest of the chain because they've got such a big store portfolio that I think some of the smaller stores have really lacked investment over time, and I think that is something that they need to kind of catch up with," Willmott says. A more "consistent" look would also be an improvement, Willmott adds. "At the moment there is a bit of a disconnect." Jackie Naghten, a retail industry veteran who has worked for the likes of Top Shop, Marks & Spencer and Debenhams, thinks Boots' stores need to be made "more functional" by not having their health hubs "squeezed in the corner". But Yasmin Trimble, 22, who buys beauty products from Boots, likes how easy the stores are to navigate. "You can get everything you need...it is not confusing. It has got a cleaner aesthetic to it as well." Katie Burrows and Yasmin Trimble both shop at Boots regularly Advantage card an 'asset to double down on' Boots was an early adopter of the loyalty cards commonly offered today by companies offering points and discounts to customers who sign up. Its Advantage card, launched in 1997, is unlikely to go away and remains popular. Naghten doesn't think they would get rid of it. "It's the best-value store card in terms of bang for your buck." The card offers shoppers three points for every pound they spend. Each point is worth 1p. Katie Burrows, 23, is a fan of building up the points to get money off. She mainly shops at Boots for skincare, first aid and medicine, but thinks prices for its sanitary products are "ridiculously expensive" - something her friend Yasmin agrees with. Lewis Harrison believes the loyalty card is also good value, but finds it "frustrating how the rewards points only cover a full transaction". "I wish you could use your points for a partial transaction like you can in Holland and Barrett," the 25-year-old says. "It would be good to use the points towards more expensive transactions." Natalie Berg, retail expert and founder of consultancy NBK Retail, suggests the Advantage card gives Boots "a unique understanding of their customers" and is an asset the new owners "will want to double down on". "As AI and social media change how people discover and buy products, that direct relationship with customers will only become more important." The new owners have already signalled they plan to expand Boots' healthcare service, a booming industry at the moment. The retailer started out as an apothecary, so health is in its roots. Today, it offers a wide range of health and wellbeing services as well as prescriptions and vaccinations through its in-store pharmacies. It also announced earlier this summer it was expanding services for weight loss drugs, which have surged in popularity. Naghten points out that the Weston family's purchase of Boots comes at a time when pharmacies are increasingly going to prescribe more medications and health services, in a bid to ease pressure on GP surgeries and hospitals. "They didn't buy this thing for no reason. They have got the blueprint," she says. While health will remain a core part of its business, Boots has other strengths, Naghten adds, in its No7 make-up and skincare products. "When you have all these people coming in for health and wellbeing services, they will also be picking up a lipstick," she says. Willmott suggests Boots has an "edge" over its rivals on the health side, given its reputation as an expert. But the company is facing tough competition, which Boots acknowledged affected revenues in its latest financial results.

events.title: Tasmanian EPA says it was not told extent of Firmus data centre generator plans
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tasmania's EPA worried AI company Firmus plans to use generators much more than first disclosed Firmus has pulled its ASX float plans following poor interest from investors. ( Supplied: Tasmanian government ) Tasmania's environmental watchdog is concerned Firmus plans on using 276 diesel generators far more often than it first disclosed. The EPA has now applied to join as a party to a TASCAT appeal, where Firmus is seeking to have conditions around its generator use removed. A Firmus submission to a federal joint select committee on AI reveals new renewable energy infrastructure it promised to power its data centres may "not necessarily" be built within Tasmania. Tasmania's environmental regulator is urging a tribunal to hear its concerns, after learning the operator of a recently approved AI data centre wants to use hundreds of diesel generators far more often than it originally disclosed. Earlier this year, the George Town Council approved a Firmus Technologies proposal to build a 288-megawatt data centre in the state's north, after the Tasmanian Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) determined it did not need to make an environmental assessment. The data centre's approval was subject to conditions, including that Firmus could only run the 276 on-site diesel generators at limited times, such as during emergencies or routine inspections. Firmus Technologies is building AI data centres in Tasmania, but most of its planned centres are not built yet. ( Supplied: Firmus Technologies ) Firmus, however, has appealed that condition through the Tasmanian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (TASCAT ), arguing it wanted to use the generators "for limited augmentation of the mains electricity supply to offset curtailment, manage energy security and maintain operational reliability during periods of energy market stress". Tasmania's Environment Protection Authority (EPA) board has now applied to TASCAT to join as a party to Firmus's appeal. EPA likely to have assessed project if proposed use was higher In its October 7 submission, seen by the ABC, the board said it was originally told the generators would be used "just for emergency use in the event of a power failure", and would not be used during normal operation other than for scheduled weekly exercise runs of less than two hours, annual load tests, and utility outage events. The board said Firmus's recent appeal showed it planned on using the generators in more circumstances than it thought. Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff (centre) with co-CEOs Tim Rosenfield and Oliver Curtis at the Firmus Technologies site. ( Supplied: Tasmanian government ) "That variation, if part of the original proposal, would likely have resulted in the Board making a different decision in relation to whether to assess the proposal," the board said. It pointed out that if Firmus's appeal against the condition around generator use is upheld, it could allow it to subvert EPA processes it likely would have been subjected to "if the proposal had been accurately presented". "And further, if upheld, the appeal has the potential to permit an activity in circumstances where the environmental risks have not been properly assessed, which may result in environmental harm including nuisance … necessitating the EPA taking enforcement action in respect of it," it said. Construction underway at Firmus's St Leonards site. ( ABC News: Morgan Timms ) The EPA board said it would not comment on matters currently being considered by TASCAT, and Firmus declined to comment on the matter. A state government spokesperson said it was supportive of private investments that created jobs and economic benefits but "projects should use resources responsibly and engage transparently with communities". Greens MP Tabatha Badger said she welcomed the EPA raising concerns and pointing out the potential for the generators to breach acceptable limits and for noise to carry across the river. Meanwhile, a submission made by Firmus to the current federal joint select committee on AI reveals its Tasmanian data centres may be powered with renewable infrastructure based interstate, rather than locally. Firmus has long said it will build two megawatts of new renewable energy generation for every 1 megawatt it uses across new data centres planned for Launceston, Long Reach and Wesley Vale. Tim Rosenfield and Oliver Curtis are the co-CEOs of Firmus Technologies. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) Firmus's co-CEO Tim Rosenfield has previously implied that new capacity would be built in Tasmania.

events.title: Trump strikes deal with Putin for Russia to supply diesel to US
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Energy minister Chris Bowen rejects Trump-Putin diesel supply plan Donald Trump (right) says he had a "highly successful" phone call with Vladimir Putin over diesel supply. ( Reuters: Kevin Lamarque ) Donald Trump says he has reached an agreement with Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply diesel to the US. Mr Trump signed sweeping sanctions against Russia last month aimed at clamping down on Russia's energy revenues. Analysts have cast doubt on how much the deal will ease near record-high diesel prices in the US. US President Donald Trump says he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, up-ending years of Washington pressuring Moscow over its war with Ukraine. The price of diesel, used for agriculture, heating homes and trucking, sits near a record high in the US. Mr Trump said on social media he had a "highly successful" discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin in which they agreed Moscow would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets. Energy minister Chris Bowen told Weekend Breakfast that Australia "doesn't need or want Russian fuel". "We have the arrangements in place as best as we possibly can with our trading partners to ensure that Russian fuel doesn't flow to Australia," he said. "We do not want Vladimir Putin to benefit from this war in the Middle East." Mr Bowen stopped short of condemning the United States but reiterated Australia was firmly against Russia being rewarded "for their illegal and immoral invasion of Ukraine by any arrangements put in place". Analyst warns diesel prices could top $4 a litre Analyst warns export ban the most worrying development since the Middle East conflict began. An envoy for Mr Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, praised the cooperation between Russia and the US in a post on X shortly after the call. Only last month Mr Trump signed a sweeping sanctions law aimed at clamping down on Russia’s energy revenues and other areas that are fuelling its war against Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy criticised the US leader's new stance. "Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilised world," he said. "Russia will repay the diesel with further terror and perfidy." The US Treasury Department issued a general licence on Friday, local time, allowing the importation of Russian diesel until April 7. Mr Trump said Russia would supply another 500,000 tonnes in November and a further 1 million tonnes "immediately thereafter". Even more would follow, Mr Trump said, "based on the condition of their diesel refineries", which have been damaged by Ukrainian attacks. What to expect on Australian fuel supply and pricing for the weekend The week's most important fuel news, analysis and pricing information. The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the diesel from Russia and when the fuel being supplied under the agreement would become available. It also did not clarify whether subsequent supplies of Russian diesel set to come next month would be supplied prior to the US midterm elections on November 3. Doubts over deal's effect on fuel prices Analysts said the agreement was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices. "I cannot overstate how much of a nothing burger this is," Rory Johnston, an oil market researcher and founder of CommodityContext.com, said on X, adding that Russia usually exported much more diesel when its refinery fleet was not under attack. The 300,000 tonnes to be immediately delivered is equal to about 2.25 million barrels of diesel. The US exports about 1.5 million barrels of diesel per day. "It's clearly not a fix, but another stream to aid a very tight diesel market," Jim Mitchell, an analyst at consultancy Wood Mackenzie, said. Diesel prices, which can drive inflation, are up 70 per cent since the US and Israel launched the war with Iran on February 28. The wars in Iran and Ukraine have triggered a severe global fuel supply crunch, pushing average US diesel prices to $US6.28 a gallon ($2.37 a litre) on Thursday, according to the AAA motorist group. The price climb is despite Mr Trump's two recent efforts to boost fuel supplies: pressuring allies ‌to release emergency reserves and expanding access to tax-exempt red-dyed diesel, which is normally used for farm equipment. US diesel futures HOc1 fell sharply following news of the deal and were trading at $US4.64 a gallon, down more than 4.8 per cent. "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Mr Trump said.

events.title: Darwin council leads China and Vietnam delegation after rate rise
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Darwin City Council to lead China and Vietnam trade delegation, after rate rise The Darwin City Council will lead an Asian trade delegation including about 10 businesses in December. ( ABC News: Hamish Harty ) Darwin lord mayor Peter Styles will lead a delegation of businesses to China and Vietnam later this year, in a bid to help bolster the Top End economy. The trip comes after rates in the city were raised above inflation, but the council has denied it is a "junket". It is the first of such overseas delegations led by the city's council since 2023. Darwin City Council has defended its decision to lead a trade delegation to Asia during a year when the city's rates have been hiked and its annual hard rubbish collection delayed to 2027. The council has confirmed about $18,000 of ratepayer funding will be spent on the mission, to be led by lord mayor Peter Styles, which aims to open economic doors for the Top End city. The council's general manager of innovation, Alice Percy, said the delegation would lead about 10 businesses to Guangzhou in China and Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam in December. Guangzhou, China's third-largest city, will be part of the council-led trade delegation. ( Getty Images ) "This is definitely not a junket for the mayor and for the council," she said. "It's an important economic opportunity for Darwin as a capital city." Ms Percy said it would be the first time the city's council had led a delegation abroad since 2023. Alice Percy says the trade mission could be lucrative for the Darwin economy. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) The delegation comes a year after China Southern Airlines began flying to and from Darwin , with the council voicing its ambition to try and convince more carriers to fly to the city. While attending businesses will fund their own trips, the council has said it will provide support and facilitate introductions and networking opportunities with businesses in Asia. Mr Styles is a previous NT government Asian engagement minister, and after he lost his seat in 2016, he held private consultancy businesses in the same field. Peter Styles will lead the delegation. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) The council was asked whether it viewed Mr Styles's previous roles as possible conflicts of interest in leading the delegation, but it did not respond by deadline. Mr Styles was unavailable for an interview. Trip follows rate rises, service delay The council's move to embark on the trip comes six months after it raised rates by 5.5 per cent, above inflation level , and ditched its annual pre-cyclone clean-up for 2026 , postponing it until next May. At the time of the rate hike, Mr Styles said the council was grappling with rising expenses and a large damage bill following a destructive cyclone season. The trip will also take in Vietnam's Ho Chi Minh City. ( ABC News: Jarrod Fankhauser ) Former Darwin lord mayor Graeme Sawyer said the council risked seeming out of touch with its ratepayers. "Particularly at a time when cost of living and everything else is so front and centre in people's minds, you're really treading on some rough country here," he said. Mr Sawyer said he had concerns about a "culture of secrecy" within the Darwin council, where discussed items were routinely being made confidential and unable to be viewed by the public. Graeme Sawyer says the council should be "open and explicit" with ratepayers about its reasons for ventures like this one. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) "If council's not being open and explicit about the benefits and the reasons for these sorts of things, then naturally people are just going to think it's another junket," he said. The Asian trade delegation was originally made confidential by the council when the resolution was passed earlier this year, but the council has confirmed it has now been made public. In the community, the ABC asked Darwin residents what they thought of the upcoming trade mission, which will fund two council staff members to travel abroad alongside the lord mayor. Kathy Carter would like to see the council focus more on rates, roads and rubbish. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) Darwin resident of more than 40 years, Kathy Carter, said she did not support the initiative. "I think it's probably not a good idea," she said. "The rates have just been put up, and we need more interest in rates, roads and rubbish. "They can do cultural ties and trading things and all that stuff with the [NT] government." Mike Sproule says the money going towards the delegation could be better spent elsewhere.

events.title: Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
events.summary: Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president. Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas. Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months. The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections. As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public – stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation – has soured. The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market. It is these states – places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio – that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress. Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky criticises 'gift to Putin' Published 1 day ago What are the US midterms? A simple guide Published 5 days ago For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain. He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves . He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking. He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms – an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having. His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort. Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return – besides much-needed hard currency – is unclear. It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy". "Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X. It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box. The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market. Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes – attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail. The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption. Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference. With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked. "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post. But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand. Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words. Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work? events.title: Long live the mechanical keyboard
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. For a writer, the mechanical keyboard is a beautiful thing. It’s certainly not necessary for everyone, but a well-designed mechanical keyboard can turn a tedious day of typing into an aesthetically pleasing experience. Given that most of my days involve sitting at a desk for hours, having a keyboard that I enjoy using is a necessity. I first got a mechanical keyboard about two years ago — the Keychron K2 — and I’ve never looked back. Keychron is one of the most prominent brands within the mechanical keyboard industry, having made a name for itself after initially launching via Kickstarter back in 2017. The company has since produced dozens of different keyboards (as well as keypads) and a variety of mouse models . Unlike other electronics, there isn’t a whole lot to owning a mechanical keyboard. The simplicity is part of the appeal. You unbox them, set them up (the K2 comes with little tilt legs that give you a slightly better angle from which to type), and plug them in. From here, you have a couple of different options. The K2 comes with a simple USB cable, but there’s also an option for Bluetooth connection. If you value a clean, minimalist workspace, Bluetooth is probably the way to go. While I am loyal to my older Keychron K2, there are a few upgraded and newer versions to consider. Keychron has released a variety of new models over the past two years, with a broad range of features and price tags. In many cases, the form factor is the draw. One of the more interesting releases, called the Keychron K8 HE Wireless Magnetic Switch Custom Keyboard, comes with an all-wood body and is equipped with an LED backlight. That one is substantially more expensive at around $200. The K2, meanwhile, costs $60. But if you’re into the look, maybe it’s worth it. If you’re a gamer, there’s also Keychron’s C0 HE One-Handed 8K Keyboard , which is a keypad built for convenience and speed and has an industrial aesthetic to it. However, interested gamers will have to wait — as it’s currently sold out. The company has also updated its K, Q, and V series keyboards, with many of those ranging in price from $100 to $200, depending on the features and model. One of the appealing elements of owning a mechanical keyboard is the versatility. You can swap out the key caps for a wide variety of others (indeed, there’s a whole submarket devoted to this) or make your own custom caps (I’ve never gone that overboard). There is also the sound, of course. Some people balk at the accentuated noise of loudly clacking keys, but I’m a fan. In fact, the sound is one of the key selling points for a lot of consumers. The distinct auditory experience produced by said keyboards has even made its way into ASMR videos . For me, the Keychron’s biggest selling point is its retro form factor. I get really nostalgic for old school electronics, and Keychron scratches this itch pretty well. It’s a beautiful-looking device, which brings to mind a different era of computing, when the style was more workman-like, less minimalist. As far as home office purchases go, you could do a lot worse than to pick yourself up a piece of hardware that makes your desk look like it just time-traveled from the 1990s. events.title: JD Vance says he won't watch livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter
events.summary: Vice President JD Vance said Friday he won't watch a potential livestream of the convicted Fort Hood shooter's execution, which President Trump told reporters he had approved. Why it matters: Vance questioned whether the execution would actually be public but joined a small chorus of Republicans opposed to watching the execution, which is set to be conducted by a firing squad in December. What they're saying: "Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance told reporters on Friday. "Now that said, I mean, look, if it's all through livestream, I'm not going to be watching it." Yes, but: Trump's comments came during a separate press gaggle on Friday, where he was asked if he had authorized or approved the livestream of the execution. "Did I approve? Absolutely, I approve." Driving the news: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in an interview Thursday that Americans would be able to watch the execution of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it. ... People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," he said. AP later reported that the execution would be livestreamed. If it goes forward, Hasan's execution will be the first public one in 90 years, and the first military execution since 1961. Zoom in: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) condemned plans to make the execution public in a Thursday night X post . "Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting. Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America," the outgoing senator said. Utah Sen. John Curtis (R) said in an X post , "Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent." "A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment. Secretary Hegseth's plan to livestream the Fort Hood execution risks feeding that appetite. The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity." The other side: Some GOP politicians, like Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.), welcomed the livestream. "Excellent. Public execution is what this terrorist deserves. We will be watching," he said in a post on X. Editor's note: This story was updated with comments from President Trump.

TypeSafe AI, the developer of Jev, a new type of AI model that gained rapid popularity after launching just a few weeks ago, has raised $870 million at a $7.5 billion valuation. The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz, with participation from Sequoia and existing investor DCVC. The massive fundraise comes as little surprise given Jev went viral almost instantly after its September 15 release . The startup claims that a third of Fortune 500 companies are already using the model, a remarkably swift adoption by enterprises. Jev is based on a transformer architecture, but it is not a large language model (LLM). It doesn’t output text, but instead produces probabilities, or what the company calls “calibrated decisions.” What has users and large corporations so excited about Jev is TypeSafe’s claim that it works significantly faster and uses far fewer tokens than LLMs. The company positions its approach as uniquely suited for automating tasks rather than generating text or code. “We have been super good at human language for four years, but it’s not useful for automation because computers speak a different language,” TypeSafe co-founder Diogo Almeida told TechCrunch last month. Along with Almeida, who was previously a researcher at OpenAI, TypeSafe was co-founded in 2024 by former Meta research engineer Sasha Sheng and Erik Gafni, an engineer and entrepreneur. events.title: Exclusive: Zelensky tells Axios Trump's diesel deal with Putin "not fair and not honest"
events.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios in a phone interview on Friday that President Trump's decision to unilaterally lift sanctions on Russia and allow it to export diesel was "not fair and not honest." "You know, it looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible," Zelensky said in frustration, referring to the Russian president's birthday earlier this week. Why it matters: Trump's announcement, which came after a call with Putin, shocked Ukraine and many European governments and created a new crisis between the U.S. and its Western allies. During the 15-minute interview, Zelensky sounded exasperated and dismayed and even expressed a sense of betrayal by the news of the diesel deal. Trump was asked several times by reporters on Friday about Zelensky's criticism but declined to comment and said he was happy about the deal with Putin. Driving the news: Trump announced the deal with Putin as his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were meeting in Miami with the Ukrainian negotiating team along with senior diplomats from Germany, France, the U.K., the EU and NATO to discuss new U.S. ideas for ending the war. Zelensky said he spoke several days ago with Witkoff about the need to continue efforts to reach a diplomatic breakthrough before winter and the midterm elections. "Steve proposed to meet in Florida. And of course I accepted to go there and speak about the possibilities of negotiations. The Americans said they have some ideas and we agreed to come to discuss," Zelensky said. At no point during his talks with Witkoff and Kushner did the U.S. suggest that a diesel deal with Russia was on the table, Zelensky stressed. He said he understood from Witkoff that the U.S. envoys planned to take messages from the Florida talks to the Russians and then potentially travel to Kyiv to try to seal a peace deal. Behind the scenes: Zelensky said that an hour before Trump's statement, his negotiators, who were meeting with Kushner and Witkoff in Florida, informed him that Trump planned to speak with Putin. They said an announcement regarding U.S. sanctions on Russia might be forthcoming, without elaborating. "It's not honest, really, because we tried to build our relations in the best way," he said. "It looks like that they used this opportunity to meet us from one side, and from the other side called Putin and negotiate this." What he's saying: The Ukrainian president said he would have supported easing sanctions on Russian energy if it was done in the context of a deal to halt attacks on energy facilities in Ukraine and Russia during the winter. "If the price is energy ceasefire, this negotiation is good," Zelensky said. But he argued that Trump presumably would have announced such a breakthrough if Putin had agreed to it. "What did [Trump] get? That he will have more diesel? For whom? More Russian diesel for Americans? It shows weakness of the world," Zelensky said. Zelensky compared the current deal to the Anchorage summit between Trump and Putin last year, which ended with the U.S. president agreeing to many of the Russian demands regarding the war in Ukraine without getting anything in return. "It looks like Alaska No. 2," he said. Between the lines: Despite his anger, Zelensky stopped short of saying the episode meant Washington could no longer mediate between Kyiv and Moscow. "It's not simple. We need the Americans," he said. "We need the Americans to try to stop this war." But he questioned whether rewarding Moscow without an apparent Russian concession would make further diplomacy more difficult. "This decision will not help us in any way," Zelensky said. "But what is bad, I think that this decision will not help Americans." What's next: Zelensky said he plans to speak with his negotiating team to get a full readout of its talks with Witkoff and Kushner. Zelensky said he also wanted to understand whether the diesel agreement was connected to a trip Trump's envoys planned to take to Russia. "If you allow them to export diesel, and you think before that you have to go to Russia to negotiate, it looks that you are buying this meeting," Zelensky said, while stressing that he did not know whether that was actually Trump's intention. "Maybe I'm not right," Zelensky said. "But it looks this way. Otherwise, why do it?"

events.title: Katie Zacharia tapped as next White House press secretary
events.summary: Katie Zacharia, a former Department of Homeland Security spokesperson, will be the next White House press secretary, President Trump said Friday. The big picture: Zacharia will take over the podium from Karoline Leavitt, a Trump loyalist who announced her departure from the administration in August. What they're saying: "It is my Great Honor to have just appointed, as Press Secretary, Katie Zacharia," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning. She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!" "I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration." Zoom in: Zacharia thanked Trump for the appointment in a Friday post on X. "Serving President Trump and the American people at this critical 250-year mark is the honor of a lifetime. President Trump has shown America that we can be great again, and he works to effectuate that greatness every single day," she wrote. "I look forward to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out. Following the fabulous Karoline Leavitt is a high standard, and one worth meeting." Catch up quick: Zacharia is a conservative lawyer and commentator who works as a senior communications adviser at Trump Media & Technology Group, which operates Truth Social. She also served for about six weeks as the Department of Homeland Security's deputy assistant secretary for public affairs and spokesperson. Zacharia announced her departure from DHS on March 31 in a post on X, saying she hoped to continue supporting the president's agenda "in other capacities." Zacharia has worked as a commentator on Fox News, CNN, Newsmax, One America News and other outlets. She holds both a law degree and a bachelor's degree from Pepperdine University, where she currently serves on the school's Dean's Council. The intrigue: Zacharia is less well-known than some of her predecessors, but she is a vocal defender of the administration on TV and online. Trump also noted Friday that Zacharia had been involved in his 2024 presidential campaign, "assisting in key Swing States." She also previously worked for Trump ally Richard Grenell at Fix California, an advocacy group that works to advance conservative values in the state. Zacharia has previously described herself as a "native Californian and lifelong conservative." She told CNN in April that she's a "huge fan of ICE and a big fan of the Border Patrol" and praised border czar Tom Homan's work on immigration. Axios' Avery Lotz contributed to this reporting. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information.

events.title: Chuck Schumer has a 2028 problem that's not even in New York
events.summary: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer is going to have his hands full next Congress, even without a threat to his leadership or a primary challenge from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.). Why it matters: Schumer (D-N.Y.) will have to grapple with the presidential ambitions of up to eight of his senators who may care more about winning the White House than following their leader. Roughly one in six Democratic senators eyeing the campaign trail would add a degree of difficulty to a job that rarely lacks challenges, as former President Obama acknowledged this week. "Being the head of the Democratic Party is a pain in the butt, because you've got people from every walk of life," Obama said of Schumer at a fundraiser Wednesday. Flashback: This year's ICE funding fights gave Schumer a taste of how presidential ambitions can complicate governing. Potential 2028 contenders competed to take the toughest stance against ICE funding, even at the risk of a government shutdown. Zoom in: The tension between individual ambition and party unity could surface early in Schumer's tenure if he becomes majority leader. Democrats are promising to lower costs and govern responsibly, while insisting they'll challenge and investigate the Trump administration at every turn. Schumer and President Trump have a long, complicated relationship — and each other's cell numbers. Between the lines: Democrats could control majorities in both chambers, giving them immense power against Trump. But majority power is dependent on members being present and unified. Presidential contenders have incentives to spend time outside Washington and show how they differ from their fellow 2028 hopefuls in the Senate. They also may want to pick high-profile fights with the party establishment to prove their progressive bona fides. But Schumer faced a similar challenge during the 2020 presidential cycle, when he was minority leader and seven sitting senators sought the Democratic nomination. Attendance was the biggest headache as candidates crisscrossed the country, complicating Senate scheduling. But Democrats didn't lose any major votes despite their presidential hopefuls being on the campaign trail. Who we're watching: Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) has visited South Carolina, New Hampshire and Nevada (twice). Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.): South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire and Iowa. Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.): South Carolina (twice), Nevada and Michigan. Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.): South Carolina, New Hampshire and Michigan. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.): Iowa and Nevada. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.): Iowa and New Hampshire (twice). Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.): Nevada (twice) and New Hampshire. Honorable mention: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) is focused on winning reelection, so he has no documented early-primary-state visits yet. That hasn't stopped presidential rumors from swirling. Zoom out: First, Schumer needs to get to at least 51 seats in November, navigate a high-stakes lame-duck session, and then win a secret-ballot election to reclaim his title as majority leader. Some of his potential new members — especially if Democrats have a good night on Nov. 3 — aren't overly enthusiastic about supporting him. Candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas have not committed to voting for him. The bottom line: Presidential candidates want to stand out. Senate majority leaders need their members to blend in — and fall in line.

events.title: Wall Street posts weekly gains with earnings, inflation data on tap
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, in New York City. Wall Street ended higher and posted weekly gains as investors looked ahead to third-quarter earnings and inflation data that could shape the Federal Reserve’s next move. Big banks, including Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase, are due to report, while analysts expect S&P 500 earnings to rise 30.6% and energy and technology to lead. Stocks were mixed by sector and company news, with AI shares rising, telecom firms falling after SpaceX’s spectrum deal, Humana jumping on Medicare ratings, and Apple slipping on weaker demand. NEW YORK - Wall Street ended higher on Oct 9 as investors shifted their focus to next week, with third-quarter earnings season set to start and inflation data expected, which could shed light on the Federal Reserve’s next policy decision. All three major US stock indexes advanced on the day, logging weekly gains. The small-cap Russell 2000, however, ended lower than Oct 2’s close. “It’s the kind of back-and-forth market we’ve been in where we have the reversal of sentiment around Iran,” said Ross Mayfield, investment strategy analyst at Baird in Louisville, Kentucky. “With conflicting headlines coming out of the White House and parties in the Middle East, there’s just no edge there.” “That’s why it’s a fairly tepid rally,” Mayfield added. Crude prices initially retreated after President Donald Trump said the US will not launch any attacks on Iran before the midterm elections, adding that talks between Washington and Tehran aimed at ending the market-rattling Iran war were “productive.” Front-month West Texas Intermediate oil and Brent crude both settled up 0.4%. Benchmark Treasury yields edged higher, but remained below Oct 7’s 24-year high. Third-quarter reporting season begins in earnest next week, with big US banks Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Morgan Stanley scheduled to release results. Analysts estimate S&P 500 annual earnings growth of 30.6%, on aggregate, for the July-September period, with energy and technology posting the largest year-on-year earnings growth of 123% and 66.5%, respectively, according to LSEG data. The mood of American consumers, who shoulder about 70% of the US economy, has soured this month, according to the University of Michigan, with near-term expectations deteriorating to an all-time low. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 423.31 points, or 0.83%, to 51,654.95, the S&P 500 gained 46.15 points, or 0.59%, to 7,811.51 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 172.83 points, or 0.64%, to 27,366.17. Among the 11 major sectors of the S&P 500, communication services was the lone percentage loser. AI-related momentum stocks were generally higher, with the Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF up 1% as the US bull market, largely driven by the AI boom, approaches its four-year anniversary. “Chips have been this year’s story,” said Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager at Founder ETFs in Dallas. “(It’s) a multi-decade technological change and just at the beginning of whatever’s happening, not at the end.” Elon Musk’s SpaceX struck a deal to acquire a nationwide low-band spectrum portfolio, posing a direct challenge to US wireless companies. Telecom firms T-Mobile US, AT&T, and Verizon dropped between 8.8% and 13.3%. Humana jumped 11.6% after US government data showed 95% of the health insurer’s members were in Medicare Advantage plans rated four stars or higher for 2027. Apple slid 1.1% after a media report that the iPhone maker has told some suppliers to cut production of components for its newly launched iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, as soaring memory chip costs and price increases dampen consumer demand. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.65-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 141 new highs and 183 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 2,756 stocks rose and 1,997 fell as advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.38-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 14 new 52-week highs and five new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 41 new highs and 209 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 14.37 billion shares, compared with the 17.76 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days. REUTERS

events.title: Trump announces major diesel deal with Putin, infuriating Ukraine
events.summary: President Trump announced Friday that he's reached a deal with Russia to increase the supply of diesel to the U.S. and global markets — angering Ukraine, which called it a gift to Vladimir Putin in the midst of their war. Why it matters: The announcement, which includes a waiver on some U.S. energy sanctions against Russia, took place as Ukrainian and European diplomats arrived in Miami for talks on ending the war with Russia. What he's saying: "I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote on Truth Social. Trump added that Russia will deliver," within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel." Combine with oil coming out of the Strait of Hormuz, Trump wrote, "Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" "Today, at President Trump's direction, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) is immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market," the Treasury Department said in a statement. Friction point: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky responded angrily to Trump's announcement, writing on X that any sanctions relief for Russia outside of a "lasting de-escalation agreement ... is an obvious weakness." "Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will repay the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis," Zelensky wrote. Zelensky added that Ukraine told Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff that it is "ready to take symmetrical de-escalatory steps" with Russia. "Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure. This is the kind of agreement we are proposing to America, and we believe the U.S. has enough power to achieve such a compromise," he said. The other side: The Kremlin said in a statement that during Putin's call with Trump, "significant attention was devoted to prospects for resolving the Ukraine crisis." The Kremlin said the two leaders discussed the situation in global energy markets. "The Russian side confirmed its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the U.S. and global markets. I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the global economy as a whole," Putin said during the call, according to the Kremlin. Putin special envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who worked on the deal, wrote on X that "Russia-US energy and economic cooperation will continue and benefit global markets and the world." By the numbers: Ukrainian strikes cut Russia's available refining capacity by as much as 60% over the summer, though the effect varies month to month, per an analysis by two Dallas Fed researchers this week. Through a combination of Middle East refinery outages, shipping constraints, damaged Russian refineries and curtailed Chinese refining, the global fuels market has seen reduction of as much as 6 million to 8 million barrels per day of capacity since late spring, or up to 10% of global refining. What they're saying: "Putin and others are trying to opportunistically shift blame for high diesel prices onto Ukraine, rather than the U.S.-Israel-Iran war devastating global supply chains," said Joseph Webster, an energy and geopolitics analyst with the Atlantic Council, a nonpartisan think tank. "These putative Russian export volumes are not only uncertain to materialize but are small in volume and wouldn't address the global diesel shortage," he said via email. Ben Geman contributed to this report.

events.title: Trump lifts US sanctions on Russian diesel amid price surge
events.summary: US President Donald Trump on Friday said Russia had agreed to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets after a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin. The move comes as Mr Trump faces growing domestic political pressure to bring down rising diesel prices, caused by supply constraints during the Iran war and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries , before November's midterm elections. Mr Trump said in a social media post that under the deal, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to the US and global market, in addition to 500,000 tonnes in November, followed by one million more tonnes “immediately thereafter”. The US President said that, “based on the condition of their diesel refineries”, Russia would deliver three million tonnes of diesel fuel “within a short period of time”. “Between our total control of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian energy, diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be coming, in record numbers down, and fast!” Mr Trump wrote. The Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control released a licence allowing the immediate “sale, delivery, offloading, or importation, including importation” of Russian origin-diesel fuel into the US until April 2027. The department said it did not authorise any debit to an account on the books of a US financial institution of Russia's central bank, its national wealth fund, or its finance ministry. The move drew quick condemnation from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said allowing Russia to sell its petroleum products “is an investment in war that needs to end, not continue”. “Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy,” Mr Zelenskyy said. Trump is doing a deal with the devil to try to help his flailing political fortunes from the shockingly high diesel prices caused by his own reckless, illegal war in the Middle East. This filthy deal will only aid and abet the same Putin who is helping the Iranians to target… https://t.co/lEILjnE38R — Chuck Schumer (@SenSchumer) October 9, 2026 US Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer and other members of the Democratic Party expressed dismay at the announcement. “This filthy deal will only aid and abet the same Putin who is helping the Iranians to target and try to kill American troops in the Middle East and who illegally and viciously invaded our ally Ukraine,” he said on X. Russia was the second-largest diesel exporter in the world after the US before imposing curbs to protect its domestic market. Those supplies have been further hampered by Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, including what Kyiv claimed to be an attack on the country's largest oil refinery on Thursday. It is unclear how Russia will supply the diesel amounts announced by Mr Trump. Russia's fossil fuel export revenue fell 8 per cent on a monthly basis in August to €604 million ($676 million) per day, with export volumes falling 7 per cent, according to the Centre for Research on Clean Air, a think tank that has previously condemned Russia's invasion of Ukraine . Mr Trump has recently acknowledged the diesel fuel crisis. In September, he publicly called on Mr Zelenskyy to halt its attacks on Russia's oil facilities “because he's causing a shortage of diesel fuel”. G7 member countries last week said they had agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and other products through the International Energy Agency to help stabilise markets following pressure from the Trump administration, which had threatened to impose a diesel export ban. IEA members on Wednesday said they had agreed to prioritise the release of diesel stocks and accelerate the release of roughly 100 million barrels of emergency oil reserves. The IEA's members in March agreed to release 425 barrels of reserves to markets as prices surged after the Iran war broke out on February 28, with roughly 325 million barrels having been released so far. Friday's surprise move also appears to defy a Russian sanctions law championed by the late senator Lindsey Graham , which Mr Trump signed into law on September 18. The law codifies the existing US sanctions regime targeting Russia and introduced new tariff authorities with a particular focus on energy exports. Don Beyer, the senior Democrat on the House of Representatives Joint Economic Committee who opposed the legislation, called the deal “infuriating”. “Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake,” he wrote on X. The average cost of diesel in the US on Friday was $6.27 per gallon, compared to $3.67 this time last year.

events.title: New York Plans Stronger Sports Betting Regulation to Curb Gambling Addiction
events.summary: DraftKings sent extensive promotional offers to ProPublica reporter Jake Pearson while he was testing the company’s safety guardrails for problem gamblers. Recreation of notifications by Chris Alcantara/ProPublica Gambling regulators in New York on Friday formally proposed two rules that they say will help curb gambling addiction in the state. The move adds the country’s largest sports betting market to a growing list of places that are seeking online gambling reforms as states that have legalized wagering on sports in recent years deal with the harmful side effects, including rising addiction diagnoses there. While the drafts have been months in the making, their official introduction follows mounting media scrutiny, including a ProPublica investigation last month that showed weaknesses in the guardrails that companies like DraftKings have erected to address problem gamblers on their platforms. That system is called “responsible gaming.” The commission’s chair, Brian O’Dwyer, said that the proposed rules “provide an opportunity for the industry to illustrate its commitment” to protecting its customers.  “The industry is on notice by me and this commission that they need to solve this problem,” O’Dwyer said. “If the industry does not address it, then we will address it and they may not like the solution that we come up with.” One of the new rules would effectively adopt guidelines that New Jersey already uses, requiring sportsbooks to follow specific thresholds to identify at-risk bettors. The company would then be mandated to check in with those users. Another rule would bar companies from using artificial intelligence to customize bonuses or wagers. DraftKings, one of the country’s largest sports betting companies, has said it already follows the New Jersey trigger thresholds. Among them: depositing more than $10,000 in a 24-hour period or wagering more than $1 million in a 90-day period. What Does Your Data Reveal About Sports Betting Apps? Help ProPublica Find Out. If you’ve bet on sports with FanDuel or DraftKings, you can help ProPublica understand how these apps work. Use our browser extension to download your betting history, then upload your files. Share Your Experience But as ProPublica recently reported, problem gambling can manifest in much smaller amounts. With the advice of recovering addicts, addiction specialists and professional sports bettors, a reporter deposited $21,600 into his DraftKings account in less than eight weeks and purposefully bet compulsively, exhibiting the hallmark signs of problem gambling throughout that time. The behavior didn’t qualify for a company review or interventions beyond responsible gaming notices, including in-app pop-ups. Some advocates for gambling reforms said that’s one big reason why the proposed rules don’t go far enough. New York and New Jersey “are clearly complacent in the status quo by endorsing and prescribing regulations that are nothing more than giving the appearance of reform and not effectuating actual change,” said Brianne Doura-Schawohl, a gambling reform advocate who lobbies for consumer and public health protections. After the commission advanced the rules unanimously on Friday, O’Dwyer said he recognized “the limitations of this proposal” and urged the state’s nine licensed mobile sports betting companies to share data so that problem gamblers can’t elude intervention by bouncing between them.  The introduction of the rules is a key step toward formal adoption. There will be a 60-day comment period for the public to weigh in on them. Barring major changes, the rules will then go back before the commission. Though the plans were first published in March and received dozens of public comments, their official introduction at the gaming commission comes on the heels of reporting by The New York Times, which found that DraftKings used artificial intelligence and data scientists to target its promotions to losing bettors , and ProPublica, which found that promotions far outweighed the responsible gaming notices sent to a reporter exhibiting problematic behavior. DraftKings made that journalist a VIP after he displayed red flags of problem gambling. Since those articles were published last month, regulators in Maine and Michigan have also said that they are reviewing some of the issues raised in the stories. Read More I Deliberately Bet Like a Problem Gambler. DraftKings Made Me a VIP. A spokesperson for Maine’s Public Safety Department said the Gambling Control Unit is “monitoring the use of AI locally and nationally” but has no rules or laws addressing the issue and declined to provide any additional information “regarding the scope of that monitoring or specific operations.” A spokesperson for Michigan regulators hasn’t responded to requests for comment. Massachusetts regulators, who have been looking into the use of AI by gambling companies, said they were also taking a look. The governor of Maryland has separately said he’d like to limit gambling companies’ use of AI to “identify and target users showing problem-gambling patterns.” Asked for comment on the New York regulations, a FanDuel spokesperson said the company “welcomes the opportunity to engage with regulators and work collaboratively to establish best practices for the industry.” A spokesperson for DraftKings referred ProPublica to its prior comments. In statements and interviews, the company has defended its responsible gaming program and disputed any characterization that it targets addicts or those prone to addiction with inducements. In an interview with ProPublica, Lori Kalani, DraftKings’ chief responsible gaming officer, said that, overall, “the system worked the way it was supposed to” during our gambling investigation, citing the more than 30 messages it sent our reporter. She added that “as a business, as an industry, we’re doing a good job of educating people, of raising awareness, of making tools and resources available, of monitoring accounts.” DraftKings told the Times it “rejects any implication that its marketing practices are unfair or improperly targets customers” and said its perks were delivered to “customers who demonstrated sustained, engaged use on our platform, not toward customers based on their losses.” The rules presented on Friday were made in response to a call by Gov. Kathy Hochul this year to address problem gambling. The Democrat, who is running for reelection, has announced a 10-year survey of residents’ gambling behavior to help “guide smart, targeted investments that protect New Yorkers and strengthen access to care.” But the commission’s proposed rules are a relatively moderate step in that direction. The measures would require a sports betting company to do more due diligence into a user’s “financial vulnerability” under certain conditions.
