events.title: The CEO who put Canary Wharf back on the map
events.summary: The Signal Interview “Everybody wrote this place off,” Shobi Khan says as he walks a visitor around Canary Wharf, the 130-acre estate he has overseen since 2019. After the UK’s banker-scaring vote to leave the European Union, and an office-emptying pandemic, the refrain he kept hearing was: “It’s over. Bad experiment. Why did we do that?” Khan still remembers his fury when a rival London property developer wrote in 2024 that Canary Wharf needed “a drastic transformation” to survive, but those doubts were widely shared at the time. Just when the east London business district might have been celebrating a post-COVID rebound, it lost a series of prominent tenants, including HSBC, Moody’s, and Clifford Chance. Fast forward to 2026, and Canary Wharf Group is reporting the highest rental rates in its history. Office occupancy now exceeds 92%, local retailers’ sales are 40% higher than they were in 2019, and visitor numbers, which fell from 54 million a year to just 20 million during the pandemic, are on track to exceed last year’s record of 76 million. Khan can also boast a string of new commitments from high-profile global tenants. Visa recently leased 300,000 square feet of office space, Barclays just bought its headquarters for £750 million, and Citi is investing more than $1 billion in its European HQ. Capping them all is JPMorgan’s proposal to erect a £3 billion, 265-meter tower that will be London’s largest office building if its plans are approved. “What kind of vote of confidence is that?” Khan asks rhetorically. What turned the tide, he says, was a multipart strategy to make Canary Wharf more competitive with the West End, the City of London, and Europe’s leading financial hubs. He now sees that approach as an intellectual property playbook that CWG could one day take to other markets. “I’ve got people from China, from the Middle East, Australia, all coming here for tours,” he says, “and we get offers.” A ‘green and blue’ diversification Canary Wharf was a product of Margaret Thatcher’s government, the centerpiece of an ambitious redevelopment of London’s crumbling docklands. But from the opening of its first towers in 1991, it suffered from a reputation as a sterile, remote outpost that appealed to few employers other than those in need of large trading floors that old buildings in the City of London could not provide. Khan joined CWG as CEO in 2019, having been chief operating officer of the US real estate investment trust General Growth Properties. Even before he moved, he recalls: “I’d keep talking to London business leaders, and they were like, ‘Oh, yeah, Canary, I remember it. So many bankers, nothing to do after five, and it’s really hard to get to.’ That was the perception for 30 years.” He has been much helped by the opening of the Elizabeth line in 2022, which he calls “a game-changer” for improving access to the site. But Khan has also invested in bringing in a much broader array of companies and government agencies, so tenants from outside financial services now account for almost half of his office space. He has simultaneously diversified a district that once had few apartments, shops, and dining options. About 3,500 residents now live in its apartment buildings — a figure he expects to double by next year. And Canary Wharf has more than doubled the number of retailers, restaurants, bars, and cafes since the pandemic. That has reduced the group’s historic dependence on the office market. Lately, Khan has focused on creating more “green and blue” spaces like parks and riverside walkways, while “curating” activities and amenities designed to make Canary Wharf feel more like a vibrant community than an office park. As he walks around the property, he points out outdoor event spaces, a padel center where the booked-up courts cost £80 to £100 an hour, and an Olympic-sized open-water pool that attracted 30,000 swimmers in the month after it opened this summer. Such attractions may sound like sideshows, but they help bring Khan’s strategy to life. It takes time to change perceptions, he notes, and he needs such tangible symbols to convince potential tenants that Canary Wharf has truly changed. “It’s like a house renovation. Some people can visualize it, but some people need to see the renovation,” he says. A playbook that could travel CWG, owned by Brookfield and the Qatar Investment Authority, is not wholly confined to its 130 acres. The group has developed projects elsewhere in London, including 20 Fenchurch Street, the curving City skyscraper nicknamed “the Walkie-Talkie.” But Khan says CWG has developed “a lot of expertise” from honing its model, which it can deploy in other districts, cities, and countries. It may do so over “the medium term,” rather than sooner, he adds, because it still has land to build another 5-7 million square feet, equivalent to seven to 10 new buildings. For now, “we’ve got enough on our hands,” he says — even as he notes that Canary Wharf Group now prefers to be known by its initials, CWG, so that future partners won’t assume that its ambitions are limited to its current home. Even as Khan worries about the impact of rising interest rates, he says the London market is “in an up cycle,” and predicts “great demand-supply fundamentals” for the coming years. Appetite for top office space remains strong across the capital, while CWG’s latest earnings showed that availability in Central London fell 20% year on year as supply in Docklands stayed broadly steady. The shortage of supply elsewhere in London will get worse next year, Khan says, blaming it on UK regulations that have driven up construction costs, deterring new development. A decade after the Brexit vote, “there’s been minimal flight” of bankers to European capitals, he notes. “But growth is less because of that. There have been jobs added in Amsterdam, Paris, and Frankfurt. But those jobs would have been here if it wasn’t for Brexit. And I think that additional regulation has put those jobs there.” It is early in Andy Burnham’s tenure as prime minister and Khan is reserving judgment. “They’re very good at listening,” he says of the Labour government, but “we haven’t seen anything that’s been implemented that would be pro-growth.” “London can still offer culture, creativity, an educated workforce, an attractive time zone, and the rule of law,” he notes. “That’s my point to the government: Just give businesses and individuals a little incentive to invest, and the city will grow.” Why offices need ecosystems Prime buildings in the City of London and the West End still charge a premium over Canary Wharf’s rents, and Khan’s business plan depends on narrowing that gap. But his task is not just to convince future tenants that his property is superior to rival offerings: Post-pandemic, he must still make the case for the office itself. events.title: "Not a fetish, not a taboo": Democrats weigh another Trump impeachment
events.summary: Democrats believe President Trump has committed impeachable offenses. But they're divided over whether they should try to impeach him if they win control of the House. Why it matters: If Democrats win the House, as expected, their 2027 decision on whether to try to impeach Trump could have major consequences for the 2028 presidential race. Zoom in: Theoretically, impeaching Trump would be easy for a unified, Democrat-controlled House. Many top Democrats note that Trump survived a record two impeachments in his first term — and that he'd be unlikely to be removed from office. That would require a two-thirds, bipartisan vote in a Senate that's likely to be closely divided. Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) said Trump has "already committed numerous impeachable offenses " in his second term, including usurping congressional authority. In 2021, Raskin led the second Trump impeachment, following the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. Raskin said top Democrats are "very sober about what that two-thirds requirement means on the Senate side. If anything, Donald Trump has tightened his control over the Republican Party since the last round. He's gotten rid of the senators that he viewed as not sufficiently loyal and sycophantic." Zoom out: Other Democrats also are cautioning against an impeachment campaign if their party takes control of the House in January. Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel, a potential presidential candidate, told NBC's "Meet the Press" last Sunday that he supports investigations, not impeachment, "because it's not going anywhere and it's going to be a food fight." Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) said recently: "Don't be impeaching anybody ... Let's just get back to work." Friction point: Democrats' more progressive wing is already talking about an impeachment drive. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) told The Floridian in March: "If you are asking me if I support impeachment, I do. I think that it's on very objective grounds of following the law or not." Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), a liberal who, like AOC, is weighing a White House run, also has argued for impeachment. " It's about setting a standard," he told NBC News , rejecting the notion that an impeachment would distract Democrats from pushing policy changes. "Democrats can impeach to uphold constitutional values, and at the same time have a first-hundred-day agenda that deals with the cost of living." What's next: Trump, who denies wrongdoing, is already preparing for his third impeachment. He told reporters Wednesday that he was "never even worried" about his first two impeachments. "I can do whatever I want, if I want," Trump said, calling the impeachments and subsequent criminal cases against him "very illegal things." "I view the presidency as a very sacred position," he said. "Very sacred position. Very important. Very sacred. A position where it has to be treated properly." Deep down , Trump might welcome an impeachment, one adviser said, "because he's in his element in chaos and when he's being persecuted." A longtime confidant said: "If Democrats win and start the investigations, he'll get more defiant ... Democrats won't be able to resist impeachment and he won't be able to resist daring them to do it. You think you control Donald Trump? Well, f*ck you. You don't." A senior administration official said the belief within the White House is that an impeachment would "just prove Democrats are all about getting Trump, and this stuff about affordability is just a hoax." Between the lines: Democrats know they face a conflict between holding Trump accountable and delivering on their campaign promises to restore Medicaid cuts and bolster the Affordable Care Act. Raskin said: "Does this make sense as a matter of law and politics and public policy to advance another impeachment? That's obviously a more complex question than whether or not he's violating the Constitution when he goes to war without congressional consent or he imposes tariffs outside of the law, or he engages in unprecedented scales of corruption in abusing his office." "So all this is to say, it is not a fetish with us," he added. "On the other hand, it's definitely not a taboo." Raskin, a law professor, is in line to lead the House Judiciary Committee, which would be involved in any impeachment. He emphasizes that "impeachment is by definition an intertwined question of both law and politics." In other words, it's not just a legal process. That's why the House impeaches and the president is then tried in the Senate, not the Supreme Court. The intrigue: Some Democrats have been at odds with themselves on impeachment. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), another potential 2028 candidate, said in April 2025 that he "strongly" supported impeaching Trump and that there's "no question" the president committed impeachable offenses. By this summer, however, Ossoff was no longer committed to it. Behind the scenes: Some Republicans have indicated that if they keep control of the Senate in the Nov. 3 election, they could bypass an impeachment trial by simply voting to dismiss the charges. Senate Democrats did that in 2024, after President Biden's homeland security secretary, Alejandro Mayorkas, was impeached by the House. Senate Republican leaders warned then that Democrats were setting a precedent they may not like when Republicans were in charge. Then there's Vice President Vance. He's likely to run for president over the next two years as Democrats debate impeachment. "JD relishes nothing more than defending the president," an administration official said. "More 'lawfare' against POTUS will unify Republicans even more." "If Democrats want JD to become president, please, impeach Trump."

events.title: Saudi Arabia faces its toughest moment of war
events.summary: Matthew’s view Riyadh was once the Gulf’s escape route from the Iran war. No longer. Several Western governments are advising against travel to Saudi Arabia. The US requires officials to obtain special approval to use the capital’s airport. I’m hearing of some executives leaving for Doha and the UAE. Here in Riyadh, we now hear booms and see fires that have largely been absent since the Iran conflict began on Feb. 28. This is a jarring reversal: Saudi Arabia has suffered fewer attacks than its Gulf neighbours, its airspace has mostly stayed open, and the kingdom has projected a business-as-usual attitude. That message is getting harder to sustain after Iran-backed Houthi fighters escalated attacks in response to the Saudi-led campaign against them in Yemen. One person was killed in a strike on Riyadh airport, a Saudia Airlines plane was reportedly left in flames , and hundreds of flights have been canceled. Some offices, schools, and the Expo 2030 construction site near the airport were evacuated on Thursday. Foreign governments suggested their citizens remain vigilant, but what can individuals do when threats come suddenly from the sky? Over the next few weeks, Saudi Arabia is hosting the World Petroleum Congress and the Future Investment Initiative, drawing CEOs from the world’s biggest energy and financial companies. While no postponements or cancellations have been announced, security teams are undoubtedly assessing what level of risk is tolerable for the titans of the global economy. Staying away could offend the kingdom, and firms that don’t stand with Saudi Arabia now risk missing out when the economy bounces back. Older residents here repeat a mantra that the country has been through worse, notably when Iraq launched Scud missiles in 1991 during the first Gulf War. But most of those strikes were on military structures. Riyadh was different then, too. It had no ambitions to be a hub for finance, trade, and tourism. Today, it needs stability. It’s harder to sell investors on its vision when the capital is under fire. Notable Explosions “rattled” Riyadh on Thursday, with this week’s Houthi attacks being the deadliest since the war in Yemen was reignited last month, The New York Times reported .

events.title: Everton owners consider selling club two years after takeover
events.summary: Everton are currently seventh in the Premier League after seven matches Everton owners The Friedkin Group (TFG) are exploring the sale of the club less than two years after taking control. The American group completed a takeover of the club in 2024 in a deal believed to be worth in excess of £400m. In a statement, TFG said after prioritising stability, investment and the opening of Everton 's new stadium last year, the time is right "to consider the next chapter". "The Friedkin Group is exploring new investment options for Everton Football Club, including the potential sale of a controlling interest," TFG said. "When TFG became custodians of Everton , the club faced significant financial uncertainty and challenges both on and off the pitch. The immediate priority was to provide the stability, investment and support needed to secure the club's future, including helping to bring the long-promised stadium to completion for its deserving supporters. "With that foundation now safely in place, the time is right to consider the next chapter for Everton ." TFG, led by chairman Dan Friedkin, outlined a vision for a "sustainable and successful" future for the club when they took over, but its leadership came under scrutiny during the summer transfer window. In September, David Moyes said he had never met or spoken to Friedkin, who is based in Houston, since returning as manager in January 2025. Friedkin leaves the day-to-day running of the club to his son-in-law Rishi Majithia, who works in tandem with chief executive Angus Kinnear. Fans reacted angrily when news broke that Everton had accepted a £40m bid from Nottingham Forest for one of their prized assets, England Under-19 midfielder Harrison Armstrong. Everton eventually pulled out of the deal, but supporters remained frustrated by the selling of Beto to Fiorentina shortly after. The move left the Toffees with just one recognisable striker in 23-year-old Frenchman Thierno Barry. TFG added that they will only "entertain interest from parties who we strongly believe will be the right stewards to take the club forward". "Throughout this process, TFG's focus will remain unchanged. We will support the club in all ways necessary to achieve success on the pitch and will continue efforts to make a positive difference in the communities the club serves," the statement continued. Everton up for sale again - so what next as owners TFG look for a way out? Published 2 days ago 'An unspectacular tenure' - analysis The decision of Everton 's owners TFG to explore selling the club comes as no great surprise after the turbulent events of recent times. A fracture opened up between TFG and Everton 's fanbase over the controversial attempt to sell highly-rated teenager Armstrong late in the transfer window, before a botched deadline day left manager Moyes with only 18 senior outfield players. The failed sale of Armstrong, as well as the departure of Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City for £65m, was bolted on to a cautious approach to the markets that suggested limited ambition on the part of TFG. It was in sharp contrast to the more hands-on approach at AS Roma, the other club owned by TFG, who bring in the additional riches of playing in the Champions League. Moyes revealing he had never spoken to Friedkin, who has not attended an Everton game since the Scot was reappointed as manager 21 months ago, strengthened the belief among supporters that TFG were effectively absentee owners. TFG secured a deal for 99.5% of the club, succeeding former owner Farhad Moshiri in 2024 after Everton had fallen into financial crisis. Since then, TFG have put the club on a stable financial footing and Everton have moved into a new stadium - although this was effectively done before their takeover - and have made the club an attractive proposition to potential buyers. This will be TFG's main achievement in what will, when Everton is sold, be regarded as an unspectacular tenure. 'It's come as a shock' - Brown-Finnis Speaking on 5 Live Breakfast, former Everton goalkeeper Rachel Brown-Finnis described TFG's plans to sell the club as a "shock". "It's come as a bit of a shock. They have stabilised the club. There was so much financial uncertainty when they arrived, it's felt like a turbulent time," said Brown-Finnis. "We [ Everton ] have a stadium to be crazily proud of, it's going to generate revenue from a commercial point of view. "If the Friedkin Group sells up tomorrow, they have left the club in a much better place. I just hope that they do their due diligence. "I hope the new owners want to drive the club forward. Everton fans have spent too much time in a financially turbulent era." events.title: Finland, the world's happiest nation, faces a glum winter
events.summary: Finns have many reasons to feel content, but the country's pile of debt is not one of them. Russia's war in Ukraine has added to the fiscal burden. Can the Nordic nation absorb another shock? There's an uneasy mood in Finland , the country that's ranked the world's happiest for nine consecutive years . A colder-than-usual winter is on the way and so is the toughest austerity budget in years. With an election due in April, the argument is no longer how much to cut, but which services, benefits and pensions will face the biggest cuts. Finland's debt and deficit levels are in their worst state since the 1990s, when a banking crash and the collapse of the Soviet Union — a key export partner — pushed the Nordic nation into its own Great Depression. Finland's debt ratio climbed sharply since the COVID-19 pandemic Last month, Finland's national statistical institution confirmed that the national debt had reached 90.3% of gross domestic product (GDP) in the second quarter. Before the pandemic, that figure was around 65%. Trouble to the east is, again, part of the reason. Finland ramped up defense spending after joining NATO a year after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine . Helsinki, which used to rely on Moscow for about a third of its energy, also faced much higher costs as it transitioned to other suppliers. The Finnish government has spent more than it earns since the 2008/9 global financial crisis, partly due to an aging population and sluggish economic growth. Last month, the State Treasury projected the fiscal deficit would reach 4.2% of GDP in 2026. Brussels has piled pressure on Helsinki to bring down the borrowing gap, as European Union rules require member states to stay below 3% of GDP. In January, the European Council opened an excessive deficit procedure and gave Finland until the end of 2028 to reach the desired target. Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's government, which took office in June 2023, said it would aim to save about €9 billion ($10.1 billion) during this parliamentary term. But whoever wins the next election will have to cut much deeper, economists warn. "The amounts currently estimated range from €8 to €11 billion," Jarkko Kivisto, an advisor to the Bank of Finland's monetary policy and research department, told DW. Earlier this year, all but one political party agreed to support a debt brake, where the next government commits to tightening the country's deficit to about 2% of GDP by 2031. Finland: Europe's race for critical raw materials National Coalition rules out tax hikes To date, Orpo's center-right National Coalition is the only party to promise a further €9 billion in cuts if he wins a second term. As well as further savings from health, social care and welfare, Orpo also plans to target workplace pensions, without reducing current payouts. While the Social Democrats plan to split the reforms between spending cuts and tax hikes, Orpo plans to achieve his target without raising taxes — meaning public services will bear the brunt. Kivisto, however, cautioned: "The deficit is so large that it would need a package that includes tax increases and expenditure cuts." While Finland's at-risk-of-poverty rate is lower than the EU average, unemployment is higher than anywhere else in the bloc. In August, Finland's jobless total stood at 10.3%, just above Spain's 10%, according to Eurostat, the bloc's statistics agency. Youth unemployment reached 23.3%, against an EU average of 15.4%. With household spending already falling, Lauri Holappa, director of the Finnish Centre for New Economic Analysis, warned that a new round of austerity would be a hard blow for the domestic economy. "More than a quarter of the population works in the public sector, so if those workers face the threat of being sacked, the savings rate will rise and private spending will drop again," Holappa told DW. Successive pressures ranging from the COVID-19 pandemic, higher interest rates and the global financial impact of two current wars have hurt efforts to cut the growing gap between income and borrowing. The 2027 budget proposal still counts on a spending gap of €12.4 billion. Finland rearms after Russia's full-scale invasion Before the Ukraine war, Finland had already committed to buying 64 F-35A fighter jets from the United States, in a deal worth about €8.4 billion. During more than four years of Russia's war in Ukraine, the Nordic nation raised military spending from $4.5 billion to over $8 billion per year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI). In April, the government said it would further increase defense spending to 3.2% of GDP, close to NATO's 3.5% target. A night in Finland's largest underground defense bunker With oil prices remaining close to $100 a barrel due to the Iran war , the government has so far resisted pressure to increase fuel subsidies. That's despite the Bank of Finland recording a 50% rise in the cost of imported energy in the early months of the Iran war.

events.title: China and EU trade envoys seek ways to ease tensions over growing imbalances
events.summary: The top trade envoys for China and the European Union are wrapping up two days of talks aimed at calming escalating tensions over growing imbalances between the two giant economies BEIJING -- The top trade envoys for China and the European Union were wrapping up two days of talks Friday aimed at calming escalating tensions over growing imbalances between the two giant economies. EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic traveled to Beijing saying it was crucial that the negotiations deliver “tangible outcomes” in rebalancing trade between China and the 27-nation bloc. It was unclear, however, if the two sides would find the will to resolve key factors behind China’s growing trade surplus, which hit 360 billion euros ($410 billion) last year. China is pushing for the EU to stop blocking its imports of advanced computer chipmaking machines, restrictions imposed on national security grounds at Washington's behest. Sefcovic said the talks this week were the culmination of three months of intensive work. He had set an October deadline for meaningful results on trade rebalancing. Earlier in the week, the Chinese Commerce Ministry issued a statement urging the EU to avoid protectionist measures, warning that such moves could backfire. Trade tensions have grown in recent months, with both sides imposing or considering curbs on each other’s imports. The EU has moved to limit imports of Chinese-made electric vehicles and EV batteries and enacted measures to protect the European steel industry. It also is limiting duty-free imports of e-commerce small parcels, essentially targeting Chinese fast fashion firms. Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Fort Hood survivors speak out on Pentagon's decision to livestream Hasan's execution Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Last week, China launched an anti-dumping investigation into imports from the EU of p-nitrotoluene, a chemical compound used in dyes and pharmaceuticals. Chinese officials and businesses have raised concerns over reports some EU members are pushing for new measures to protect local industries. Worries over surging Chinese exports to Europe and other parts of the world in what some are calling a China shock 2.0 have deepened as the U.S., especially since President Donald Trump returned to the White House, has raised tariffs and enacted other measures to try to reduce its own huge trade deficit with Beijing. Despite the backlash from some of its trading partners, China's global trade surplus hit $1.2 trillion in 2025 and is forecast to surpass $1 trillion again this year. The EU's trade deficit with China widened to 103.34 billion euros (about $116 billion) in the April-July quarter, as imports rose to 153.63 billion euros ($172.3 billion) ,while European exports to China climbed to 50.3 billion euros ($56.4 billion), according to EU statistics. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters SPONSORED POST: Vendor roadmaps set the pace of change in most enterprise software estates. Origina argues the business should. Most enterprise software estates run to somebody else’s calendar. End-of-support dates, license model changes and needless upgrades arrive on the vendor’s schedule, and the IT team absorbs them: the migration nobody budgeted for, the re-platforming that displaces a project the business actually asked for, the patch cadence that is really a product roadmap in disguise. Origina, an independent provider of software maintenance and support, puts figures on the pressure. As a rule of thumb, up to 90 percent of IT budgets go on “keeping the lights on”, leaving only 10 percent for anything new. Enterprise software costs, it says, are on course to rise 40 percent by 2027, and most of that increase is driven by vendors rather than by customers. The alternative it argues for is not standing still. It is to decide, on the business’ terms, what changes and when. A system that is stable, compliant and doing its job does not need upgrading because of a vendor-driven deadline. It needs to be supported, secured and kept in step with the business until the business has a reason to move. That reason might be a merger, a new operating model or a real step change in capability. It should not be a support deadline. That is the case for building flexibility into long-term planning from the start, rather than buying it back later at a premium. On the estate’s biggest lines, this is how it looks. Perpetual VMware licenses stay supported for as long as they are useful, instead of moving to a subscription bundle on someone else’s timetable. SAP environments run beyond standard support windows, and modernization programs are planned properly and executed when it makes business sense. Plus, the whole estate is protected against the vulnerabilities that are actually exploited, not the tens of thousands that are merely disclosed. In 2025, 48,000-plus vulnerabilities were published, but only around one percent of these were ever used in an attack. Origina’s OPTAS service proactively identifies, prioritizes and addresses issues before they become a problem. Beyond the budget, one of the constraints most IT leaders feel first is people. The engineers who understand a long-lived SAP estate or a sprawling VMware footprint are scarce, and every unnecessary migration keeps them tied up with work the business never asked for. Independent support helps you to free up resources you can invest in innovation and growth. Control, in the end, is the ability to say not yet, and to mean it. Explore your options: find out how Origina supports VMware and SAP on your timetable, and how OPTAS protects the estate in between. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Chap who took the job left a trail of wreckage – and invaluable case studies – in his incompetent wake Techie was stung by a wasp, held overnight by Chinese police, then trapped in a 13-hour meeting 9 days ago Techie assumed boss knew what they were talking about and killed Exchange by deleting data 13 days ago Project leader thought his team understood the plan, ended up fixing their 'interpretation' of it 16 days ago Your cloud survived everything except the real world 20 days ago Techie fixed Wi-Fi dead zone with a drill 23 days ago Welcome to another installment of On Call, The Register's reader-contributed Friday column which often shares your stories of what happens when incompetent people climb the greasy pole and send their failures straight back down into the lap of tech support. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Preston," who wrote to share his story of working as a field service tech in the late 1990s. "I'd risen to the rank of senior field service engineer and was offered a position in consultancy," Preston told The Register . He turned it down because he liked working at the coal face, and the people he worked with there appreciated his skills. "As soon as I arrived at clients, someone was making me a coffee just as I liked it," Preston explained, "so I turned down the consultancy position." One of Preston's colleagues took the promotion and was soon working on projects such as reconfiguring Windows NT 4.0 and the servers it ran on to handle two CPUs, configuring backup systems, and ensuring uninterruptible power supplies (UPSes) were in place to keep things alive. Preston kept doing his own thing, but the character of his job soon changed. "Within weeks, I was getting assigned calls where upgrades had gone wrong, UPSes were failing, and backups were not working." Preston realized the chap who took the promotion was making basic mistakes on almost every job – some of them so bad that one customer refused to work with the newly minted consultant. One of the jobs that eventually landed on Preston's to-fix list saw the consultant wipe a customer database that his backup regime did not protect. At another site, he created a system that pointlessly powered down every day and botched the installation of the UPS that would have saved his bacon. Preston covered as best he could to protect his company rather than the incompetent "consultant." He eventually quit the IT services caper and became a trainer. "I used these incidents as examples of what to look out for when installing and fault finding on customer sites, and also as a lesson on why you should never rely on the person who does a job before you getting things perfectly right." events.title: Oil posts weekly gain as Hurricane Isaias rips through US Gulf coast
events.summary: Oil prices settled higher on Friday to post weekly gains as Hurricane Isaias hit the US Gulf coast, forcing oil companies to significantly taper down their operations. Crude was trading lower earlier in the session after US President Donald Trump ruled out launching attacks on Iran before the midterm elections next month. Brent , the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, added 0.42 per cent to settle at $104.72 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, climbed 0.39 per cent to close at $91.85 a barrel. From last week's close Brent, which settled more than 4 per cent higher on Thursday amid continuing tensions in the Middle East, jumped 2.41 per cent, while WTI added 0.81 per cent. “Brent crude rose ... as renewed Middle East tensions coincided with disruption to US Gulf of Mexico production from Hurricane Isaias,” said Nick Stadtmiller, chief economist and group head of research at Emirates NBD. “Around 63 per cent of US Gulf oil production has been shut in ahead of the storm, while prices came off their intraday highs after President Donald Trump said the US was holding productive discussions with Iran.” The US Gulf coast is home to offshore oil production sites, as well as refining infrastructure and export terminals. The hurricane is forecast to lead to heavy rain and potentially flash floods. About 500,000 barrels per day of capacity are at risk from the hurricane, said Soojin Kim and Edward Bell from MUFG. "Ongoing fighting between Saudi Arabia and its allies against the Houthis are keeping the geopolitical risk in oil markets elevated while shipping in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz continues to be threatened," they said. The Houthis carried out deadly attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia's southern region and Riyadh this week, with debris from an intercepted ballistic missile damaging civilian sites in the kingdom's capital. Meanwhile, Mr Trump on Thursday said he had no intention of ordering attacks on Iran before the midterm elections take place next month, which has temporarily eased supply concerns. In a post on Truth Social, he said Iran was in a “very bad condition” economically and militarily and the US blockade on Iranian shipments through the Strait of Hormuz would remain in “full force”. He added that the countries were holding "productive discussions". Impact on oil prices Oil prices have remained volatile this week as attacks on ships in the strait, a vital route for global crude shipments, increased. The US also announced new sanctions on 17 vessels responsible for transporting millions of barrels of Iranian crude oil, as well as petroleum and petrochemical products, to markets in southern and eastern Asia. The US is looking to squeeze Iran’s oil revenue and put pressure on Tehran as the regional war continues. The US Treasury is "starving the tyrannical regime in Tehran of the money it uses to wage war in the region, and we will continue exposing those who enable the regime’s oil sales", Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. Gold, meanwhile, ended higher on Friday on bargain hunting and as investors weigh the possibility of further interest rate hikes from the US Federal Reserve. The precious metal, widely regarded as a safe-haven asset, added 1.52 per cent to a one-week high of $4,194.40 an ounce. Silver jumped 2.82 per cent to $60.82 an ounce.

events.title: Nvidia-backed data centre firm scraps IPO as AI valuation concerns deepen
events.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) data centre company Firmus has scrapped its plans for what would have been one of Australia's biggest-ever stock market listings. The Nvidia-backed firm said it had made the decision due to "recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions" and that going public would not be in the company or shareholders' best interests. Firmus had initially announced plans for a stock market debut that valued the company at more than $30bn (£22.65bn). One investment firm told the BBC that it had decided not to take part in the initial public offering (IPO) over concerns about its valuation. "Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options. We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress," the company said. Firmus builds and operates liquid-cooled data centres, or what it calls "AI factories", for clients including OpenAI and Meta. It has operations in Australia, Singapore and other parts of the Asia-Pacific region. The company's backers include Nvidia and major investment firms Blackstone and Jane Street. Blackstone declined to comment when contacted by the BBC. Nvidia and Jane Street have also been contacted for comment. The decision by Firmus to scrap its stock market listing comes as investors and industry analysts have raised concerns about the hundreds of billions of dollars being poured into AI as the prospects for long-term returns remain unclear. A humming annoyance or jobs boom? Life next to 199 data centres Published 26 October 2025 AI data centres are booming in Australia - but at what cost? Published 3 September UniSuper, one of Australia's biggest pension funds, was among the institutional investors that decided not take part in the IPO. "We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn't have a compelling valuation," UniSuper's chief investment officer John Pearce said in an update to investors. He also said UniSuper was concerned that Firmus would have to go further into debt to fund its growth plans. "It's disappointing. The [Australian Securities Exchange] needs new stories and this could have been one if it was correctly priced," Pearce told the BBC. This kind of listing is a test of how willing companies are to keep "ploughing money" into AI, said Phillip Wool, chief research officer from Rayliant Investment Research. Investors in Firmus would be buying into a company that is still in its early stages and is likely to need to borrow large sums of money, Wool said. "It's more like a bet on a dream", he added. Australia has become an attractive destination for data centre investment , thanks to the country's abundant clean energy, natural gas supplies and land availability. Australia has become an attractive destination for data centre investment OpenAI boss Sam Altman said earlier this year that Australia could become a world leader in the data centre industry if it wanted to. There are currently over 160 data centres in the country and plans for more. That is despite resistance from some Australians who have raised concerns about their environmental impact and the noise they create . In September, Altman said OpenAI did not aim to list on the stock market this year, citing concerns over the technology's safety that make it "an ill-advised moment" to go public. The ChatGPT-maker, along with rival Anthropic, have been eyeing blockbuster stock market debuts that would value the firms at more than $1tn each. AI-related stocks, Nvidia and Oracle, fell in US trading on Thursday after reports that OpenAI's revenues were lower than previously thought. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mundella yoghurt returns to shelves as deal revives collapsed WA dairy brands Mundella yoghurt was established in Western Australia in 1974. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) Emerging processor Artisanal Market has bought the brands and assets of collapsed Mundella Foods and Margaret River Dairy Company. The companies were put into liquidation in August, leaving creditors owed millions of dollars. Yoghurt production is expected to start near Margaret River before the Christmas period. A late rescue deal and sale is set to keep two landmark West Australian dairy brands on supermarket shelves. Mundella Foods and the Margaret River Dairy Company went into liquidation in August, with creditors owed millions of dollars. Local processor Artisanal Market has bought the brands and assets, including processing facilities in Perth and Margaret River, for an undisclosed sum. Mundella Foods' operations near Mundigjong will not be used for processing by the new owners. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) Artisanal Market managing director Kevin Sorgiovanni founded another well-known WA dairy and juice brand, Harvey Fresh. He said he had been interested in buying the companies back in 2023, when they were sold by Chinese-owned Manassen Foods to The Cheeky Cow, which has since collapsed. "We saw the Mundella and Margaret River business as a great opportunity for the South West and also to add some value back to the WA dairy market." Mr Sorgiovanni said both brands of yoghurt would be manufactured at the export-approved Metricup processing facility near Margaret River. Artisanal Markets will mothball Mundella's original manufacturing facility at Mundijong, near Perth, because of its poor condition. Artisanal Markets is jointly owned by PenAgri Group and Research Corporation. Mr Sorgiovanni told the ABC the new ownership had plans to target the Asian market for broader sales. There are hopes to export Mundella yoghurt to Asia. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) "We want to do more than just the WA market," he said. Mr Sorgiovanni said production at the Metricup facility would start at 2 million litres a year, but it had the capacity for 10 million litres. The revival is welcome news for dairy farmers across southern WA, but challenges remain. WA Farmers Dairy Council president Ian Noakes said he was keen to see how Artisanal Market would secure milk supply. Ian Noakes has welcomed the sale. ( ABC South West WA: Anthony Pancia ) "Most of the milk in WA is contracted, and the main companies are not very good at letting a bit of milk go to somebody else," he said. "So it would be a matter of waiting probably until somebody comes out of contract to get a milk supply." Mr Noakes hoped the additional competition would improve the price points for local dairy farmers. events.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
events.summary: Top of the Week TSMC and GF inked a $2B manufacturing agreement , under which GF will manufacture silicon interposers for TSMC’s CoWoS advanced-packaging ecosystem at its Malta, New York fab. Volume production is expected to ramp in the first half of 2028. Applied Materials and Intel are expanding their R&D collaboration to develop next-gen transistors, interconnects, and advanced packaging technologies, combining work at Applied’s EPIC Center in Silicon Valley with Intel’s R&D operations in Hillsboro, Oregon. Rapidus launched Rapidus CORE , a global ecosystem framework intended to support customers from chip design through manufacturing for its planned 2nm foundry business. The first phase includes 17 design-service partners. Xanadu and GF formed a multi-year manufacturing partnership to move ultra-low-loss silicon nitride photonics and superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors onto GF’s 300mm production line in Malta, New York. Big hauls Wolfspeed received a conditional commitment for up to $1.5B in 30-year U.S. government financing to expand domestic SiC materials and wide-bandgap power-device production. Vinci raised $250M in Series B funding at a $1.5B valuation to expand its AI-powered physics simulation platform . The platform models thermal, thermo-mechanical, and fluid behavior during design, with simulations reportedly running in minutes rather than hours or days. Oratomic raised $475M for its neutral-atom quantum computing hardware. VEIR raised $110M for superconducting power delivery technology for AI data centers. Atomic Machines launched with $250M for its Matter Compiler system that builds micro-machines from code , including an electromechanical micro-relay to cut power in 800VDC data centers during a fault. Financials TSMC (Sept. revenue) and Samsung (Q3 guidance). Analysis Global semiconductor sales reached $159.7B in August, up 8% from July, with year-to-date sales topping $1T , reports SIA/WSTS . McKinsey expects inference to account for about 60% of AI compute by 2030, driving demand for custom accelerators, HBM, chiplets, advanced packaging, and silicon photonics. Silicon photonics, CPO, and optical networking are emerging as the next U.S.–China semiconductor battleground as AI data centers outgrow electrical interconnects, says Wilson Center , which estimates China accounts for 56% of global optical-transceiver manufacturing capacity. Brookings estimates the U.S. AI buildout could require $10.3T through 2032 for data centers, power, networking and specialized chips, but it warned that increasingly complex financing could obscure financial risks. Lithography ASML and Carl Zeiss researchers outlined a hyper-NA EUV lithography architecture with a numerical aperture of at least 0.75, potentially enabling features as small as 5nm, more than one-third smaller than current high-NA systems. The technology could be ready in about a decade, although commercial production remains uncommitted. Canon says its nanoimprint lithography technology is entering the final stage toward full-scale mass production. DUV immersion lithography is the strongest remaining chokepoint on China’s AI-chip production, contends think tank Center for Technology & Statecraft . It estimates Chinese-owned fabs had accumulated more than 330 DUVi systems by 1Q26 and says continued imports could significantly narrow the U.S.-allied AI-chip manufacturing advantage. The report calls for a China-wide ban on DUVi exports, servicing restrictions and tighter controls on critical components. Memory Samsung is reportedly planning ~$3.9B in investment in memory-chip testing facilities in Vietnam . Netlist and Micron entered into patent license and settlement agreements covering Netlist’s portfolio for server DIMMs and high-bandwidth memory, ending all pending legal proceedings between the companies. Micron faces a potential walkout at its Taiwan facilities after workers voted overwhelmingly to authorize a strike over profit sharing. Toshiba plans to invest approximately $380M to double HDD production capacity for AI data centers by fiscal 2027, compared with 2025 levels, reports Nikkei Asia. Security and export controls Arteris won an additional $3.3M through the U.S. government’s Trusted and Assured Microelectronics initiative to expand its third-party IP (3PIP) security assurance program in collaboration with BAE and SiFive . The U.S. DOJ charged the owner of California-based Earthmade Computer with allegedly smuggling more than $300M in export-controlled computer servers to China . Prosecutors allege the servers contained high-end U.S.-manufactured GPUs and were routed through Malaysia and Singapore using false end-user and destination information to evade U.S. export controls. Meanwhile, CSET researchers modeled more than 10 million scenarios for detecting diverted AI chips and found ping-based location verification to be the most cost-effective approach. However, they cautioned that implementation costs and complexity could limit its usefulness, and said that combining PLV with targeted physical inspections could improve enforcement. Recognition Silvaco CEO Wally Rhines was inducted into the National Academy of Engineering for his co-invention of the blue-light-emitting diode and decades of leadership in the semiconductor/EDA industry. Quick links to more news: In-Depth Reports and Deals New Technologies Security Vehicles, Batteries Research Quantum Workforce | Education Events and Webinars Global Europe SEMI Europe joined the European Commission’s new STEAM Executive Panel to represent semiconductor workforce needs and advise on industry-education partnerships, STEM participation, re-skilling, and up-skilling. In Germany, X-FAB broke ground on a new cleanroom in Erfurt, and Mitutoyo opened a new semiconductor measurement and inspection center in Dresden. HCSS warns that Europe risks losing its strong position in polysilicon unless production capacity grows fast enough to meet rising domestic and global demand. Asia Elephantech plans to open an advanced packaging center in Tokyo in March to support process development, prototyping, and scale-up for AI-server packaging and PCBs. AMD is working with 14 South Korean AI semiconductor and technology companies to develop heterogeneous computing systems that combine AMD CPUs and GPUs with Korean AI processors, reports SBS News. Cadence and Jilin University unveiled their CAE Multiphysics Joint Laboratory in China . The organizations also have a computational fluid dynamics joint lab. Towa plans to invest approximately $32M in a new molding equipment plant near Kyoto, Japan , to expand production capacity for advanced packaging. Americas Nvidia, AMD, Micron , and eight other companies committed a combined $2.4B in AI tools and compute credits to the U.S. government’s Genesis Mission. events.title: So long, Spokes: GitHub rewrites storage to restore reliability, just in time for agentic hordes
events.summary: Responding to unprecedented demand from AI agents, GitHub is rebuilding its Git storage architecture from scratch. Early tests with the new architecture show a promising 35x write improvement in internal tests. GitHub will need a miracle of that proportion just to keep up with customer demand. The plan involves decoupling writes from reads, offloading maintenance, and letting object storage manage redundancy. Most impressive is that the redesign is happening under the hood, with the goal of a non-disruptive change that won't alter developer workflows, review processes, or security controls. Running an enterprise-grade code repository means supporting “large engineering teams running busy CI pipelines alongside growing fleets of agents. Supporting these teams means building Git infrastructure for sustained, concurrent reads and writes at a scale few repositories reach today,” wrote Brian Celenza, GitHub principal software engineer, in a blog post describing the updates. Celenza did not offer a timeline for this ambitious migration. When GitHub’s customers shifted their coding focus to AI agents, activity on the platform spiked significantly. Between September 2025 and August 2026, GitHub traffic doubled, from 218.2 billion events per month to 473.3 billion. In September alone, commits hit 7.38 billion, a 5x increase from September 2025. This shift in traffic is stressing the system. According to the GitHub Availability Report, the service suffered 10 incidents in April alone that degraded performance. Another nine incidents landed in May, with each generating more bad publicity than the previous one. So long, Spokes GitHub's current storage architecture, nicknamed Spokes, uses a three-phase commit protocol, storing full repo copies across multiple local disks and requiring a quorum of replicas to acknowledge each write. While this approach ensures strong reliability, it bottlenecks write speed, as every push is bounded by the slowest replica required for quorum. The new architecture writes a commit only once, to Azure Blob Storage, an object store service that automatically handles replication (and hence redundancy) on its own, eliminating the quorum bottleneck. GitHub also gooses performance by separating read requests into their own channel, a job handled by lightweight compute workers. The only coordination between reads and writes is over the reference branch pointers. Maintenance duties – such as compaction and garbage collection — are moved from the serving path to operate as background processes, further reducing system lag. Git in the age of agents GitHub seems to be on the same page with others in rethinking Git for the agentic age. Former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke launched a Git-hosting service called Entire, which offloads agent traffic to mirror repositories, allowing a customer’s core GitHub repos to just serve the core development traffic. SpaceX subsidiary Cursor, which uses Git to back its agent-support service, also refined the storage layer for better performance. Cursor engineers also rejected Spokes’ three-phase commit in favor of uploading pushes into an object storage write-ahead log (WAL), which captured all changes as immutable objects, caching at least one copy on super-speedy solid-state disks. Respect for the Octocats While it's cathartic to hate on a service that often goes down, you have to feel empathy for the GitHub engineers who, when they created the service, couldn’t have guessed what they signed up for. “I've worked at extreme scale before and seen companies spend three months just preparing for events that will increase their traffic by 10% or 20% [...], which is nothing compared to what GitHub's facing now,” wrote PlanetScale CEO Sam Lambert in an X message. We can all hope the new storage architecture will give GitHub's engineers some well-earned rest. ®

events.title: JD Vance’s comments about immigrants 'unwarranted' and ‘deeply offensive’, India's Foreign Ministry says
events.summary: India's Ministry of External Affairs on Friday called comments by US Vice President JD Vance on Indian immigrants "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive". A day earlier, Mr Vance announced that Microsoft and some of India ’s biggest IT services were suspended from a programme allowing workers on H-1B visas to apply for green cards. He accused the companies of abusing the system, comparing foreign workers to “indentured servants”. "The history of the United States itself has been shaped by generations of immigrants whose labour, enterprise and innovation have contributed to its growth and prosperity," the ministry said in a statement. It added that Mr Vance's comments were "unwarranted" and ignore the contributions of Indian professionals to the US economy. Roughly 70 per cent of the H-1B visas approved in 2025 went to people from India. "Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive," the ministry said, appearing to refer to Mr Vance's use of the term "indentured servants", which carries a heavy historical burden for Indians. During the colonial period in India, more than 1.6 million people were transported as indentured servants to serve on British, French and Dutch plantations around the world following the abolition of slavery. Many workers, who typically signed five-year contracts for unpaid labour, were tricked or coerced into service. The indenture system is also a painful feature of American history. During the American colonial period, poor workers and convicts were bound to an employer for up to seven years, receiving no wages for their labour, in return for food, shelter and transport to the colonies. Similar to the Indian system, abuse was rampant. "When I say indentured servants, here's what I mean: When somebody comes in on an H-1B, they are completely subordinate to that company," Mr Vance said at the Department of Labour on Thursday. "If they lose that job, they have to leave the country." The Vice President accused Microsoft, Adobe and six other companies of fraudulently utilising the H-1B visa programme, which he said is meant to allow firms to bring in "the best of the best" from outside the US to fill jobs that are impossible to fill with American workers. This "pernicious system" is a "fundamental insult to the American way of life", he said, as it lets companies lower wages and block Americans from jobs, while also allowing for the abuse of foreign workers. As a result of the alleged fraudulent use of the system, the companies have been removed from the Permanent Labour Certification programme, which allows firms to hire foreign workers permanently and offers the workers the chance to apply for green cards. The tech industry, Wall Street firms and telecoms companies have come to rely heavily on the H-1B programme through their use of IT contractors from staffing and outsourcing agencies, which have developed a lucrative business in recruiting professionals from abroad for US clients. In the first nine months of the 2026 fiscal year, Microsoft was the fifth-highest user of H-1B visas, with 3,688, according to Bloomberg. In a statement, Microsoft said it pays H-1B employees “the same as any other employees doing comparable work”, that its wages are among the highest of all visa filings and that the vast majority of its employees in the US are Americans. Mr Vance’s comments came hours before US President Donald Trump gave Microsoft chief executive, Satya Nadella , the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at a summit in Washington intended to highlight US scientific leadership. And last week, Mr Nadella, alongside other tech industry leaders, visited the White House for a discussion on safeguards for AI. “Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company," Mr Vance said. "It’s that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans.” Washington has been engaged in an across-the-board immigration crackdown since Mr Trump returned to office last year. The State Department said earlier this month that more than 250,000 visas have been revoked under the Trump administration. Along with companies with high issuance of H-1B visas, Mr Vance also took aim at universities he said had engaged in J-1 visa fraud. He accused nine institutions, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford universities, of bringing "in foreigners to undercut the wages" of American researchers and graduate students. J-1 visas are granted to people approved to participate in work and study programmes in the US. "They're using these visas way too much. They're using them to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers, and it simply has to stop," he said.

events.title: Contribution of high value residents discussed
events.summary: Mary O'Keeffe was one of several business people who said high value residents contribute positively to the island's economy More than 260 industry leaders from business, finance and law have held a meeting to discuss the role high value residents play in Jersey's economy. Jersey's high value residency programme , external grants residential status to highly skilled and economically active high net worth individuals. One attendee at the Chamber of Commerce lunch on Thursday, Mary O'Keeffe, said high value residents "were extremely important" to the island. However, one former economic advisor to the government described the tax contribution of high value residents as "piffling". About 260 families currently live in Jersey having relocated through the scheme. O'Keeffe who runs Mary O'Keeffe relocation , external to help high value residents settle in the island said they contributed a lot to the economy and philanthropic causes. "They are extremely important, so here today the room is full of private bankers, tax accountants, lawyers, people like myself and professionals who all work with high net individuals. "So, they bring an enormous amount to the economy and that doesn't even touch on what they bring in regard to philanthropy." High value residents pay a 20% tax rate on the first £1.25m of worldwide income , external . They then pay a 1% on any income above £1.25m and there are some who feel these individuals should be paying more tax , external . O'Keeffe said: "I can understand that but that's not looking at the argument the right way. "First of all, the basic pay that they pay is £250,000 and that's before you even look at their worldwide income. "And the 1% often equates to many millions and that's what people don't understand. "High net worth individuals are extremely mobile, they are fluid, they can pick up and go wherever they want and they want to go somewhere that's safe, that's secure, that their wealth is going to be looked after and they're not going to feel that they're going to be ripped off." Industry leaders from law, finance, business and real estate met at a Chamber of Commerce lunch to discuss the role of high value residents in Jersey Garry Bell, a tax advisor to high value residents, said if tax for wealthy individuals was increased he believed Jersey would lose them. He said if the money they made above £1.25m was taxed at 20% instead of 1% it could damage the economy. Former economic advisor to the government of Jersey John Christensen said the amount of tax paid by high value residents was "piffling" "If we tax those individuals at 20% the numbers would reduce dramatically. So instead of having a net increase of say 18 or19 individuals a year you're probably only looking at one or two," Bell said. "So, we're sacrificing by seeking to tax them more, we're sacrificing that the direct income tax take, the stamp duty take, the employment, the GST, there's a whole raft of economic benefits that we sacrifice by actually seeking to tax those individuals at 20%. "We are competing with a number of other jurisdictions, Dubai - zero tax. Monaco - zero tax. "We're already one of the most expensive jurisdictions." John Christensen, a former economic advisor to Jersey's government in the 1980s and 1990s was critical of the High Value Residents programme. He said the amount of tax they pay is "piffling, frankly". "I think it's quite divisive, particularly in such an unequal island community. "As a development strategy, who benefits? They benefit because they're paying very little tax on their income but is it going to benefit young Jersey people? Not at all. "I suspect its going to contribute more to ratcheting up of house prices, ratcheting up of prices in the shops, and a higher cost of living generally. "And where they contribute to the island's economy, outside paying frankly minimal amounts of tax, lies with construction work. "They've built endless, frankly, rather ugly and inappropriately sized houses." Follow BBC Jersey on X , external , Facebook , external and Instagram , external . events.title: British households would be £5,000 richer if we were more innovative. Let’s unleash our talents | Gordon Brown
events.summary: We have a deep reservoir of assets, but struggle to turn small companies into global success stories. Innovation needs to be at the heart of government policy Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010 The coming 10 years are almost certain to be the decade that sees the greatest scientific breakthroughs in a century. The question is whether advances now under way in AI, quantum computing and biology can address cancer, find ways to treat or prevent dementia, and overcome the growing resistance to antibiotics. Can we find sustainable ways to address our energy needs and protect the environment at the same time? Can AI transform the way we deliver education, health and social care to the benefit of millions, as well as advance modern manufacturing strength? And what role can Britain’s inventors, investors and industrialists play in developing these transformative technologies? While the US and China are the world’s obvious innovation powerhouses, the UK also has enormous assets, as the Innovation Nation Conference in Manchester addressed by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will hear today. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Firmus wobbles have data centre opponents relieved, critics questioning Tasmanian sports deals Firmus has abandoned its ASX float after lacklustre demand, with the news welcomed by Tasmanian opponents of its plans. ( Supplied: Firmus Technologies ) The news of data centre builder Firmus' share market float being pulled after lacklustre demand has been met with a mixed reaction. While there has been disappointment from some investors, for the opponents of Firmus' data centre plans in northern Tasmania, the response has been relief. The news of data centre operator Firmus's share market float being pulled has been met with disappointment from some investors. But in one community where Firmus had big plans, the response was relief. Firmus was attempting to raise cash from investors to fund its data centre plans until this week's development . A group based in northern Tasmania, called the Environmental Awareness Association, has been campaigning against the company's three projects in the region. Anti-data centre protesters pictured in August outside George Town Council building, ahead of the vote on whether to approve Firmus' proposed data centre. ( ABC News: Emily Smith ) Nicholla Thompson from the association lives at Rowella, across the Tamar River from Firmus' proposed Bell Bay site, and said community backlash had contributed to investor concerns. Nicholla Thompson believes community opposition to Firmus contributed to investor hesitancy. ( ABC News: Emily Smith ) "The dominoes are starting to fall," she said. "They wanted it to sneak through and not be seen by people; it was thanks to the little group that we've got that really highlighted what was happening over here." The opponents' group was relieved by the news, but was not yet celebrating it as a win for their campaign. "A big company shouldn't be able to come in and change substantially how we choose to live in a beautiful community like this and put an AI factory up in the middle of it and have us have to endure the sound, the diesel fumes and the total destruction of our properties in value and in peace and how we live," Ms Thompson said. Firmus 'well-positioned' to continue plans, company says When asked about any impact on its Tasmanian projects, a Firmus spokesperson said nothing had "fundamentally changed" about the business. Firmus searches for private funding as it withdraws its application to list on the ASX just a day after closing its books to investors. Sam Baker, from Shadforth Financial Group, said it was hard to tell if the community opposition had contributed to the IPO failing, but it would have been considered by investors. He said it would be important to watch what Firmus did over the coming weeks and months to see if it could raise the capital. "Firmus not being able to get this ASX listing off the ground has cast some doubt over the funding of their potential rollout of data centres in northern Tasmania," he said. Deputy Premier Guy Barnett said the IPO was a matter for Firmus, but the Tasmanian government had been supportive "all the way through" the company's plans in the state. "That relationship is positive and we look forward to it continuing in a collaborative, positive way," he said. Data centre company's deal with AFL team defended by club boss The Tasmania Devils AFL club has signed a six-year sponsorship deal with a data centre builder. The Tasmanian Greens said the state government should be embarrassed by its support of Firmus, saying investors, academics and communities had been raising concerns for months. "The big question for Tasmania is why our government was so easily pulled into uncritically supporting this company despite the furiously waving red flags surrounding it," Tabatha Badger, the Greens' information and technology spokeswoman, said. Ms Badger said the government should pause any planning decisions on Firmus's three proposals in Tasmania. Firmus was also named a sponsor for Tasmania's NBL team, the JackJumpers. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) The Tasmanian-founded company had recently announced sponsorships with the Tasmania Devils AFL club, several cricket teams, including the Hobart Hurricanes, and the JackJumpers and Tasmania Jewels basketball teams. Dr Andrew Hughes, a political marketing specialist at ANU's College of Business and Economics, said the Firmus IPO falling over was a golden opportunity for the Devils to walk away from the deal. He said he was surprised the Devils had signed with Firmus, given the club was already exposed to community backlash over the proposed AFL stadium in Hobart .

events.title: India’s tech giants shrug off changes to USA’s skilled visa program
events.summary: India’s peak technology industry body, NASSCOM, has shrugged off changes to the USA’s skilled visa regime, and Microsoft has denied it abuses the program. The changes, announced on Thursday by US vice president JD Vance and Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, mean that Microsoft and Adobe can no longer use the Program Electronic Review Management (PERM) program to convert holders of the H-1B visa for skilled workers to permanent residents. Sonderling also revoked access to PERM for Indian companies Infosys, Tata, Wipro, and HCL, plus Capgemini. The secretary said the change followed criminal investigations and alleged “fraud and abuse.” “Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost three million foreign workers,” he said. “They've received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications. That's hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers.” Vice President Vance weighed in with what he called a “message to Microsoft.” “You’re a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.” Critics of the H-1B visa have often alleged that US companies use it to bring in foreign workers who are prepared to work for less than Americans. The theory even extends to an allegation that India’s outsourcers use H-1B visas to bring in workers whose main agenda is offshoring more work to India. Some observers suggest skilled workers have a secondary motivation of using their time in the US to seek visas for family members. Microsoft, whose CEO Satya Nadella once held an H-1B visa, and which has fired over 20,000 staff since early 2025, took issue with the administration’s decision in a strongly worded post. “Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category,” the company wrote. “We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings. We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.” “Microsoft succeeds as a global technology leader by developing the world’s best technology workforce,” the company’s post continues. “We do this by strengthening this country’s talent pipeline, hiring American workers, and attracting the best talent from around the world.” That’s essentially the same argument used by NASSCOM, and Indian politicians such as minister of state Vardhan Singh, who last year said that “skilled talent mobility has long played a significant role in promoting technology advancement, innovation, economic growth, and wealth creation in both India and the United States.” NASSCOM, which has never found a reason to doubt that Indian tech companies are anything other than excellent corporate citizens, took to X to share its view that “immigration and skilled talent mobility are two distinct issues and should not be viewed through the same lens.” The lobby group also argued “Over a number of years, Indian technology companies have significantly reduced their dependence on H-1B visas, while steadily expanding local hiring and building a strong domestic workforce in the U.S.” “They work with majority of the US fortune 500 companies, enable them to innovate and grow, and generate more local jobs. Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited.” Microsoft vowed to provide the Trump administration with more information about its migration initiatives. ®

events.title: Judge issues arrest warrant for Eduardo Bolsonaro, brother of presidential candidate
events.summary: A Brazilian Supreme Court justice issued a warrant on Thursday for the arrest of Eduardo Bolsonaro SAO PAULO -- A Brazilian Supreme Court justice issued a warrant on Thursday for the arrest of Eduardo Bolsonaro, one of the brothers of presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro. Eduardo Bolsonaro was sentenced in June to four years in prison for lobbying the Trump administration. Bolsonaro, a 42-year-old former lawmaker who lives in Texas and is a green card holder, was sentenced for lobbying to impose sanctions against members of the Brazilian government and implement higher tariffs on the country’s exports during the trial of his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, for a coup attempt. His lawyer didn't immediately respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press. Members of the Trump administration have never made comments about Eduardo Bolsonaro's conviction. Justice Alexandre de Moraes' decision came less than three weeks before a runoff for the country’s presidency between incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, who won the most votes in the first round on Sunday. Eduardo Bolsonaro has been a key link between his brother and the Trump administration. De Moraes, who the Bolsonaro family regards as a political enemy, also canceled Eduardo Bolsonaro's Brazilian passport. The judge chaired the investigation that led to Jair Bolsonaro being sentenced last year to 27 years in prison for a coup attempt, but has since been involved in corruption accusations. The justice said in his ruling that Eduardo Bolsonaro should start serving his sentence immediately and warned the country's federal police that he should be arrested if he returns to Brazil. “The defendant cannot benefit from his own wrongdoing by fleeing the national territory to an unknown location for the purpose of thwarting the application of criminal law,” the judge said. Eduardo Bolsonaro has lived in the U.S. since 2025, which has caused him to lose his seat in the Brazilian National Congress and his job as a federal police investigator because of his long absence. The U.S. and Brazil signed an extradition agreement in 1961, but the Trump administration would have to approve an extradition request for Bolsonaro, which is unlikely, said Raphael Vieira da Fonseca Rocha, a law professor at the Federal University of Juiz de Fora. Due to the unlikeliness of an extradition being granted, “requesting it through the existing diplomatic channels of international legal cooperation would weaken the Supreme Court,” Fonseca Rocha said. He said the Supreme Court probably won’t even try and instead appeared to be applying pressure by cancelling his passport. Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Fort Hood survivors speak out on Pentagon's decision to livestream Hasan's execution Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Coercion in the course of judicial proceedings is not included on the list of offenses that may give rise to extradition in the treaty between the U.S. and Brazil, said Joao Pedro Padua, a law professor at the Fluminense Federal University, adding that the list tends to be interpreted as exhaustive. As a consequence, “the United States would have no legal basis to extradite Eduardo Bolsonaro,” he said, adding that there was also a territorial question since Eduardo Bolsonaro was in the U.S. when he committed the crimes which led to his conviction in Brazil. The former lawmaker gave his brother's presidential bid a boost on May 26 by taking him to the White House to meet Trump. At the time, Flávio Bolsonaro was under fire for his confessed links to a disgraced banker , which analysts believed could derail his candidacy. AP journalist Eléonore Hughes contributed to this report from Rio de Janeiro.
